primary_models.equation: logit P(ED_symptom_Y2[i] = 1) = b0 + b1*SM_hours_baseline[i] + b2..b6*race/ethnicity + b7*sex + b8*income + b9*parent_ed + site fixed effects + b10*parent_ED_symptom_baseline[i] + b11*BMI_percentile + b12*anxiety_tscore + b13*BAS_reward; OR = exp(b1) per 1 hour/day
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal. Social media use is measured at the ABCD baseline visit (2016-2018, ages 9-10); the five eating disorder symptoms are measured once, by youth-report KSADS-5, at the year-two follow-up (2018-2020). Each symptom is a single binary follow-up outcome (no repeated measures, no time interaction). Because youth were not asked the ED items at baseline, the parent-reported baseline KSADS-5 version of the same symptom is entered as a covariate. Social media and total screen time are reported in separate columns of Table 2; the paper does not state that social media models adjust for other screen modalities.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, right-hand 'Social media use' columns (p. 6); results text p. 4; interpreted in Discussion pp. 6-7

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted logistic regression of year-2 eating disorder symptoms on concurrent problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic mobile phone use (MPIQ), adjusted for BMI percentile, anxiety and BAS reward responsiveness
primary_models.estimation: Same as M1: Stata 18.0 svy logistic regression with ABCD ACS-based propensity weights; site as covariate; no random effects; alpha 0.05 with no multiple-comparison correction; sex interactions tested and non-significant (not printed). Age named as a confounder in Methods text but absent from the Table 3 covariate footnote. SMAQ and MPIQ are entered in separate models (no mutual adjustment reported).
primary_models.sample: Subsamples of the N = 10,246 ABCD Release 4.0 analytic cohort: SMAQ models n = 5,587 (only youth reporting at least one social media account were asked the SMAQ); MPIQ models n = 7,280 (only youth reporting having a mobile phone were asked the MPIQ). Demographics are reported only for the full 10,246 (Table 1; see M1), not for these subsamples.
primary_models.dv: Same five binary year-two KSADS-5 youth-reported symptoms as M1 (fear of obesity, self-worth tied to weight, inappropriate compensatory behaviors, binge eating, distress with binge eating). Prevalence within the SMAQ and MPIQ subsamples is not reported; full-sample prevalence is 1.4%, 1.6%, 0.7%, 7.5%, 2.9%.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. SMAQ and MPIQ were first administered at the year-two follow-up (2018-2020), the same visit at which the youth-reported KSADS-5 eating disorder symptoms were measured. Each problematic-use scale and each symptom is modeled separately (2 IVs x 5 DVs). Baseline covariates are included, but unlike M1 the baseline parent-reported ED symptom is not in the Table 3 covariate list. Authors note they could not test prospective associations because problematic use was not measured at baseline.

primary_models.iv: (a) Problematic social media use: 6-item adolescent Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), modeled after the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, items rated 1 (never) to 6 (very often); Table 1 score 1.9 (SD 0.9). (b) Problematic mobile phone use: 8-item Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire (MPIQ), items rated 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree); Table 1 score 3.1 (SD 1.1). d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: per 1 additional hour/day of baseline social media use. M2: per 1-unit increase in SMAQ or MPIQ score (unit not explicitly stated; item-mean scale assumed from Table 1 means).
d_transformation.notes: Both models report adjusted ORs with 95% CIs, so the Chinn conversion applies directly and p0 is not needed. p0 values given in dv_axis are the full-sample (N = 10,246, weighted) year-two prevalences from Table 1 (p. 5); prevalences within the SMAQ (n = 5,587) and MPIQ (n = 7,280) subsamples are not reported. SD_IV values from Table 1 (p. 5): social media 0.4 hours/day (baseline), SMAQ 0.9, MPIQ 1.1; these are full-sample/subsample descriptives as printed and could be used to rescale ORs to a per-SD contrast (ln OR x SD_IV) if a per-SD comparison is wanted. Because social media hours have a very small SD (0.4 h), the per-hour OR of 1.55 corresponds to a much smaller per-SD effect; per-hour d values are not directly comparable to per-SD d values from other papers. [complete stage] All 15 ORs have printed 95% CIs; no SEs printed anywhere. M2 estimates now carry subsample n (5,587 SMAQ; 7,280 MPIQ) from Table 3 header. iv_type set to continuous for both models. primary_models.design: Prospective (longitudinal) analysis with two waves. The IV is screen time at the ABCD baseline visit (year 0, 2016-2018, ages 9-10) and the DV is the MIND diet score from the caregiver-reported Child Nutrition Assessment at the 1-year follow-up (year 1, 2017-2019, ages 10-11). The outcome is a single follow-up measurement, not repeated measures. There is no baseline nutrition score (the nutrition assessment was only collected at year 1), so the model does not adjust for prior diet; the authors list this as a limitation. Each screen modality was entered in its own regression (the paper reports 16 separate regression models in Table 2: 7 continuous IVs plus the categorical total-screen-time IV, at each of two waves), so each phone/SM estimate comes from a model containing only that one modality plus covariates.
primary_models.iv: Baseline (year 0) self-reported hours per day on one phone/SM modality per model: texting, video chat (eg, Skype, FaceTime), or social media (eg, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). Instrument: ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, weekday and weekend items combined as a weighted daily average ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2]) / 7. Continuous, units of hours per day, so B is the change in MIND score per additional hour per day. Baseline distributions from Table 1: texting 0.23 (SD 0.53), video chat 0.19 (SD 0.47), social media 0.11 (SD 0.39) h/d. The same survey items are listed as the year-1 screen variables; texting and social media are activity-defined items (device not restricted to phone).
primary_models.estimation: Multivariable linear regression in Stata 15.1, with ABCD propensity weights applied to match the ACS (US Census) on key sociodemographic variables. The paper does not state the variance estimator, clustering by family, or how site was modeled. Significance at P < .05 (bold in Table 2). No multiple-comparison correction reported. No interaction or stratified analyses reported. Covariates measured at year 0.

primary_models.iv: Year-1 self-reported hours per day on one phone/SM modality per model: texting, video chat, or social media, from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, weekday/weekend weighted daily average ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2]) / 7. Continuous, hours per day. Year-1 distributions from Table 1: texting 0.41 (SD 0.73), video chat 0.28 (SD 0.63), social media 0.23 (SD 0.60) h/d.

papers.extraction_flags:
The PDF at the listed path is the wrong paper...) is actually Nagata et al., "Neighborhood Quality and Screen Use", Acad Pediatr 2026;26:103164...), and the extraction comes from that file. The copy in docs/pdfs should be replaced; I did not change it. The same mismatch exists in the archive data/pdfs/ folder, so other papers' PDFs may have been swapped the same way.

On the extraction: the prospective model (year-0 IV) and the cross-sectional model (year-1 IV) are split into M1 and M2 because they have different designs. The authors interpret both, but stress the cross-sectional findings for texting and social media. Texting and social media are significant only cross-sectionally (M2). In the prospective model (M1) all phone/SM estimates are null.

Three things need human checks:
- SD_DV = 2.45 is the Table 1 "MIND diet sum score" row. It sits under the "Baseline" heading, but MIND was only measured at year 1, so the label is ambiguous.
- How study site was modeled (fixed or random) is not stated.
- Supplementary Appendix A (the exclusion flowchart) is not bundled in the PDF.

Each modality is its own single-IV regression, so the estimates are not mutually adjusted for other modalities. All 6 B values, CIs, p-values and all 6 SD_IV values were checked against Table 2 and Table 1.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 5.0, 21 U.S. sites. Children with available demographic, screen time and cognitive data were included. Per-cell N is not printed in Table S1; the Satterthwaite d.f. for texting and video chat cells range 9742.772 to 9955.263, consistent with roughly 10,000 children (main-text total screen time models had n = 9954-9979). Full-sample descriptives (Table 2, p. 3; n varies by variable): age 119.00 +/- 7.50 months (n = 11,867); 6,188 male and 5,677 female; White 6,173, Black 1,784, Hispanic 2,410, Asian 252, Other 1,247; parental education 15.20 +/- 2.61 years; parental income <49,999 USD 3,222, 50,000-74,999 1,498, 75,000-99,999 1,570, 100,000-199,999 3,311, >=200,000 1,250. Continuous variables, including screen time and cognition, were trimmed to within 3 SD of the mean before analysis.
primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of NIH Toolbox cognitive domain scores on per-device daily screen time (texting, video chat), adjusted for demographics, puberty, physical activity and sleep

iv_axis.label: Texting

iv_axis.label: Video chat
iv_axis.note: SD not printed: article Table 2 (p.3) reports only total screen time (3.79 +/- 3.07 h/day, n=11,843); no per-device descriptives in article or supplement (mmc1.docx Tables S1-S2, Fig S1).

primary_models.iv: Two phone/SM-specific IVs, each analyzed as daily hours: texting and video chat, from the ABCD youth screen time questionnaire (self-report of time spent on each activity, weekday and weekend reported separately). Daily average computed as (5/7 x weekday time) + (2/7 x weekend time), applied per device (Section 2.2, p. 2). Descriptive statistics for texting and video chat are not reported; only total screen time is described (3.79 +/- 3.07 hours/day, n = 11,843, Table 2). Table S1 also includes video games, television and videos, which are not phone/SM modalities and are listed under excluded_models.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Supplementary Table S1 (supporting information file, mmc1.docx; plotted in Fig. S1); referenced in Results 3.1, p. 3 ('almost all of the screen time on each digital device is negatively associated with cognitive function, even after FDR correction'). Specification described in Section 2.6, pp. 2-3.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Screen time and NIH Toolbox cognition taken from the same ABCD assessment (the paper calls the design cross-sectional in the Limitations, p. 5; mean age 119.00 months matches the baseline visit, although the wave is not named explicitly). One observation per child, no repeated measures, no time interactions. Each cognitive domain is a separate DV. The per-device analysis in Table S1 is a supplementary breakout of the headline total-screen-time model; the paper does not say whether each device was entered in its own model or all devices jointly, but the slightly different r2 values per device within a domain suggest separate models per device.
primary_models.dv: Five NIH Toolbox cognitive domains, age-corrected scores (Table 1, p. 2): executive function (average of Dimensional Change Card Sort and Flanker; 96.07 +/- 12.22, n = 11,710), processing speed (Pattern Comparison; 93.78 +/- 22.07, n = 11,697), working memory (List Sorting; 100.55 +/- 14.79, n = 11,672), episodic memory (Picture Sequence Memory; 100.96 +/- 16.10, n = 11,709), language (average of Oral Reading Recognition and Picture Vocabulary; 104.65 +/- 15.62, n = 11,702). Descriptives from Table 2, p. 3.
primary_models.estimation: R 4.3.1, lmerTest package (linear mixed-effects models; t tests with Satterthwaite-type fractional d.f.). Random effects for family ID, multiple data collections and twin/triplet status. No sampling weights reported. Outliers in screen time, cognition and all continuous variables trimmed to within 3 SD. Alpha = 0.05. Table S1 applies FDR correction across all 25 p-values in the table (5 devices x 5 domains); the main text applies FDR within each domain (Benjamini-Hochberg). No interaction or stratified analyses by sex or other variables are reported. A separate mediation analysis (R package printed as 'lanvnn', presumably lavaan; 10,000 bias-corrected bootstraps) of putamen volume uses total screen time only.

papers.authors: Shou Q, Yamashita M, Mizuno Y

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta / sqrt(1 - beta^2) (guidelines section 4a); applied to each CI endpoint for the d CI.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 SD increase in daily texting or video chat hours, assuming the Table S1 'beta' is standardized
d_transformation.notes: Table S1 column is labeled 'beta' without stating whether it is standardized. The main text distinguishes unstandardized b from standardized beta for total screen time (e.g., executive function b = -0.212, beta = -0.051), and the Table S1 magnitudes (-0.024 to -0.071) match the scale of those standardized betas, so beta_std is assumed. If the betas were instead unstandardized per hour, B -> d would need SD_IV for texting and video chat, which the paper does not report (only total screen time SD = 3.07 h, Table 2). SD_DV values in dv_axis come from Table 2, p. 3 (full sample, not the per-cell analytic sample) and are given for reference only. Table S1 comes from the online supporting information (mmc1.docx from the publisher's site), not the article PDF. [complete-stage check] Main text: total screen time EF b=-0.212 with beta=-0.051; b*SD_IV/SD_DV = -0.212*3.07/12.22 = -0.053, consistent with the main-text beta being standardized and supporting the beta_std reading of Table S1. No per-device SDs anywhere, so B-scale conversion remains impossible if Table S1 were unstandardized. Supplement is not stored in docs/pdfs; values verified from scratchpad copy p84_mmc1.docx.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The article PDF is only 6 pages and does not contain the qualifying estimates. They are only in Supplementary Table S1. I got that table from the publisher's open-access supplement (ars.els-cdn.com, 1-s2.0-S0001691826005433-mmc1.docx), saved a copy to the scratchpad as p84_mmc1.docx, and parsed the values directly from the docx table, so they match it exactly. A human should confirm this is the official supplement and consider saving it next to the PDF. 2) The Table S1 column is just labeled 'beta' and the supplement never says whether it is standardized. I coded it as beta_std because its magnitudes (-0.02 to -0.07) match the standardized betas in the main text, and the main text reports unstandardized b of about -0.2 to -0.4. If the betas are actually unstandardized, d cannot be computed: the paper reports no SD for texting or video chat, only for total screen time (3.07 h/day). 3) Table S1 does not print per-cell N. The paper also never says whether each device was modeled on its own or all devices were entered together; the r2 values differ by device, which suggests separate models. 4) I set significance using the FDR p, which the authors corrected across all 25 tests in Table S1. On that basis texting is not significant for executive function (raw p .017, FDR .071) or processing speed (raw p .023, FDR .064). 5) The covariate list follows Section 2.6. Section 2.5 points to the Table 2 variables as covariates, and those also include total brain size and handedness, so the exact covariate set is somewhat ambiguous. Section 2.5 actually cites 'Table 1', which looks like a typo for Table 2. 6) The paper does not name the ABCD wave. Mean age 119 months points to baseline, and the authors describe the design as cross-sectional. 7) The SD_DV values come from the full sample in Table 2, not the analytic sample. They are listed for reference only, since a standardized-beta conversion does not need them.json

papers.title: The association between screen time and cognitive function in children: The partially mediating role of putamen volume

primary_models.estimation: Generalized estimating equations (Liang & Zeger 1986), Stata 17.0 xtgee, binomial family, logit link, autoregressive working correlation structure. No site or family clustering terms, no weights, no imputation. Alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. Non-significant predictor x time interactions dropped; significant ones followed by simple-effects tests of time within each predictor level. Post-hoc sensitivity analysis refitting all models in substance-naive youth is extracted separately as M2. No sex, race, or other effect-modification tests reported.
primary_models.dv: Three binary time-varying outcomes, each modeled separately: any alcohol use, any nicotine/tobacco use, any cannabis use since the prior assessment. At annual visits (ages 11-12, 12-13) from the interviewer-assisted Timeline Followback; at the two mid-year phone assessments from a brief past-6-month substance use questionnaire. Prevalence at age 11-12 (Table 1): alcohol 9.9%, nicotine/tobacco 0.9%, cannabis 0.5%.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (release not stated); all participants with substance use data at one or more of the four assessments, n = 10,907 (from the 11,880 enrolled). No imputation; all observed data used ('intent-to-treat'). Table 1 (age 11-12): mean age 12.0 years (SD 0.67); 52.5% male; 53.5% non-Hispanic white, 19.7% Hispanic or Latino, 14.2% Black or African American, 10.5% other; household income 11.1% < $25,000, 36.3% $25,000-$99,999, 31.1% $100,000-$200,000; grade 13.7% 5th, 44.2% 6th, 35.4% 7th; 67.8% of parents married. Per-model analytic N not reported.
primary_models.equation: logit(P(SubUse[i,t] = 1)) = b0 + b1*PhoneOrSM[i] + b2*time[t] + b3*age[i] + b4*female[i] + b5*Black[i] + b6*Hispanic[i] + b7*Asian[i] + b8*Other[i] + b9*income[i] (+ b10*PhoneOrSM[i]*time[t] in the SM-alcohol and SM-nicotine/tobacco models only); t = 0..3; within-person correlation handled by AR working correlation in GEE.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Predictor (phone ownership or social media use) and covariates measured once at the ABCD Year 2 annual visit (age 11-12, analytic baseline, time = 0) and treated as time-invariant. Outcome (any use of the substance since the prior assessment, binary) is time-varying across four assessments: Year 2 annual (time 0), Year 2 mid-year (1), Year 3 annual (2), Year 3 mid-year (3), roughly ages 11-12 to 13-14, data collected September 2018 to January 2022. Outcomes enter as repeated measures, not averaged. Six separate models, one per predictor x substance combination. Each model initially included predictor, linear time, and predictor x time; the interaction was dropped when non-significant. It was retained (significant) only for SM x alcohol and SM x nicotine/tobacco, so in those two models the SM main effect is the group difference at time 0 (age 11-12) and the interaction is the per-timepoint change in that log-odds difference. In the other four models the predictor main effect is the average group difference across all four timepoints.

primary_models.iv: Two binary predictors, each from a single youth-report item at the age 11-12 (Year 2) annual visit, modeled in separate models: (1) mobile phone ownership, 'Do you have your own mobile phone?' (0 = no, 1 = yes), endorsed by 71.2%; (2) social media use, 'Do you have at least one social media account?' (0 = no, 1 = yes), endorsed by 54.9%. d_transformation.notes: OR converts directly via Chinn; no SDs needed. p0 values in M1 dv_axis are the marginal age 11-12 prevalences from Table 1 (p. 3), not the unexposed-group rate, and are not needed for the OR conversion. Caveats: (1) In M1 SM-alcohol and SM-nicotine/tobacco, the SM OR is the difference at time 0 with an interaction retained, so it is not comparable to averaged effects in the other cells. (2) The SM-alcohol main effect in Table 3 (OR 1.50) conflicts with the Results text (OR 1.06, non-significant). (3) The sm_x_time interaction ORs are not a group contrast and probably should not be converted to d alongside the main effects. (4) Five of the six M1 models come from supplementary tables not included in the PDF; values were copied from the Results text. Completion pass: both models iv_type binary; ORs with printed CIs for all 14 cells, no SDs needed. Table 3 SE (0.04) added for SM and SMxtime alcohol rows; the SM row SE does not match its CI width. Phone x alcohol p corrected to p_label '<0.001' (p null).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The values for social media and alcohol disagree within the paper. Table 3 gives the SM main effect as OR 1.50 (1.31, 1.72), b 0.41. The Results text on p. 3 gives OR 1.06 [0.92, 1.21], b 0.04, not significant. The draft uses the table value, so a human needs to decide which is correct. 2) The supplementary tables (Supp Tables 1, 3, 4 and the one printed as 'S') are not in the PDF. Five of the six full-sample models were therefore copied from the Results text, and their p-values and SEs are missing. 3) In the SM-alcohol and SM-nicotine/tobacco models the SM x time interaction was kept. That makes the SM main effect the difference at time 0, not an average over follow-up. The two interaction ORs are entered as a separate 'sm_x_time' IV row and probably should not be converted to d alongside the main effects. 4) M2 is the post-hoc sensitivity analysis in substance-naive youth (n=9,628). It is reported in the text only, but the authors interpret it in the Discussion. Its covariates are assumed to match M1 because the text only says the models were 're-fit'. 5) For phone and alcohol, p was entered as 0.001 with the label '<0.001'. The p0 values are the marginal age 11-12 prevalences from Table 1, not the rates in the unexposed group. 6) There are typos in the source: the CI '[1.01, 1.017]' for the SM x time OR, and '[0.06. 0.37]'. 7) The ABCD release is not stated, and per-model analytic N is not reported; only the total of 10,907 is given.

primary_models.iv: Two qualifying exposures, each measured at Year 2 and analyzed as a continuous mean score. (1) Problematic mobile phone use: 8-item Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire, item sum divided by number of items, range 1-7, Cronbach alpha 0.84; weighted mean 3.08 (SD 1.10) among the n=6,158 phone users. (2) Problematic social media use: 6-item Social Media Addiction Questionnaire modeled on the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, mean score range 1-6, alpha 0.80; weighted mean 1.84 (SD 0.89) among the n=4,633 youth with a social media account. The coefficient is per 1-point increase in the mean score. Higher scores indicate more addiction-like use.
primary_models.sample: ABCD 5.0 release, Year 2 and Year 3 follow-up. Analytic sample N=8,119 participants with complete sociodemographic data, any reported mobile phone, social media, or video game use, and at least one outcome. The MPIQ was asked only of phone users (n=6,158) and the SMAQ only of youth with at least one social media account (n=4,633) (Table 1 footnotes), so the per-exposure analytic N is smaller than 8,119; exact per-model Ns are not printed in the main text. Mean age at Year 2 12.04 (SD 0.66). 47.5% female, 52.5% male. Race/ethnicity: 5.1% Asian, 14.7% Black, 19.5% Latino or Hispanic, 3.3% Native American, 1.2% Other, 56.2% White (43.8% non-White). Household income: 13.5% <=$24,999; 16.4% $25,000-49,999; 16.9% $50,000-74,999; 15.1% $75,000-99,999; 28.1% $100,000-199,999; 10.1% >=$200,000. Parent education 89.5% college or more, 10.5% high school or less. Excluded participants were more likely to be younger, female, higher income, higher parental education, and less likely to be White (Appendix Table 1). Table 1 values are ACS-weighted.
primary_models.equation: Y_Year3[i] = b0 + b1*PSU_Year2[i] + b2*Y_Year2[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*household_income + b15*parent_education + site terms + e[i], where PSU is either the MPIQ mean score or the SMAQ mean score and Y is one of the six CBCL T-scores or sleep duration. Focal coefficient b1.

primary_models.name: Weighted multiple linear regression of Year 3 CBCL T-scores and sleep duration on Year 2 problematic phone use (MPIQ) or problematic social media use (SMAQ), adjusted for sociodemographics, site, and Year 2 outcome
primary_models.dv: Seven continuous Year 3 outcomes. Six parent-reported CBCL DSM-oriented scale T-scores (Table 1 weighted means/SDs): depressive problems 54.18 (6.26), anxiety problems 53.69 (6.26), somatic problems 54.72 (6.18), attention/deficit 53.36 (5.38), oppositional defiant problems 53.10 (4.99), conduct problems 52.34 (4.71). Sleep duration from the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire, a weighted average of school-day and free-day sleep durations; Table 1 reports average sleep duration 8.91 (SD 1.58) hours per night, while Figure 1 labels the outcome 'Weekly sleep duration'.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Figure 1 (p. 5), point estimates printed beside each forest-plot row; full table in Appendix Table 3 (online supplement, not bundled in this PDF); described in Results p. 4 and Discussion pp. 4-7
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal, two waves. Problematic use exposures measured at ABCD Year 2 follow-up (ages 11-12, 2018-2020); continuous outcomes measured at Year 3 follow-up, one year later. Each outcome model adjusts for the same outcome measured at Year 2, so the coefficient is the association with Year 3 level net of Year 2 level. Single follow-up per child, not repeated measures. No time interaction. Problematic phone, social media, and video game use are each presented as a separate exposure block; the paper does not state explicitly whether the three were entered in separate models or jointly, but the different eligible subsets (phone users vs. SM account holders) imply separate models.
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18. Multiple linear regression. Sampling weights based on the American Community Survey applied. Study site entered as a covariate; no random effects or clustering described. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction applied for multiple testing; adjusted p/q values not printed in the main text. Assumptions of linear regression checked. No sex, race, or other interaction tests or stratified results reported. No sensitivity analyses reported. Significance below is judged from the text and from whether the Figure 1 CI excludes zero.

Stata 18. Multiple logistic regression. ACS-based sampling weights. Study site as covariate; no random effects described. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction; adjusted p values not printed in main text. Assumptions of logistic regression checked. No interaction tests, stratified estimates, or sensitivity analyses reported. Significance judged from text and from whether the Figure 2 CI excludes 1.
primary_models.dv: Six binary Year 3 outcomes (Table 1 weighted prevalence): suicidal behaviors from the youth KSADS (passive ideation, nonspecific active ideation, active ideation with plan/method/preparation/intent, or attempt), 2.9%; total sleep disturbance, Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children total score at or above 39, 25.7% (continuous total score M 36.30, SD 8.10); alcohol initiation (tried a sip), 11.6%; tobacco initiation (a puff of a tobacco product), 2.5%; marijuana initiation (a puff), 1.0%; any substance initiation, 12.8%.
primary_models.sample: Same as M1: ABCD 5.0, analytic N=8,119 overall, with the MPIQ restricted to phone users (n=6,158) and the SMAQ to youth with a social media account (n=4,633). Same demographic profile. Per-model Ns not printed in the main text.
primary_models.equation: logit(P(Y_Year3[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*PSU_Year2[i] + b2*Y_Year2[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*household_income + b15*parent_education + site terms, where PSU is the MPIQ or SMAQ mean score. Reported AOR = exp(b1).
primary_models.design: Same prospective two-wave design as M1: problematic use at Year 2 (ages 11-12), binary outcomes at Year 3, adjusting for the respective outcome measured at Year 2. Differs from M1 in using binary outcomes and logistic regression.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The PDF has only 10 pages, and Appendix Table 3 (the full results with numeric CIs and p values) is in the online supplement, which is not included. All 26 point estimates come from the values printed next to the forest-plot rows in Figures 1 and 2. CIs and p values are null and need filling from Appendix Table 3. 2) Significance is judged from the text and by looking at the figure CIs. The ones to check against the supplement: SMAQ->somatic and SMAQ->anxiety (lower bounds near 0), and MPIQ->marijuana and SMAQ->tobacco (lower bounds near 1). Benjamini-Hochberg FDR was applied, but the adjusted values are not shown. 3) Figure 1 labels the coefficient 'beta', but nothing says it is standardized, so I treated it as unstandardized B (per 1 point of the MPIQ/SMAQ mean score). 4) The sleep duration unit is unclear: Figure 1 says 'Weekly sleep duration', but Table 1 gives 8.91 (SD 1.58) hours per night. 5) SD_DV for the CBCL T-scores is set to 10 by rule. The weighted sample SDs in Table 1 are 4.71-6.26, so the derived d will be smaller than with sample SDs. 6) The paper says N=8,119, but the MPIQ was asked only of phone users (n=6,158) and the SMAQ only of SM account holders (n=4,633). The per-model Ns are not printed, and the paper never says whether the phone, SM and gaming exposures were modeled separately or together. 7) The p0 values are weighted marginal Year 3 prevalences, not rates in an unexposed group. Problematic video game use is excluded (generic gaming).json

d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). M2: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000).
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 4): MPIQ 1.10 (n=6,158 phone users), SMAQ 0.89 (n=4,633 social media account holders); these are ACS-weighted descriptives. SD_DV for CBCL DSM-oriented T-scores set to 10 by construction per guidelines; the observed weighted Year 3 SDs in Table 1 are smaller (depressive 6.26, anxiety 6.26, somatic 6.18, attention 5.38, ODD 4.99, conduct 4.71), so using 10 will give smaller d values than using the sample SDs. SD_DV for sleep duration 1.58 (Table 1, 'hours per night'), but Figure 1 labels the outcome 'Weekly sleep duration', so the unit of B for sleep is uncertain. Figure 1 is labeled beta; the IV is an unstandardized mean score and the DV is in T-score units, and the paper never says the coefficients are standardized, so they are treated as unstandardized B. Because all M1 models adjust for the Year 2 outcome, the derived d reflects association with Year 3 level conditional on Year 2 level. p0 for M2 are the weighted marginal Year 3 prevalences from Table 1 (not unexposed-group rates) and are not needed for the OR-to-d conversion. No numeric CIs are printed in the main PDF (only graphical CIs in Figures 1-2), so d CIs cannot be computed until Appendix Table 3 is obtained. [complete stage 2026-10-01] Re-read entire PDF: no numeric CI, SE, exact p or test statistic printed for any cell; all 26 CIs confirmed missing (Appendix Table 3 online only). iv_type set to continuous for M1 and M2. [audit 2026-10-01] sd_dv for the six CBCL scales changed from 10 to the analytic-sample weighted Year 3 SDs printed in Table 1 p.4 (6.26, 6.26, 6.18, 5.38, 4.99, 4.71).
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1-point increase in the MPIQ (1-7) or SMAQ (1-6) mean score; after the M1 conversion, per 1 SD of the exposure.
d_transformation.native_metric: B (M1, unstandardized linear coefficient labeled beta in Figure 1) + OR (M2, adjusted odds ratio)

primary_models.sample: ABCD data from the Year 2 (Time 1, ages 11-13) and Year 4 (Time 2, ages 13-15) follow-ups; release version not stated (NDA study 2313 cited). From the original 10,964 participants, exclusions were missing basic demographics (sex, age, race/ethnicity, family income), missing VGA or SMA data, missing MID fMRI data, or imaging flagged for exclusion by the ABCD analytic core (Hagler et al., 2019). 2,400 met criteria at Year 2 and 1,578 at Year 4; the final sample is N = 543 who met criteria at both time points. SMAQ/VGAQ were administered only to youth reporting at least one social media account or video game use. Final sample (Table 1): age 11 = 244 (44.9%), 12 = 298 (54.9%), 13 = 1 (0.2%); 331 male (61.0%), 212 female (39.0%); White 261 (48.1%), Black 80 (14.7%), Hispanic 132 (24.3%), Asian 10 (1.8%), Other 60 (11.0%). Authors report no significant demographic differences between final and original samples.

primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed models in R lme4; random intercept for research site only (no participant random effect is stated despite repeated measures). Coefficients reported as standardized betas with 95% CI. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across models; significance judged at p_FDR < 0.05. No weights. For significant VGA x Time interactions, simple slopes were probed at -1 SD, mean and +1 SD of VGA; no SMA simple slopes because no SMA x Time effect survived FDR. No sensitivity analyses reported.

primary_models.equation: BetaWeight_ROI[i,t] = b0 + b1*VGA[i,t] + b2*SMA[i,t] + b3*Time[t] + b4*VGA[i,t]*Time[t] + b5*SMA[i,t]*Time[t] + b6*Age + b7*Sex + b8..b11*Race/ethnicity + b12*FamilyIncome + b13*MeanFD + u_site + e[i,t]; focal estimate b5 (SMA x Time).
primary_models.dv: MID task fMRI ROI beta-weights from the ABCD curated tabulated data (Hagler et al., 2019): Reward Anticipation vs. Neutral (reward contrast) and Loss Anticipation vs. Neutral (loss contrast), averaged across the two runs, in 8 bilateral ROIs (nucleus accumbens, amygdala, caudate, putamen, insula, caudal ACC, medial OFC, rostral ACC labeled vmPFC), left and right separately, giving 32 DVs each modelled separately. Units are GLM beta coefficients; no descriptive statistics reported.

primary_models.name: Linear mixed model of MID-task ROI beta-weights on SMA x Time, adjusted for VGA x Time, demographics and head motion
primary_models.iv: Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), 6 items adapted from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, each rated 1 (Never) to 6 (Very often), summed score (range 6-36 per Fig. 2). McDonald's omega = 0.86. Administered only to youth reporting at least one social media account. Means and SDs are not tabulated; Fig. 2 shows violin distributions only. SMA was significantly lower at Time 1 than Time 2 (paired t = -5.34, p < .001, Cohen's d = -0.23). Time is coded as the two waves (coding not stated). The estimate is the SMA x Time interaction coefficient, reported as a standardized beta.
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, two waves: ABCD Year 2 follow-up (Time 1, ages 11-13) and Year 4 follow-up (Time 2, ages 13-15). SMA, VGA and ROI beta-weights are measured at both waves and entered in long format as repeated measures (two rows per participant). The focal SMA estimate printed in the paper is the SMA x Time interaction, i.e. whether the SMA-brain association differs between Time 1 and Time 2. The SMA main effect is in the model but its coefficients are not printed (text only says it did not reach significance, p_FDR > 0.05). Each of 32 ROI-by-contrast DVs fitted in a separate model.

primary_models.estimation: Partial correlations; software not separately stated (analyses in R). Table note says correlations are conditioned on age, sex, race/ethnicity and family income; mean framewise displacement and site are not listed. p-values appear uncorrected (bolded at p < .05) even though the text says all models were BH-corrected; no FDR values are printed for Table 2. No CIs.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, SMA columns under Time 1 and Time 2 (p. 5); Results 3.1 p. 4; interpreted in Discussion p. 5 (positive correlation between SMA and loss sensitivity at both times and reward sensitivity at Time 2).

primary_models.iv: Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), 6 items adapted from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, each rated 1 (Never) to 6 (Very often), summed score (range 6-36 per Fig. 2). McDonald's omega = 0.86. Administered only to youth reporting at least one social media account. Means and SDs are not tabulated; Fig. 2 shows violin distributions only. SMA was significantly lower at Time 1 than Time 2 (paired t = -5.34, p < .001, Cohen's d = -0.23). Direction is symmetric (correlation); SMA treated here as the IV column.
primary_models.sample: ABCD data from the Year 2 (Time 1, ages 11-13) and Year 4 (Time 2, ages 13-15) follow-ups; release version not stated (NDA study 2313 cited). From the original 10,964 participants, exclusions were missing basic demographics (sex, age, race/ethnicity, family income), missing VGA or SMA data, missing MID fMRI data, or imaging flagged for exclusion by the ABCD analytic core (Hagler et al., 2019). 2,400 met criteria at Year 2 and 1,578 at Year 4; the final sample is N = 543 who met criteria at both time points. SMAQ/VGAQ were administered only to youth reporting at least one social media account or video game use. Final sample (Table 1): age 11 = 244 (44.9%), 12 = 298 (54.9%), 13 = 1 (0.2%); 331 male (61.0%), 212 female (39.0%); White 261 (48.1%), Black 80 (14.7%), Hispanic 132 (24.3%), Asian 10 (1.8%), Other 60 (11.0%). Authors report no significant demographic differences between final and original samples. N per correlation is not stated; assumed to be the 543 final sample.
primary_models.dv: MID task fMRI ROI beta-weights from the ABCD curated tabulated data (Hagler et al., 2019): Reward Anticipation vs. Neutral (reward contrast) and Loss Anticipation vs. Neutral (loss contrast), averaged across the two runs, in 8 bilateral ROIs (nucleus accumbens, amygdala, caudate, putamen, insula, caudal ACC, medial OFC, rostral ACC labeled vmPFC), left and right separately, giving 32 DVs each modelled separately. Units are GLM beta coefficients; no descriptive statistics reported.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional within each wave: SMA at Time 1 (Year 2) correlated with ROI beta-weights at Time 1, and SMA at Time 2 (Year 4) correlated with ROI beta-weights at Time 2 (concurrent pairing inferred from Table 2 layout and Results text; not stated explicitly). One correlation per ROI x contrast x wave.

papers.extraction_flags:
Things to check by hand:

(1) For M1, the SMA estimate the paper prints is only the SMA x Time interaction (Table 3). The paper says the SMA main effect is "not significant" but prints no coefficient for it. So M1's d values describe how the association changed between waves, not the association itself. Coders should decide whether M1 belongs in the d comparison at all.

(2) M2 uses the Table 2 partial correlations (SMA with ROI beta-weights at Time 1 and Time 2). These are conditioned on demographics only, with no head motion and no site term. The p-values appear uncorrected even though the text says all models were BH-corrected. I coded sig at p < .05 to match the paper's bolding. Two things are inferred from the table layout and Results text, not stated: that SMA and brain were measured at the same wave, and that N = 543 per correlation.

(3) The SMA-as-DV model (hypothesis 2) went to excluded_models. The paper reports SMA results only as "no significant interaction" and gives no numbers.

(4) M1 significance is coded on p_FDR < .05. Right insula loss is p = .017 uncorrected but p_FDR = .089, so it is coded sig = false.

(5) The paper does not say how Time was coded or which variables were standardized. The LMM has only a site random intercept; no participant random effect is stated even though the data are repeated measures.

(6) No SDs or means for SMA or beta-weights are reported anywhere, so all sd fields are null.

(7) The pdftotext extraction labels the second row of each ROI pair as only "R" for the vmPFC rows. I mapped them by order to vmPFC R, and spot-checks against the page images matched.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: M2: d = 2r / sqrt(1 - r^2). M1: treat standardized beta as approximate r, d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2), applied to CI endpoints as well.
d_transformation.native_metric: M1: standardized beta (interaction coefficient); M2: partial r
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: change in the standardized SMA-brain slope from Time 1 to Time 2 (difference in association between waves), not a simple per-SD association. M2: per 1 SD of SMA (correlation) at a single wave.
d_transformation.notes: M2 partial correlations convert directly via r to d, though no CIs are printed so d CIs cannot be formed. M1 coefficients are standardized interaction terms (Table 3 note: 'standardized beta coefficients'); converting them to d is mechanically possible but the result describes a between-wave difference in slope, not a main association, and the SMA main effect itself is unreported, so M1 d values are not comparable to per-SD association d's from other papers. Time coding and standardization procedure (which variables standardized) are not stated. No means or SDs for SMA or beta-weights are reported anywhere (Fig. 2 shows distributions only), so sd_iv and sd_dv are null; none are needed because both metrics are already standardized. Complete pass (2026-10-01): full 9-page PDF re-read (no supplement file exists). M1 values/CIs/p re-verified against Table 3; M2 r/p re-verified against Table 2 and n = 543 added to each M2 estimate so Fisher-z CIs can be derived.

primary_models.location_in_paper: Methods 3.4 (p. 4); network plots Figs. 1-3 (pp. 4-5); edge weights Table 2 (T1, p. 5), Table 3 (T2, p. 5), Table 4 (T3, p. 6); edges interpreted in Results 4.2, 4.4, 4.6 (pp. 7-8) and Discussion p. 9.
primary_models.equation: Gaussian graphical model per wave t: precision matrix K_t estimated by graphical LASSO, minimizing -log det(K) + tr(S_t K) + lambda * sum|k_ij| over the 13 nodes {ScrOnlineV, ScrTV, ScrVG, ScrText, ScrVChat, ScrSM, PLE_5, PLE_10, PLE_14, PLE_16, PLE_19, PLE_20, PLE_21}. Edge weight w_ij = -k_ij / sqrt(k_ii * k_jj) = partial correlation between node i (phone/SM) and node j (PLE item) given all 11 other nodes; small edges shrunk to exactly 0. Tuning-parameter selection (e.g. EBIC gamma) not reported.
primary_models.iv: Three phone/SM screen-time nodes from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey: ScrText (texting), ScrVChat (video calling on services such as Skype and Discord), and ScrSM (social media, e.g. Facebook, Instagram). Youth reported hours/minutes spent on each activity on a typical weekday, with a second set of questions for weekends. The paper does not say whether the node uses weekday, weekend, or a combined value, and does not report means or SDs for any screen variable. The same network also contains three non-phone screen nodes (ScrOnlineV online video such as YouTube/Twitch, ScrTV, ScrVG video games on any device) that are partialled out of every phone/SM-PLE edge.

covariates.detail: Each edge is a partial correlation conditional on the other 11 nodes: the three non-phone screen nodes (online video, TV, video games), the other two phone/SM nodes, and the remaining six PLE items.
covariates.name: All other network nodes

covariates.detail: None. No age, sex, SES, site, or family adjustment is reported.
covariates.name: Demographic covariates

primary_models.design: Three separate cross-sectional networks, one per ABCD wave (T1 at ages 9-10, T2 and T3 at roughly 12-month intervals; the last wave was collected in 2019 when participants were 11-12). Each network is estimated on that wave's data only; there are no cross-lagged or temporal (between-wave) edges, so every edge is a same-wave undirected association. The paper calls the approach longitudinal network analysis, but longitudinal content is limited to comparing the three cross-sectional networks with the Network Comparison Test. Phone/SM nodes and PLE nodes are both nodes; neither is formally an IV or DV. For this extraction the phone/SM nodes are placed on the IV axis and the PLE nodes on the DV axis.

primary_models.name: Regularized (graphical LASSO) partial-correlation network of six screen-time nodes and seven PLE item nodes, estimated separately at three ABCD time points; phone/SM-to-PLE edges
primary_models.estimation: R packages qgraph (network estimation, graphical LASSO) and networktools (centrality, bridge indices). The correlation type (Pearson vs. polychoric/Spearman), lambda selection criterion, and missing-data handling are not reported. Stability assessed by case-dropping bootstrap (correlation-stability coefficient; acceptable > 0.25, preferable > 0.5): edge CS = 0.75 at each of T1, T2, T3. Edge and centrality difference tests used bootnet (Figs. S8, S10, S12 in the supplement, not in this PDF). No p-values, CIs, or significance flags are printed for individual edges in Tables 2-4. Network Comparison Test (NetworkComparisonTest package, alpha = 0.05) compared global structure and strength between wave pairs. No multiple-comparison correction beyond LASSO regularization. No sex or other moderation tests. Centrality (expected influence, betweenness, closeness) and bridge centrality reported in Figs. 4-9; the authors state closeness and betweenness were too unstable to interpret.

primary_models.dv: Seven item-level nodes from the Prodromal Questionnaire - Brief Child Version (PQ-BC; 21 items, each with a follow-up distress question rated 1 [strongly disagree] to 5 [strongly agree]; reported alpha = 0.84, omega = 0.92): PLE 5 delusion of control, PLE 10 auditory hallucinations, PLE 14 experiential hallucinations, PLE 16 somatic delusions, PLE 19 visual hallucinations, PLE 20 struggling to concentrate, PLE 21 difficulty communicating. The paper does not explain why these 7 of the 21 items were chosen, and does not say whether each node is the yes/no endorsement or the 1-5 distress rating. No item descriptives reported.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study data accessed from the NIMH Data Archive; data release not stated. N = 11,876 adolescents (mean age 9.92, SD 0.62; 6,196 male [52.2%], 5,680 female [47.8%]). Retention 94.5% from Wave 1 to Wave 2 and 87.7% from Wave 1 to Wave 3; the paper states 10,414 participants at the smallest time point. Per-wave analytic Ns and missing-data handling are not otherwise reported. Race/ethnicity not reported. An attrition t-test (Table 1, p. 3) found retained vs. lost participants did not differ on age or sex but differed on all screen-time variables and some PLE items, with small effects (Cohen's d < 0.2).

papers.extraction_flags:
1. How the model card is built. There is one model card: a glasso network fit separately at T1, T2 and T3. It has 9 IV rows (texting, video chat and social media at each of the 3 waves) and 7 PLE item columns, so 63 edges. All edge values come from Tables 2-4. The 28 nonzero edges match the pdftotext output of the PDF; the 35 others are exactly 0. A reviewer might prefer three cards, one per wave.

2. sig and p are null for every edge. The paper prints no p-values, CIs or significance flags for single edges; the bootnet difference tests are only in the supplement. If the renderer requires a boolean for sig, this needs fixing. Each edge's note says whether it was shrunk to 0 or kept as nonzero.

3. Missing details:
   - The paper does not say whether each screen node is weekday time, weekend time or a combination.
   - It does not say whether each PLE node is the yes/no endorsement or the 1-5 distress rating, or why these 7 of the 21 PQ-BC items were chosen.
   - Not reported: ABCD release, correlation type, lambda/EBIC tuning, per-wave N, missing-data handling, race/ethnicity breakdown, and any descriptives or SDs for the nodes.

4. Design. The paper calls itself a "longitudinal network analysis", but it fits three same-wave networks. There are no cross-wave edges.

5. Possible later use. Bridge expected influence and centrality for the phone/SM nodes appear only as figure points (Figs. 4-9) and were excluded. These figures are the authors' main interpretive output, so a later review level might want values read off them.

6. All phone/SM-PLE edges are tiny (largest 0.037). The authors' claims about texting's centrality rest mostly on its edges to other screen nodes, not to PLEs.

7. Cohen's d was not computed. Section 4a of the guidelines lists network edge weights as non-convertible.

d_transformation.contrast_type: Edge = partial correlation between a phone/SM screen-time node and a PLE item node at the same wave, conditional on the 11 other nodes and shrunk by L1 regularization; no unit contrast on the IV.
d_transformation.notes: Guidelines section 4a lists network edge weights as non-convertible. Formally an edge is a partial correlation and r -> d (d = 2r / sqrt(1 - r^2)) could be applied, but the values are LASSO-shrunk (many set to exactly 0), conditioned on the other screen nodes and PLE items, and lack CIs and p-values, so a derived d would not be comparable to regression-based d's. No SDs for screen-time or PLE nodes are reported anywhere in the paper. All 63 phone/SM-PLE edges are small: the largest is 0.037 (video chat - somatic delusions, T3); the rest range from -0.007 to 0.031, and 35 are exactly 0. Complete-pass (2026-10-01): full PDF re-read; no edge CIs, SEs, p-values, per-wave N or node SDs are printed anywhere in the article; bootnet edge CIs exist only in the online supplement (Figs. S8/S10/S12), which is not available locally.

primary_models.iv: Screen media activity items from the ABCD youth screen time questionnaire, each asked for a typical weekday and a typical weekend day: TV shows or movies; watching videos (e.g., YouTube); video games; texting ('Text on a cell phone, tablet, or computer (GChat, Whatsapp, etc.)'); video chat ('Video chat (Skype, Facetime, etc.)'); and social networking sites ('Visit social networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, etc.'). 7-point response recoded to hours: None = 0, <30 min = .25, 30 min = .5, 1 h = 1, 2 h = 2, 3 h = 3, 4+ h = 4 (p. 294). The qualifying phone/SM items are Text_wkdy, Text_wknd, VideoChat_wkdy, VideoChat_wknd, SocMedia_wkdy, SocMedia_wknd as labelled in Figs. 5-6. Item-level descriptives are not in the PDF (OSM-1).
primary_models.estimation: Group factor analysis following Klami et al. (2015) and Paulus et al. (2019); software not named in the PDF (code at github.com/Miller-Jack/cortex-rsfmri). The GFA identified 67 latent variables; three explained >4% of variance (together 22.7%). Factor 3 loaded only on resting-state variables and was dropped per the preregistration, leaving GFA grouping 1 (9.34% of variance) and GFA grouping 2 (8.56%). Loadings are shown with 95% CIs; a loading is called 'significant' when its 95% CI lies outside the mean of the metric, without multiple-comparison correction (p. 297). No covariates or random effects enter the GFA. Registered Report (Stage 1 protocol https://osf.io/z4eyv); deviation: models run on full baseline and replicated on the full 2-year follow-up rather than split-half of Release 1.1/2.0.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Methods 2.5 (p. 296); Results 3.2 (pp. 297-298); Fig. 4 (p. 298), Fig. 5 (GFA grouping 1, p. 299), Fig. 6 (GFA grouping 2, p. 300); replication at 2-year follow-up in OSM-2 (not in PDF); interpreted in Discussion p. 302
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional at ABCD baseline. The GFA jointly decomposes two groups of variables measured at the same visit: the screen media activity items (weekday and weekend) and the Gordon-parcellation within- and between-network rs-fcMRI correlations. There is no IV/DV direction in this model; texting, video chat and social media items are observed variables whose loadings on latent factors are estimated alongside the brain network variables. A separate GFA was run on the same participants at the 2-year follow-up to test whether the factor structure replicated (reported in OSM-2; the paper says GFA 1 partly replicated and GFA 2 did not).
primary_models.name: Group factor analysis of 12 self-reported screen media activity items (including texting, video chat and social media) with resting-state network connectivity
primary_models.equation: GFA: X_g = W_g * Z + E_g for each variable group g in {screen media items, rs-fcMRI network correlations}, where Z holds latent factor scores shared across groups, W_g the group-specific loadings, and E_g residual noise. Factors retained if they explain >1% of the variance (Methods p. 296; Results p. 297 states the three retained factors each explained >4%) and load on both groups.
primary_models.dv: Resting-state functional connectivity: ABCD-curated average Fisher-z correlations within and between Gordon-parcellation networks (auditory, cingulo-opercular, cingulo-parietal, default, dorsal attention, fronto-parietal, retrosplenial-temporal, sensorimotor hand, sensorimotor mouth, salience, ventral attention, visual), with sensorimotor mouth as a control network (pp. 294-295). In the GFA these are the second variable group rather than a dependent variable.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 4.0 baseline (11,878 participants). Participants needed >10 min of resting-state data with framewise displacement <0.2 mm and a T1 that passed DAIC QC; 86 had no MRI and 3,983 failed at least one benchmark, leaving 7,809 for confirmatory analyses (Fig. 1, p. 294; text p. 293). Ages 9-10 at baseline. 11,309 participants had valid screen time data, with mean weekly screen time 26.50 h (SD = 21.52) (p. 297). Sex and race/ethnicity breakdowns are in OSM-1, not in the PDF.

primary_models.iv: Average weekly time on social networking sites ('Visit social networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, etc.'), child self-report at baseline, built from weekday and weekend items recoded 0-4 h (p. 294). How weekday and weekend were combined into a weekly value is not stated in the PDF. Descriptives not reported in the PDF.
primary_models.name: Generalized additive mixed models of 2-year follow-up cognitive and CBCL outcomes on baseline social media time, adjusted for demographics with site and family random effects

primary_models.estimation: Generalized additive mixed models with data-acquisition site and family as random effects, estimated by maximum likelihood; compared with a covariate-only null GAMM by AIC and likelihood-ratio tests (pp. 296, 298). Coefficients reported as standardized betas. The main GAMM series used alpha = .05/12 = .004; the paper says the social media series extends 'the same GAMMs and covariate measures'. Inference anchored to a smallest effect size of interest of r = .20 (p. 295). Software not named in the PDF. No interaction or stratified analyses reported for social media.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0. Inclusion criteria stated to be the same as the preregistered analysis (baseline N = 7,809 after imaging QC; complete-case on covariates and outcome). The analytic N for each social media model is not reported in the PDF (OSM-4).

papers.extraction_flags:
M1 is the group factor analysis. It covers the texting, video chat and social media items (weekday and weekend) together with resting-state connectivity. Their loadings appear only on the radial plots in Figs. 5 and 6 (pp. 299-300), with no printed values. Its 12 estimate cells are therefore all null. Each cell has a note with the direction the text gives: GFA 1 loads negatively on all screen media variables, and GFA 2 loads on video games. Factor loadings also cannot be converted to Cohen's d.

M2 is the exploratory GAMM series: baseline social media time predicting cognitive and CBCL outcomes at the 2-year follow-up. The main text gives only the range "b's ranging from .013 to .026" (p. 301). The per-outcome values are in online supplement OSM-4, which is not bundled in the PDF, so estimates is empty. A human should retrieve OSM-4 from the Cortex site. Its standardized betas would make the paper partly transformable. OSM-1 should also be retrieved for the social media SD and the sample demographics.

Other items to check:
- Social media variable: the PDF does not say how weekday and weekend were combined into "average weekly social media usage."
- Which outcomes: the analytic N per model is not given. The scope of "all study outcomes" is my reading, taken as the 2 CBCL scales plus the 8 cognitive tests in Table 1.
- Covariates: the Methods list sex, ethnicity, age and caregiver education. Results 3.3 lists a longer set: parental age, marital status and income in 4 strata are added. I used the Results list.
- Factor threshold: the Methods say a factor was retained at >1% of variance; Results say >4%.
- Number of screen items: the Discussion says "ten metrics," but the Methods describe 6 activities on weekdays and weekends, which is 12 items.
- M1 as a primary model: whether a GFA should be a primary model or excluded is a judgment call. The Stage 2 inclusion was based on the GFA loadings.

papers.extraction_flags:
It holds one model (M1) with 12 estimates: 3 IVs (texting, social media, video chat) by 4 outcomes (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, any substance). All 12 ORs and CIs were checked against a zoomed render of Fig. 1, and they match.

What a human should verify:
(1) Every estimate comes from the printed labels on the Fig. 1 forest plot. The paper has no results table. 11 of the 12 also appear in the Results text, but video chat -> alcohol (OR 1.04, CI 0.98-1.11, not significant) appears only in the figure. The figure label for texting -> alcohol is missing its opening parenthesis.
(2) The paper prints no p-values. "sig" comes from the Fig. 1 asterisk, which marks significance after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. p is null and p_label is "*" when significant.
(3) The paper never says whether each modality was fitted in its own model or all modalities were entered together. I assumed one modality per model.
(4) Study site is listed as a covariate, but the paper doesn't say whether it is a fixed or random effect.
(5) The ABCD release version is not stated in the PDF. Appendix A, which compares included and excluded participants, is an online supplement and was not in the PDF.
(6) The p0 values are weighted marginal Year 3 prevalences from Table 2. They are not unexposed-group rates, and the OR conversion doesn't need them.
(7) The derived d is per 1 hour/day, not per SD. Year 2 SD_IV values from Table 1 (texting 1.5, social media 1.6, video chat 1.3) are recorded in case they are needed.
(8) Cannabis at Year 3 is rare (N=65, 1.0%).

primary_models.estimation: Stata 18 (StataCorp). Multiple logistic regression with ABCD sampling weights based on the American Community Survey. Adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction across tests; asterisks in Fig. 1 mark significance after correction. No p-values printed. Effect modification by sex and by race and ethnicity was tested; the Results state there was no evidence of effect modification, and no stratified estimates are reported. No sensitivity analyses reported.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Fig. 1 (p. 4), forest plot with OR (95% CI) printed for each modality x outcome; described in Results p. 3; interpreted in Abstract and Discussion pp. 3-5.
primary_models.dv: Year 3 youth-reported substance use experimentation, four binary outcomes analysed separately: alcohol (ever had a sip of alcohol such as beer, wine or liquor), nicotine (a puff from a tobacco or electronic cigarette, Juul, vape pen, e-hookah, cigar or pipe), cannabis (a puff or eaten any marijuana), and any substance use experimentation (tried any of the three). The alcohol sipping item is adapted from the iSay Sip Inventory. Weighted prevalence (Table 2, p. 3), Year 2 / Year 3: alcohol 10.4% / 12.0%; nicotine 1.0% / 2.5%; cannabis 0.3% / 1.0%; any substance 11.1% / 13.2%. Cannabis experimentation at Year 3 had N = 65 (Discussion p. 5).
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal analysis over two ABCD follow-up waves. Screen time modalities measured at the Year 2 follow-up (2018-2020, participants mostly 11-12 years old); substance use experimentation measured at the Year 3 follow-up, one year later. The same experimentation outcome at Year 2 is entered as a covariate. Single follow-up outcome per person (no repeated measures). Each outcome (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, any substance) is a separate binary DV. The paper says 'multiple logistic regression models' were run and the forest plot lists one OR per modality; it does not state explicitly whether each modality was entered in its own model or all modalities together, but the format (total screen time and each component listed in parallel) is consistent with one modality per model.

primary_models.equation: logit(P(SubstanceExp_Y3[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*Modality_hours_Y2[i] + b2*SubstanceExp_Y2[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*household_income + b15*parent_education + b16*family_conflict + b17*COI_z + site terms; OR = exp(b1) per additional hour/day of the modality. Fitted separately for each outcome (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, any) and, as presented, for each modality.
primary_models.name: Weighted multiple logistic regression of Year 3 substance use experimentation on Year 2 phone/SM modality hours per day, adjusted for Year 2 substance experimentation and sociodemographic covariates
primary_models.iv: Year 2 hours per day on one screen modality, from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey. Youth reported average daily time on weekdays and weekends for each of eight modalities; the qualifying ones here are texting, video chatting (e.g., Skype, Facetime), and social media (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). Daily hours = ((weekday average x 5) + (weekend average x 2)) / 7. Entered continuously; OR is per additional hour per day. Weighted Year 2 means (SD), Table 1: texting 0.7 (1.5), social media 0.7 (1.6), video chat 0.5 (1.3) hours/day.

papers.title: Prospective association between screen use modalities and substance use experimentation in early adolescents

d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 additional hour/day of the Year 2 modality (texting, social media, or video chat)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.notes: The ORs are per hour/day, so the Chinn d is a per-1-hour contrast, not a per-SD contrast. Year 2 SD_IV values come from Table 1 (p. 3): texting 1.5, social media 1.6, video chat 1.3 hours/day; these can be used to rescale ln(OR) to a per-SD contrast if needed (ln(OR) x SD_IV). p0 values are the weighted marginal Year 3 prevalences from Table 2 (p. 3), not unexposed-group rates; they are not needed for the OR -> d conversion. Outcomes are rare (nicotine 2.5%, cannabis 1.0% at Year 3; cannabis N = 65), so ORs approximate risk ratios. All values were read from the printed labels on the Fig. 1 forest plot, and 11 of the 12 also appear verbatim in the Results text (video chat -> alcohol appears only in the figure). No p-values are reported. Completion pass (2026-10-01): re-read all 7 PDF pages; all 12 ORs and CIs confirmed against Fig. 1; no SEs or exact p-values exist in the paper; no supplement file bundled. iv_type set to continuous.

papers.title: Cannabis expectancies mediate the association between social media use and cannabis experimentation in early adolescents: A prospective cohort study

d_transformation.native_metric: M1: unstandardized logit coefficient (log-odds); M2: unstandardized linear B; M3: indirect effect on the logit scale
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV = 1.5 h/day and SD_DV = 3.0 (positive expectancies) and 2.6 (negative expectancies) are the weighted Table 1 descriptives for the N = 7691 analytic sample (p. 3). M1 B is on the log-odds scale because the gsem outcome equation is a binomial logit (Methods 2.5); it is not an OR and should not be run through the linear B formula. M2 has no CI, so only a point d can be derived. M3 indirect effects are products of coefficients across a linear and a logit equation; they are kept in native units and marked non-convertible per the guidelines for mediation indirect effects. Baseline event rate for the binary DV is the marginal weighted 5.1% at Year 4. Completion pass: whole PDF re-read (6 pp.); no supplementary file in repo; M2 a-path CIs/SEs and M1 SE are not printed anywhere in the article. All IVs continuous (hours/day).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: ln(OR) = B, so d = B * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to B and to each CI bound. M2: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). M3: not converted (mediation indirect effect).
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1 and M3: per 1 hour/day of Year 2 social media time. M2: per 1 hour/day, converted to per 1 SD of social media time via SD_IV.

primary_models.estimation: Stata 18, generalized structural equation modeling (gsem) with binomial logit regression for the binary outcome. Sequential modeling: covariates and Year 2 cannabis experimentation first, then the direct association, then expectancy paths and mediation. ACS-based sampling weights applied. Assumption checks reported: VIFs < 2, Box-Tidwell p > 0.05, all Pregibon's dbeta < 1. Alpha = 0.05, two-tailed. No multiple-comparison correction. No sex or race interaction tests or stratified estimates reported. Clustering/random effects not described beyond study site as a covariate.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study participants with complete data on Year 2 social media use, cannabis variables and covariates; N = 7691 (ABCD release not stated; excluded participants with missing data, flowchart in online Appendix A, not bundled in the PDF). Weighted descriptives (Table 1): mean age at Year 2 12.0 years (SD 0.7); 47.9% female, 52.1% male; race/ethnicity 57.4% White, 18.9% Latino/Hispanic, 14.0% Black, 5.2% Asian, 3.3% Native American, 1.3% Other (42.6% racial/ethnic minorities); household income 13.1% <=$24,999 to 10.6% >=$200,000; 89.5% parent college education or more. Friends' cannabis use at Year 2: 2.7% yes.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort, three ABCD waves. Social media time measured at Year 2 follow-up (2018-2020), cannabis expectancies (mediator) at Year 3 (2019-2021), cannabis experimentation at Year 4 (2020-2022). Single follow-up outcome per child, not repeated measures. Year 2 cannabis experimentation enters as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with new or continued experimentation by Year 4 net of Year 2 status. Mediation was run as two separate models, one with positive expectancies (Fig. 1a) and one with negative expectancies (Fig. 1b) as the mediator; the direct effect of social media time is printed as B = 0.18 in both panels. No time x IV interaction.

primary_models.iv: Social media time at Year 2, continuous hours per day. ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey: typical hours per day on social media (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X) reported separately for weekdays and weekend days, combined as ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2]) / 7. Weighted M = 0.7, SD = 1.5 h/day (Table 1).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The headline B=0.18 (95% CI 0.13-0.24) is the gsem direct effect from a binomial logit equation, so it is on the log-odds scale; I coded it as other:logit_B (d = B*sqrt(3)/pi). Please make sure the pipeline does not run it through the linear B formula. Fig. 1a and 1b both print direct B = 0.18, and the text does not say which mediation model the CI comes from. 2) The M2 a-paths (SM to positive expectancies B=0.16, to negative B=-0.16) come only from the Fig. 1 labels: there is no CI, no exact p, and the paper does not say whether they are unstandardized. The indirect effects (0.16x0.29=0.046 and 0.16x0.18=0.029) are consistent with raw-scale coefficients. Expectancies (beliefs about cannabis) were counted as an individual-level psychosocial DV, so check that they are eligible. 3) M3 indirect effects are kept in native units and marked non-convertible. 4) SDs come from Table 1 and are weighted (SM 1.5 h/day; expectancies 3.0 and 2.6). p0 = 0.051 is the weighted marginal prevalence of Year 4 experimentation, not the rate among non-users. 5) The ABCD release is not stated. The Appendix A flowchart and Appendix B (expectancy scoring) are online supplements that are not in the PDF. The paper does not say whether study site enters as a fixed or random term.

d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of the media-specific IV (if standardized); the authors' own wording for the general-SMA LMM is per additional hour of screen time
d_transformation.notes: M3 is unambiguously standardized (all variables z-scored, Table 4/5 footnotes), so the direct effect c' (0.035, CI 0.0229-0.0456) converts; the indirect a*b effect should not be converted as a total association. M1 and M2 report beta without saying whether it is standardized; for the general-SMA CLPM the authors describe beta = 0.03 as the increase in internalizing per additional screen hour (p. 6), which suggests unstandardized slopes, but a per-hour change of 0.03 t-points is implausibly small relative to t-score scaling, so standardized coefficients are likely. SD_DV values recorded in M1 are baseline sample SDs from Table 1 (p. 5): externalizing 9.543, internalizing 10.516, stress 5.694; year-3 SDs are not reported. SD_IV for texting, social media and video chat is not reported (Table 1 gives only total SMA 3.530 +/- 2.896 h). M1 and M2 report no CIs (M2 gives SE only, recorded in notes), so d CIs cannot be derived for them. Five of nine M1 cells are not reported and are recorded as null. Complete-pass (verification): M2 SEs moved into 'se' fields (0.011, 0.014, 0.014; p.6) so CIs can be derived for M2; all models set iv_type continuous. Re-read entire PDF: no media-specific SDs, no SE/CI for M1, no supplement bundled. Verified p.6 values: video chat -> internalizing beta -0.021, SE 0.011, pfdr 0.069. Complete-pass 2 (supplement now bundled: 10.1016_j.ijchp.2025.100589_supplement.docx): Table S2 prints t, R2, pfdr and Pearson r for each FDR-significant media-specific LMM; t added for the 4 printed M1 cells (texting-stress 3.39; SM-internalizing 2.08, -externalizing 3.55, -stress 3.57). Non-significant M1 cells are not in S2. Table S2 also gives texting/social media/video chat -> 2YFU brain (total brain volume, area, RSFC) t and r values, relevant to the excluded media-specific brain-outcome model; no betas there. No media-specific SDs anywhere.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta / sqrt(1 - beta^2). If M1 betas were in fact unstandardized B (t-score points per hour), beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV would be required, and SD_IV for the individual media types is not reported.
d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (reported as beta; M3 explicitly standardized, M1/M2 standardization not stated)

Descriptive statistics per media type are not reported; Table 1 gives only total SMA (all six types including TV, videos and video games) at baseline, 3.530 +/- 2.896 hours. Parental education: primary school 24 (0.5%), high school or less 199 (4.4%), college 1469 (32.2%), higher than college 2865 (62.9%). The N for each media-specific model is not separately reported.

primary_models.dv: Parent-reported CBCL sex- and age-normed t-scores at the 3-year follow-up, three outcomes run separately: internalizing problems (anxious/depressed, withdrawn/depressed, somatic complaints), externalizing problems (rule breaking, aggressive behavior), and stress problems. primary_models.design: Longitudinal, two time points used for this model. Media-specific weekly-average screen time measured at baseline (age 9-10) predicts CBCL internalizing, externalizing and stress problem t-scores at the 3-year follow-up. One model per outcome, with each media type entered in separate media-specific models (the paper repeats the general-SMA linear mixed model replacing general SMA with media-specific SMA time). Outcome is a single follow-up, not repeated measures. Baseline CBCL is not listed as a covariate. No time x IV interaction.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Results, 'SMA's differential effect on mental health and the brain' (p. 6, right column, continuing from left column); method in 'Predicting mental health problems with baseline SMA' and 'Media-specific analysis' (p. 4). primary_models.equation: CBCL_DV_3y[i] = b0 + b1*SMA_mediatype_BL[i] + b2*age + b3*gender + b4*race + b5*household_income + b6*parental_education + b7*pubertal_level + u_site + u_family(site) + e[i]; fit separately for each media type and each of the three CBCL outcomes.
primary_models.estimation: Three-level linear mixed model (participants within families within sites). Software for the LMM not stated (R 4.3.2 and MATLAB R2022b are named for the CLPM and mediation analyses). No weights reported. Two-sided tests; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at q = 0.05 across all analyses, with pfdr reported. Only the significant media-specific estimates are printed in text; neither SE nor 95% CI is given for these media-specific LMM estimates. No sex or other interaction tests or stratified results reported. The authors interpret the general-SMA LMM beta as the change in t-score per additional screen hour (p. 6), but whether the media-specific betas are standardized is not stated.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) M1 and M2 never say whether the beta is standardized. For the general-SMA CLPM, the authors read beta = 0.03 as "per additional hour" (p. 6), which would mean an unstandardized slope. I coded beta_std because the mediation analysis is explicitly standardized and a per-hour effect of 0.03 t-points is implausibly small. A human should decide this. If the betas are unstandardized, d cannot be computed: the paper gives no SD for texting, social media or video chat (Table 1 has only the total SMA SD, 2.896). 2) All media-specific LMM (M1) and CLPM (M2) estimates appear only in the text. There are no CIs (M2 gives SEs, which I put in notes), and only significant or near-significant cells are printed. Five of the nine M1 cells (texting with internalizing and externalizing, all three video chat cells) are null and marked as implied non-significant. 3) Supplement Table S2 holds the media-specific SMA-to-brain estimates for texting, video chat and social media. It is not bundled in the PDF, so I did not extract them. Obtain the supplement and extract them. 4) The sd_dv values in M1 are baseline SDs from Table 1, not year-3 SDs. 5) M2 includes reverse paths where phone/SM is the DV (baseline externalizing to 2-year texting and social media). Those are cross-lagged, so they qualify, but a human should confirm. 6) The tables look internally inconsistent. Table 2 reports a direct effect of 0.676 for total SMA via CON-RTN on externalizing, which is implausible against the LMM beta of 0.058. Table 4 also lists one row with pfdr 0.5715, even though the table claims all rows are significant. This casts some doubt on how the mediation tables were reported. In M3, both the texting c' (0.035, Table 4) and the indirect a*b (0.005, Table 5) are extracted; the indirect effect should not be converted to d. 7) The N for each media-specific model and for the imaging mediation subsample is not reported (cohort N = 4557).json

533) says social media was significantly associated with self-harm and suicidal ideation among boys, but the adjusted Table 3 CIs include 1 (SI 1.22 [0.60, 2.45]; SH 1.83 [0.95, 3.51]); only the unadjusted rows are significant. I coded sig from the adjusted CIs. (2) The model is described only as a "univariate general linear model with covariates"; the link function, software, and clustering are not stated, so it is unclear whether these are true risk ratios. (3) No p-values are printed. sig = 95% CI excludes 1 (bold in the table). (4) Video chat is included as a qualifying phone/SM IV per FT-IC2, even though the authors leave it out of their "digital media" composite. It comes from Table 2, not Table 3. (5) M2 (any vs. no social media use) exists only in the text, with no table. I made it a separate card because the contrast is different. (6) dv_axis p0 is the gender-specific marginal prevalence from Table 1. Each estimate also has a non-standard field, p0_cell, holding the printed rate in the unexposed group. That is the better p0 for converting RR to OR, especially for video chat and M2, where exposure prevalence is 12-21%. The converter may need to be pointed at p0_cell. (7) Sex is coded on the DV axis (8 DV columns = 4 diagnoses x girls/boys). (8) Supplementary Figs. 1-4 (exposure-response curves) are not in the PDF but cover composites only. primary_models.iv: Binary indicator of spending 2 or more hours per day (coded 1) vs. less than 2 hours per day (coded 0) on one activity, analyzed one at a time: video chat ("video chat (Skype, Facetime, etc.)"), social media ("visit social networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, etc."), and texting ("Text on a cell phone, tablet, or computer (e.g., GChat, WhatsApp, etc.)"). Youth-reported ABCD screen time questionnaire, weekday and weekend items; responses coded none = 0, <30 min = 0.25, 30 min = 0.50, 1 h = 1, 2 h = 2, 3 h = 3, 4+ h = 4; daily average = (weekday x 5 + weekend x 2) / 7. 2 h/day cutoff follows AHA/AAP recommendations. Continuous hours/day M (SD), girls / boys (Table 1): video chat 0.79 (1.02) / 0.89 (1.07); social media 0.14 (0.45) / 0.09 (0.39); texting 0.26 (0.57) / 0.19 (0.50).
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2 (video chat column, Adjusted rows, pp. 532-533) and Table 3 (social media and texting columns, Adjusted rows, pp. 533-534); described in Results p. 532-533 and Discussion p. 534.
primary_models.estimation: Relative risk (adjusted relative risk, ARR) estimated with what the authors describe as a univariate general linear model with covariates; link function, error distribution, and software are not reported. No survey weights, no random effects or clustering for site or family reported. Alpha implied as .05 (95% CIs excluding 1 shown in bold); no p-values printed and no multiple-comparison correction. Analyses stratified by gender rather than testing gender interactions. No sensitivity analyses reported.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 2.0, baseline (first wave) data collected 2017-2018. N = 11,780 youth with valid data on the measures (girls n = 5633, boys n = 6147). Mean age 9.91 (SD 0.62); 48% female; 59% white, 9% Black, 19% Hispanic, 2% Asian, 10% other race or ethnicity. Adjusted-model ns are smaller than the full sample because of missing covariate data and vary by cell (e.g., girls social media 5004 vs. 79; boys social media 5445 vs. 60; girls texting 4951 vs. 132; boys texting 5403 vs. 102; girls video chat 4492 vs. 588; boys video chat 4729 vs. 769). Exclusion rules beyond complete data are not described. The proportion of youth at 2+ h/day was 1.7% of girls and 1.2% of boys for social media, 2.8% and 2.0% for texting, and 11.9% and 14.3% for video chat (Table 1).
primary_models.name: Gender-stratified adjusted relative-risk model of lifetime K-SADS-5 internalizing diagnoses on 2+ vs. <2 h/day of video chat, social media, or texting, adjusted for demographics
