primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit. Screen time and K-SADS-5 diagnoses measured at the same visit; diagnoses are lifetime (past or current), so temporal order is not established. One observation per child. Each screen activity and each diagnosis is analyzed in a separate model, separately for girls and boys.
primary_models.dv: Four binary lifetime DSM-5 diagnoses from the youth self-report computerized abbreviated K-SADS-5: depressive disorders, anxiety disorders (generalized and social anxiety sections), suicidal ideation or attempt, and non-suicidal self-injury (self-harm). Coded 1 if the youth met criteria in the past, currently, or currently in partial remission; 0 if never. Lifetime prevalence in Table 1 (girls / boys): depressive 4.8% / 5.3%; anxiety 1.4% / 1.3%; suicidal ideation or attempt 7.6% / 9.7%; self-harm 4.6% / 7.4%. Each diagnosis analyzed separately within each gender.

primary_models.equation: RR = P(diagnosis = 1 | IV = 2+ h/day, covariates) / P(diagnosis = 1 | IV = <2 h/day, covariates), estimated within each gender from: g(P(diagnosis[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*phoneSM_2plus[i] + b2*age + b3*race_nonwhite + b4*hispanic + b5*family_income + b6*caregiver_education + b7*caregiver_employment; ARR = exp(b1) under a log link. The paper does not state the link function; it describes the model as a univariate general linear model with covariates.

primary_models.iv: Binary social media use: any time on social networking sites (users, coded 1) vs. no time (non-users, coded 0), from the same youth-reported weekday/weekend social media item as M1 averaged to hours/day.
primary_models.estimation: Same as M1: adjusted relative risk from a univariate general linear model with covariates; software, link, and error distribution not reported; no weights, no clustering, no multiple-comparison correction; significance judged by 95% CI excluding 1.
primary_models.design: Same cross-sectional ABCD baseline analysis as M1, with the social media IV recoded as any use vs. no use because few children reached 2+ h/day. Separate models by diagnosis and by gender.
primary_models.sample: Same ABCD Release 2.0 baseline sample as M1. Adjusted analytic ns printed in text: girls 1081 users vs. 4002 non-users (4001 for suicidal ideation or attempt); boys 824 users vs. 4681 non-users (822 vs. 4680 for suicidal ideation or attempt).
primary_models.equation: g(P(diagnosis[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*SM_any[i] + b2*age + b3*race_nonwhite + b4*hispanic + b5*family_income + b6*caregiver_education + b7*caregiver_employment, within each gender; ARR = exp(b1) under a log link (link not stated in the paper).
primary_models.dv: Four binary lifetime DSM-5 diagnoses from the youth self-report computerized abbreviated K-SADS-5: depressive disorders, anxiety disorders (generalized and social anxiety sections), suicidal ideation or attempt, and non-suicidal self-injury (self-harm). Coded 1 if the youth met criteria in the past, currently, or currently in partial remission; 0 if never. Lifetime prevalence in Table 1 (girls / boys): depressive 4.8% / 5.3%; anxiety 1.4% / 1.3%; suicidal ideation or attempt 7.6% / 9.7%; self-harm 4.6% / 7.4%. Each diagnosis analyzed separately within each gender.
primary_models.name: Gender-stratified adjusted relative-risk model of lifetime K-SADS-5 internalizing diagnoses on any vs. no social media use, adjusted for demographics

d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR = RR * (1 - p0) / (1 - RR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000). Apply to RR, RR_lo, RR_hi.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: 2+ h/day vs. <2 h/day of the activity (binary group contrast). M2: any social media use vs. none.
d_transformation.notes: p0 in dv_axis is the gender-specific lifetime prevalence of each diagnosis from Table 1 (p. 532): depressive 0.048 girls / 0.053 boys; anxiety 0.014 / 0.013; suicidal ideation or attempt 0.076 / 0.097; self-harm 0.046 / 0.074. Exposure prevalence is low for social media and texting (1.2-2.8%) so the marginal rate approximates the unexposed rate, but for video chat (11.9-14.3% exposed) and M2 social media users (about 16-21% of the analytic n) the marginal rate is less exact. Each estimate also carries p0_cell, the unexposed-group rate printed in the adjusted row of Tables 2-3 (or in text for M2); this is the preferred p0 for the conversion. SD_IV and SD_DV are not needed because both IV and DV are binary. These d values reflect a high-vs-low group contrast, not a per-SD or per-hour slope, and are not directly comparable to continuous-IV d's from other papers. The authors do not state the link function; ARR is treated as a ratio of risks. Completion pass (2026-10-01): each estimate now carries p0 (= p0_cell, the unexposed-group rate from the adjusted row) and group sizes n1/n0. All RR CIs are printed; no SE/p are printed.

primary_models.design: Prediction (classification) design using ABCD prepandemic data plus the ABCD COVID-19 Rapid Response surveys. Prepandemic predictors (CBCL externalizing, BPM internalizing, Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children, Munich Chronotype Questionnaire) come from the Year 2 assessment, with change scores Baseline to Year 1 and Year 1 to Year 2 for sleep subscales; demographics from the prepandemic baseline year. Pandemic predictors (>200 youth- and parent-reported psychosocial and lifestyle items, including screen-time items) and outcomes come from the same COVID-19 survey, so pandemic features and outcomes are cross-sectional. Separate models per outcome: positive affect, perceived stress and anxiety from Survey 2; depressive symptoms from Survey 1 (and from Survey 3 in Supplementary Figure A4, not in this PDF). Surveys were administered approximately 40 days apart between May and August 2020. Not a repeated-measures model; each outcome-survey combination is fit as its own classifier.
primary_models.name: XGBoost gradient-boosted tree classifiers of binary pandemic mental-health outcomes on ~230 prepandemic and pandemic features, with mean |SHAP| feature importance (texting and online-communication features)
primary_models.equation: logit P(Y_outcome = 1) = F(x) = sum_k f_k(x), f_k = regression trees fit by extreme gradient boosting on all retained features x (including texting / on-line communication); importance_j = mean over participants of |phi_j(i)|, where phi_j(i) is the TreeSHAP contribution of feature j to participant i's predicted log-odds
primary_models.estimation: XGBoost gradient-boosted trees (GBT) implemented in Python 3.6.8 with scikit-learn 18.2; regularized logistic regression fit in parallel for comparison. Hyperparameters chosen by grid search, aiming for interpretability by limiting model complexity. Model comparison by nested cross-validation, evaluated with AUC; mean AUC >= 0.70 for both GBT and LogReg in all four outcomes (Table A1, supplementary, not in this PDF). Because GBT performed higher or roughly equal, the final GBT models were refit on the entire dataset with the best hyperparameters and interpreted with SHAP values (mean absolute SHAP in log-odds units). Only the top 20 features per model are printed; bar colour indicates direction (red: higher feature values associated with higher SHAP scores, i.e., higher predicted probability of the elevated outcome; blue: lower). No significance tests, confidence intervals, sampling weights, clustering by site/family, or multiple-comparison correction apply. Models were not stratified by sex.

primary_models.sample: ABCD 3.0 data release, participants who completed the Year 2 assessment by February 2020 and the COVID-19 youth surveys (May-August 2020). Respondents with <65% survey completion for both youth and parent report were removed (~20% of youth data and ~7% of parent data excluded; Appendix A). Table 1 analytic subsets: Survey 1 N=3,091 (mean age 12.86, range 11-14; 49.3% female; race 80.2% White, 6.8% Black, 5.5% Asian, 0.8% multiracial, 5.4% other, 1.0% unknown; 16.5% Hispanic/Latino), Survey 2 N=3,193 (mean age 12.94; 48.9% female; 78.9% White, 8.3% Black, 5.3% Asian; 16.3% Hispanic/Latino), Survey 3 N=2,934 (mean age 13.05; 48.9% female). Model-specific n from figure captions: positive affect n=2,896 (Fig. 1); stress n=3,193 (Fig. 2); anxiety n=3,193 (Fig. 3); depressive symptoms Survey 1 n=3,063 (Fig. 4B). Compared with the full ABCD baseline sample, the subsample was less Hispanic/Latino, less Black, more Asian, and had more highly educated parents (42% vs. 34% postgraduate degree).

primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Screen time (IV) measured at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10); OCD diagnosis (DV) measured at the 2-year follow-up (2018-2020, ages 11-12). primary_models.dv: Binary OCD diagnosis at the 2-year follow-up from the caregiver-completed computerized KSADS-5, scored to DSM-5 criteria: presence of obsessions or compulsions plus at least one of time-consuming obsessions, time-consuming compulsions, impairment, or distress. With baseline OCD cases excluded, a positive outcome is new-onset OCD. Results text: 6.1% of the sample met OCD criteria at year 2 and 4.4% developed new-onset OCD from baseline to year 2 (denominator not stated; appears to be the 9,208 sample).
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3, Model 3 (p. 394); reported in Results p. 392 and Abstract; interpreted in Discussion pp. 392-394 (texting, video chat and social media discussed as nonsignificant on p. 394).
primary_models.iv: Baseline self-reported hours per day of each screen modality from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (typical hours per day on weekdays and weekends). Weighted daily average = (weekday x 5 + weekend x 2) / 7, entered as a continuous variable in hours/day. Qualifying modalities: texting; video chatting (e.g., Skype, FaceTime); social media/social networking (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). Baseline means (SD) in the Model 3 sample (Table 1, No OCD baseline column, n = 8,542): texting 0.21 (0.43); video chat 0.19 (0.48); social networking 0.11 (0.40) hours/day. Each modality is a separate IV; the OR is per additional hour per day.
primary_models.estimation: Multiple logistic regression in Stata 15.1. Propensity weights applied to yield estimates representative of the American Community Survey. Site entered as a covariate; no clustering or random effects for site or family described. Significance at p < .05 (bold in Table 3). No multiple-comparison correction reported across the 7 screen modalities. No interaction or stratified analyses reported. Model 1 (unadjusted, n = 9,208) and Model 2 (adjusted plus baseline OCD as covariate, n = 9,208) reported alongside in Table 3; the Abstract and Results anchor the reported aORs to Model 3, stating findings were mostly similar to Model 2.
primary_models.equation: logit(P(OCD_Y2[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*phoneSM_hours[i] + b2..b6*race_ethnicity + b7*sex + b8..b12*income + b13*parent_ed + b14..b33*site + b34*baseline_MDD + b35*family_history_psychopathology (+ b36*age, per Statistical analysis text), estimated among participants without OCD at baseline, with ACS propensity weights. OR = exp(b1) per additional hour/day; phoneSM_hours is texting, video chat, or social networking in separate models.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0, 21 U.S. sites. Of 11,875 enrolled, 2,667 were excluded for missing screen time, OCD or confounder data, leaving 9,208; Model 3 further excludes the 666 participants with OCD at baseline, giving analytic N = 8,542. Table 1 (No OCD baseline column, n = 8,542): age mean 9.93 (SD 0.63); 49.7% female, 50.3% male; White 56.9%, Latino/Hispanic 18.5%, Black 14.9%, Asian 5.3%, Native American 3.0%, Other 1.4%; parent with college education or more 84.4%; baseline major depressive disorder 0.2%; family history of psychopathology 58.9%. Full 9,208 sample: 48.9% female, White 56.5% (Abstract says 43.5% non-White; Results text says 47.8% non-White). Table 1 percentages are propensity weighted.

primary_models.location_in_paper: Supplementary Table A7 (online supplement only; not bundled in the local PDF). Described in Discussion p. 501, right column: exploratory analyses of weekend screen-time categories and withdrawn/depressed symptoms, reported as not associated.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0 (September 2021), baseline and one-year follow-up, collected before the COVID-19 pandemic. Main analytic N = 10,828 with complete exposure and outcome data at both time points and complete baseline covariates; 243 youth reporting >18 h/day total screen time on weekdays or weekends were removed beforehand. Analyses stratified by gender: females N = 5,177, males N = 5,651 (gender queer N = 2 and different gender N = 4 not analyzed). Mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6) at baseline; 54.3% non-Hispanic White, 19.8% Hispanic, 13.3% non-Hispanic Black, 10.4% other/mixed race, 2.2% non-Hispanic Asian (Table 1). The N for Table A7 is not known from the PDF; the Discussion context suggests females (N = 5,177).
primary_models.name: Exploratory multilevel logistic regression of follow-up withdrawn/depressed symptoms (CBCL t >= 65) on baseline weekend screen-time categories, including texting, video chatting and social networking (supplementary Table A7; values not in the available PDF)
primary_models.iv: Baseline weekend screen time by category from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, youth self-report of usual hours/day for six screen types (TV shows or movies; watching/streaming videos such as YouTube; videogames; texting; video chatting; social networking sites), with response options none, <30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, 3 hours, 4+ hours. Only texting, video chatting and social networking qualify as phone/SM IVs here; the TV, video and videogame categories are excluded below. How each category was coded in Table A7 (hours/day continuous or dichotomized) is not stated in the PDF. No per-category descriptive statistics are printed in the main text.
primary_models.estimation: Multilevel logistic regression with study site as a random effect, SAS GLIMMIX procedure, SAS version 9.4. All analyses performed separately by gender a priori. No multiple-comparison correction reported; significance flagged at p < .05. Main models: sleep duration, weekday and weekend screen time as simultaneous predictors; sleep x screen-time interactions tested and not significant. Sensitivity analyses (survey-weighted SAS SURVEYLOGISTIC with ACS-raked weights, Tables A1-A2; pubertal status instead of age, Tables A3-A4; continuous CBCL t-scores, Tables A5-A6) all use the total screen time composite.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal, two waves. Baseline (ABCD Y0, age ~9.9) weekend screen-time category predicts withdrawn/depressed symptoms at the one-year follow-up (Y1, age ~10.9). Single follow-up outcome, not repeated measures. The exploratory analysis was run to unpack the main finding that >2 h/day of total weekend screen time predicted withdrawn/depressed symptoms in females (Table 3). The Discussion does not state whether the A7 models were female-only, gender-stratified, adjusted, or whether categories entered separately or simultaneously; all of this needs checking against Table A7.
primary_models.dv: Withdrawn/depressed symptoms at one-year follow-up, caregiver-reported CBCL/4-18 subscale t-score (mean 50, SD 10), dichotomized at >= 65 (borderline clinical and above, at or above the 93rd percentile) vs < 65. Follow-up prevalence: females 282 (5.5%), males 550 (9.7%); baseline prevalence females 236 (4.6%), males 529 (9.4%) (Table 2).
primary_models.iv_type_note: Not set: coding of weekend texting/video chat/SNS in Supplementary Table A7 (hours/day continuous, ordinal categories, or dichotomized at a threshold) is not stated anywhere in the article PDF (Methods p.498 describes only the summed total screen time dichotomized at >2 h/day). Set after reading Table A7.
primary_models.equation: logit(P(WithDep_t65[i, Y1] = 1)) = b0 + b1*WeekendCategory[i, Y0] + (b2*SleepDuration[i, Y0]) + b3*WithDep_t65[i, Y0] + b4*age + b5..b8*race/ethnicity + b9..b12*income-to-needs + b13*overweight/obesity + b14*physical_activity + u_site(i) + e[i]. Covariate set is taken from the main adjusted models and is unconfirmed for Table A7; whether the screen categories enter one at a time or jointly is unknown.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) Which IVs count as phone/SM. I included 'Talk on the phone or text', 'Spend time online on social media', the three phone-action categories (ringer silent/vibrate, ringer on, phone outside room, each vs. turning the phone off) and 'Woken up by phone calls, text messages, or e-mails'. The phone-action and woken-by items are phone-specific but are not texting/SM time as such, so please check they belong. I excluded 'Spend time in chat rooms' (not on the FT-IC2 list, device not specified) and 'Used phone or other device when woke up during the night' (bundles other devices and mixed activities). Both are borderline; their numbers are recorded in excluded_models. 2) The IV coding is unclear. Methods describe a 1-5 Likert scale, but Table 2 shows four night-count categories, so 'per one step' is ambiguous. The paper also does not say whether each exposure was fit in its own model or entered jointly. 3) No SDs are reported for any IV, so the M3 (linear, sleep duration) frequency-item cells cannot be converted to d. The phone-action dummies are converted with B/1.62, using the total-sample SD rather than the pooled SD. 4) M2 reports raw ordered-logit coefficients (log-odds) labelled B, not ORs. I stored them in the value fields and convert them with B*sqrt(3)/pi. 5) The DV is called 'weekly sleep duration', but Table 1 gives it in hours per night (SD 1.62). 6) Appendices A-D (supplement) are not in the PDF. Appendices C and D are described only in the text, and the supplement may hold extra phone/SM numbers. 7) The ABCD release version is not stated. pdftotext drops non-bold minus signs, so every sign was checked against a 220-dpi render of Table 3. For p shown as '< .001', p is set to null and only p_label is kept.

primary_models.design: Prospective cohort, two waves. Bedtime screen behaviors measured at Year 2; sleep outcome measured at Year 3 (one year later), adjusting for the same sleep variable at Year 2. One observation per participant; no repeated-measures structure, no time interaction.
primary_models.iv: Phone/SM bedtime behaviors from the ABCD Screen Usage Around Bedtime measure, youth self-report at Year 2 (Table 2, p. 653). (a) 'What do you usually do with your phone when you are ready to go to sleep?' entered as a categorical variable: turn the phone off (reference, 54.9%), put the ringer on silent or vibrate (18.4%), leave the ringer on (11.2%), put it outside of the room where I sleep (15.5%). (b) Past-week frequency of 'Talk on the phone or text' and 'Spend time online on social media (e.g., Facebook)' while already in bed before going to sleep. Methods describe a five-point Likert scale from 1 (never) to 5 (every night), but Table 2 tabulates four categories (0, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights); one coefficient per item is reported, implying the item was entered as a single ordinal/continuous term (per one-step increase), but the exact coding is not stated. Distribution: talk/text 66.7% 0 nights, 19.6% 1-2, 7.4% 3-4, 6.3% 5-7; social media 70.1%, 16.5%, 7.1%, 6.2%. (c) 'In the past week, how often have you had phone calls, text messages, or e-mails that wake you up after trying to go to sleep?' (83.8% 0, 10.6% 1-2, 3.4% 3-4, 2.2% 5-7 nights), same coding caveat. No means or SDs reported for any IV. Each exposure appears as its own row in Table 3; the paper does not state whether exposures were entered in separate models or jointly.
primary_models.name: Weighted logistic regression of binary total sleep disturbance (Year 3) on Year 2 bedtime phone/SM behaviors, adjusted for Year 2 sleep disturbance and sociodemographic/clinical covariates
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18 (StataCorp). ABCD propensity weights based on the American Community Survey applied. Study site entered as a covariate; no random effects or family clustering described. Significance at p < .05 (bold in Table 3); no multiple-comparison correction reported. No interaction or stratified analyses reported. Binary logistic regression; ORs with 95% CIs reported. A supplemental ordinal logistic model on the total sleep disturbance score (Appendix D) is described only narratively.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3, 'Total sleep disturbance' OR column (p. 654); Results p. 652-653; Discussion p. 653
primary_models.equation: logit(P(SleepDisturbance_Y3[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*PhoneSM_Y2[i] (or b1a..b1c for the three phone-action dummies) + b2*SleepDisturbance_Y2 + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race/ethnicity + b10*income + b11*parent_ed + b12*ACEs + b13*CBCL_depression + b14*melatonin + b15..*site dummies; weighted by ABCD ACS propensity weights
primary_models.iv_type_note: Mixed IVs in this model: phone-action rows are categorical dummies vs. 'turn the phone off' (estimate-level iv_type='categorical'); talk/text, social media and woken-by-phone rows are single per-step frequency terms (continuous). Model-level set to 'continuous' conservatively; estimate-level iv_type overrides.
primary_models.dv: Total sleep disturbance at Year 3, caregiver-reported 26-item Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (each item 1 never to 5 daily, past six months), summed and binarized at the clinical cutoff of 39. 25.5% of the analytic sample met the cutoff at Year 3 (Table 1). Year 2 binary total sleep disturbance enters as a covariate.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (release not stated in the paper), Year 2 follow-up (2018-2020) used for exposures and Year 3 (2019-2021) for outcomes. Analytic N = 9,398 participants with complete data; 2,564 of the 11,875 baseline participants were excluded (comparison of included vs. excluded in Appendix A, not bundled in the PDF). Year 2 mean age 12.02 (SD 0.66). 48.4% female, 51.6% male. Race/ethnicity: 54.9% White, 19.6% Latino/Hispanic, 15.4% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.1% Native American, 1.4% Other. Household income: 15.9% <$25K, 19.9% $25-50K, 18.0% $50-75K, 14.2% $75-100K, 24.3% $100-200K, 7.7% >=$200K. Parent education: 17.5% high school or less, 82.5% college or more. Mean ACEs 1.84 (SD 1.70); mean CBCL depression t-score at Year 2 53.89 (SD 6.07); melatonin use at Year 2 4.4% (Table 1, p. 652). Same N printed for all Table 3 cells.

primary_models.iv: Phone/SM bedtime behaviors from the ABCD Screen Usage Around Bedtime measure, youth self-report at Year 2 (Table 2, p. 653). (a) 'What do you usually do with your phone when you are ready to go to sleep?' entered as a categorical variable: turn the phone off (reference, 54.9%), put the ringer on silent or vibrate (18.4%), leave the ringer on (11.2%), put it outside of the room where I sleep (15.5%). (b) Past-week frequency of 'Talk on the phone or text' and 'Spend time online on social media (e.g., Facebook)' while already in bed before going to sleep. Methods describe a five-point Likert scale from 1 (never) to 5 (every night), but Table 2 tabulates four categories (0, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights); one coefficient per item is reported, implying the item was entered as a single ordinal/continuous term (per one-step increase), but the exact coding is not stated. Distribution: talk/text 66.7% 0 nights, 19.6% 1-2, 7.4% 3-4, 6.3% 5-7; social media 70.1%, 16.5%, 7.1%, 6.2%. (c) 'In the past week, how often have you had phone calls, text messages, or e-mails that wake you up after trying to go to sleep?' (83.8% 0, 10.6% 1-2, 3.4% 3-4, 2.2% 5-7 nights), same coding caveat. No means or SDs reported for any IV. Each exposure appears as its own row in Table 3; the paper does not state whether exposures were entered in separate models or jointly.

d_transformation.native_metric: OR (M1); ordered-logit coefficient on log-odds scale (M2); unstandardized B in hours (M3)
d_transformation.notes: M1 (OR) and M2 (ordered-logit B) convert to d without SDs. p0 for M1 = 0.255 is the Year 3 marginal rate of total sleep disturbance (Table 1, p. 652); not needed for OR conversion. SD_DV for M3 = 1.62 h (Table 1, 'Sleep duration at Year 3 (hours per night)'); M3 phone-action dummy cells convertible via B/SD_DV (uses total-sample SD in place of pooled within-group SD). M3 frequency-item cells (talk/text, social media, woken by calls/texts) are not convertible from reported statistics because the paper gives no mean/SD for the items; SD could be approximated from the Table 2 category percentages only under an assumed coding, which was not done. ABCD propensity weights used throughout. [complete-stage check 2026-10-01] Re-read full PDF (6 pp.). All 18 native values and 95% CIs present and verified against Table 3 p.654. No SEs, t/z, or exact p for '< .001' cells printed. No SD for any bedtime-frequency item (sd_iv) printed; M3 frequency cells remain non-convertible. Supplement (Appendices A-D) not bundled.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000). M2: OR = exp(B); d = B * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn applied to the proportional-odds OR). M3, phone-action dummies (binary contrast vs. phone off): d ~= B / SD_DV with SD_DV = 1.62. M3, frequency items: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein 2009 eq 7.1), requires SD_IV which is not reported.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Phone-action rows: each category vs. 'turn the phone off'. Talk/text, social media and woken-by-phone rows: per one-step increase on the bedtime frequency item (coding not explicitly stated; Likert 1-5 per Methods vs. 4 night-count categories in Table 2).

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Categorical (dummy-coded group) IV on continuous DV: d = B / SD_DV, i.e., adjusted mean difference between the trajectory group and the no/very low use reference divided by the DV SD; applied to B_lo and B_hi for the CI.
d_transformation.notes: SD_DV taken from Table 1 (p. 5) Year 2 cognitive performance measures for the full analytic sample (N = 7528): LMT accuracy 0.2, RAVLT Initial Learning Trials 9.1, RAVLT Retroactive Interference 2.7, RAVLT Long Delay 2.9. These are total-sample SDs, not pooled within-group SDs, and Table 1 notes weighted estimates, so d is approximate. The LMT SD is printed to one decimal (0.2) and B to two decimals, so derived d for LMT is coarse (e.g., -0.03/0.2 = -0.15). Because the model adjusts for the baseline score of the same test, B is a residualized (change-like) adjusted difference; dividing by the raw Year 2 SD gives a d on the outcome scale. SD_IV is not applicable (categorical IV). [complete stage] Verified all 8 B, 95% CI and P values against Table 2 p.6, Abstract p.1 and Results p.5; all agree. No SE printed anywhere; CIs are complete so not needed. Group sizes (n1/n0) added from Table 2 row labels. No supplementary file available in docs/pdfs.

papers.title: Associations of adolescent social media use trajectories with spatial and verbal memory: a prospective cohort study
papers.extraction_flags: The IV is a 3-group trajectory from a group-based trajectory model (GBTM), not hours per day, so d = B / SD_DV is a group contrast. SD_DV values are the Year 2 total-sample SDs from Table 1 (LMT 0.2, RAVLT 9.1 / 2.7 / 2.9), not pooled within-group SDs. The LMT SD is printed to only one decimal, so its d is coarse. The model adjusts for the baseline score on the same test, so B is a residualized difference. The trajectory window (baseline to Year 2) overlaps the Year 2 outcome wave. The Research-in-context panel says N = 7582, which conflicts with the N = 7528 used everywhere else. The supplement (Tables S1-S4) is not bundled in the PDF, so it is unverified whether Table S4 contains any sex-stratified social media estimates; the text and limitations suggest it does not. Software for the regression stage is not stated separately (GBTM is Stata 18.0). All 8 Table 2 values were checked against the pdftotext extraction.json

primary_models.iv: Social media time trajectory group (3 categories) from GBTM. Underlying measure: ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey item for hours per day on social media (e.g., Instagram, Facebook, Twitter), reported separately for weekdays and weekends and combined as ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2])/7 hours/day, at baseline, Year 1 and Year 2. GBTM fit in Stata 18.0 'traj'; best model by BIC was a sex-adjusted three-group solution (one linear and two cubic trajectories; Table S2). Groups: no/very low use (reference; n = 4289, 54.7%; about 0.1 h/day by age 13; legend '+0.1 hours/day' change baseline to Year 2), low increasing use (n = 2822, 38.8%; about 0.8 h/day by age 13; '+0.8 hours/day'), high increasing use (n = 417, 6.4%; about 3.1 h/day by age 13; '+3.1 hours/day'). Dummy coded against the no/very low use group.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1. Of 11,962 baseline participants, excluded those missing Youth Screen Time Survey from baseline to Year 2 (n = 2333), cognition assessments at baseline and Year 2 (n = 1372), baseline mental health (n = 1) and baseline sociodemographics (n = 728), giving analytic N = 7528 (Figure S1; included vs excluded compared in Table S1, excluded more often racial/ethnic minority, lower income, lower parent education). Mean baseline age 10.0 years (SD 0.6); 48.9% (3617) female, 51.1% (3911) male. Race/ethnicity: 58.2% White (4350), 14.2% Black (1240), 18.1% Latino/Hispanic (1159), 5.3% Asian (455), 3.1% Native American (267), 1.1% other (57). Parent education college or more 85.3%. Counts unweighted; analyses weighted to the American Community Survey. The 'Research in context' panel states N = 7582, which conflicts with the 7528 used everywhere else.

primary_models.dv: Four Year 2 cognitive scores from the ABCD neurocognitive battery: (1) Little Man Task (LMT) accuracy, proportion correct over 32 trials (0-1), visuospatial attention/mental rotation; Year 2 mean 0.7 (SD 0.2). (2) RAVLT Initial Learning Trials, total words recalled over five learning trials of a 15-word list (0-75); Year 2 mean 44.2 (SD 9.1). (3) RAVLT Retroactive Interference (short delay recall after distractor list), 0-15; Year 2 mean 9.7 (SD 2.7). (4) RAVLT Long Delay (30-min) recall, 0-15; Year 2 mean 9.1 (SD 2.9).
primary_models.equation: Cog_Y2[i] = b0 + b1*LowIncreasing[i] + b2*HighIncreasing[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..*race_ethnicity + b..*income + b..*parent_ed + b..*CBCL_ADHD + b..*CBCL_depression + b..*nonSM_screen_time + b..*Cog_baseline[i] + b..*site + e[i], with no/very low use as the reference trajectory; weighted by ACS-based sampling weights. b1 and b2 are adjusted mean differences in the Year 2 score relative to the no/very low use group.
primary_models.name: Weighted multiple linear regression of Year 2 cognitive performance (LMT, RAVLT) on baseline-Year 2 social media time trajectory group, adjusted for baseline cognition and sociodemographic, mental health and non-social media screen time covariates
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort, two-stage analysis. Stage 1: group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) of average daily social media hours across three waves (baseline 2016-2018, Year 1 2017-2019, Year 2 2018-2020) classified each participant into one of three trajectory groups. Stage 2: the trajectory group (spanning baseline to Year 2) is the IV and cognitive performance at Year 2 is the DV, with the respective baseline cognitive score entered as a covariate. One Year 2 outcome per participant; no repeated-measures DV and no time interaction. Note that the IV window overlaps the DV wave (Year 2 social media time is part of the trajectory).
primary_models.estimation: Multiple linear regression in Stata (GBTM in Stata 18.0 'traj'; the regression software is not stated separately). ABCD sampling weights approximating the American Community Survey applied to all analyses. Site entered as a covariate; no random effects or family clustering described. Two-sided tests, alpha = 0.05; Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, with bold in Table 2 marking significance after correction. Sex-stratified descriptive cognitive scores are mentioned (Table S4, supplement not in the PDF) but no sex- or race-stratified regressions were run; limitations note small subgroup sizes prevented this. No interaction tests reported.

d_transformation.native_metric: Standardized beta x 100 (beta_std scaled by 100), with SEM
d_transformation.notes: Only SE (SEM) is printed, no CIs, so d CIs cannot be derived without computing from SE (not done here). DV is z-scored thickness (SD_DV = 1 by construction, Table 2 header). SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 3): social media time SD = 1.5 h/day; SMAQ SD = 0.8. The paper calls these 'standardized beta coefficients' (Results p. 4, Fig. 1 caption, Discussion p. 7: 'standardized beta coefficients ... ranged from -0.051 to -0.026'), consistent with a fully standardized metric, but Methods do not state the IV was z-scored. All effects are small (|beta_std| <= 0.051). [complete stage] Every estimate now carries 'se' (SEM printed in Table 2 as value +/- SEM, same x100 scale; volume estimate SE = 0.931 from Results 3.1 text) and exact raw p, so CIs on beta and d can be derived as value +/- 1.96*se. N = 7,614 (Table 1). SD_DV = 1 (z-scored thickness); SD_IV in iv_axis from Table 1 (1.5 h/day; 0.8 SMAQ). No supplement bundled; article p.8 says supplementary material is online only (Supplemental Figures A.1-A.3 are not in the PDF). Fig. 1B bars are the same SM-time coefficients /100 (unlabelled bars, not used).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = value / 100; treat beta_std as approximate r; d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009). If coders determine the IV was not standardized (i.e., coefficient is change in z-thickness per 1 h/day or per 1 SMAQ point), use beta_std = (value/100) * SD_IV / SD_DV with SD_DV = 1.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of the social media variable (assuming fully standardized beta)

primary_models.name: Generalized additive mixed model (gamm4) of z-scored ROI cortical thickness on daily social media hours or social media addiction score, adjusted for demographics, SES, genetic ancestry, non-SM screen time and scanner, family random effect
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2 (p. 4) for all ROI cortical thickness estimates; Fig. 1 (p. 5) plots the same social media time coefficients; right-hemisphere cortical volume estimate in Results 3.1 text (p. 4). Methods 2.4 and 2.6.1 (p. 3); interpreted in Discussion pp. 6-7.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study 6.0 release, Year 2 visit, 21 U.S. sites. Of 10,973 participants, 8,059 had sMRI, 7,866 passed the ABCD recommended imaging inclusion criteria, and 7,614 remained after removing missing covariates (age, sex, race, caregiver partnership, household income, caregiver education, non-SM screen time, genetic ancestry). Mean age 12.0 (SD 0.7); 53.3% male, 46.7% female. Race: White 69.0%, Black 14.1%, more than one race 11.0%, Asian 1.8%, Native American/Alaska Native 0.5%, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander 0.2%, other/not reported 3.4%. Household income: 31.7% $100,000-$199,999, 12.8% >= $200,000, 10.0% <= $24,999. Caregiver education: 33.4% graduate/professional degree. 75.1% partnered caregivers.
primary_models.estimation: R 4.4.2, gamm4 package (generalized additive mixed model); family ID random effect. No survey weights reported. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across ROIs; significance in Table 2 shown at Q < 0.05 (dark shading), with raw p < 0.05 shown in light shading. No interaction or stratified analyses. Sensitivity analysis adding CBCL ADHD T-score as a covariate reported only for vertexwise maps (Supplemental Figure A.3, not in this PDF); authors state the ROI relationships persisted after adjusting for ADHD score (Discussion p. 7) but no numbers are printed. A complementary vertexwise FEMA analysis (MATLAB R2025a) with the same fixed and random effects is shown only as Z-score maps (Fig. 2).
primary_models.iv: Two IVs, each in its own model. (1) Social media time: ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey item asking hours and minutes per day on social media (e.g., Instagram, Facebook, Twitter), reported separately for a typical weekday and weekend day; daily average = (weekday*5 + weekend*2)/7; 14 participants winsorized at 16 h/day. Mean 0.6 h/day (SD 1.5) (Table 1). (2) Social media addiction: six-item Social Media Addiction Questionnaire adapted from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, 1 (Never) to 6 (Very often), averaged across items; youth with no social media account assigned 1. Mean 1.4 (SD 0.8) (Table 1). The paper describes the coefficients as standardized betas; whether the IV itself was z-scored is not stated explicitly in Methods.
primary_models.equation: z_thickness_ROI,hemi[i] = b0 + b1*SM[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4..*race + b..*PC1..PC10 + b*caregiver_partnership + b..*income + b..*caregiver_education + b*nonSM_screen_time + b..*scanner_serial + b..*scanner_software + u_family(i) + e[i], where SM is either daily social media hours or social media addiction score (separate models). Table 2 reports 100*b1 (standardized).

primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Social media use, social media addiction, and structural MRI all come from the ABCD Year 2 follow-up visit (2018-2020, ages 10-13). One observation per participant. Social media time and social media addiction were entered in separate models (Spearman rho = 0.67 between them) to avoid collinearity. Each ROI-by-hemisphere measure is a separate dependent variable; the paper also fit the same models to cortical surface area, cortical volume and subcortical volume ROIs, but only the thickness results are tabulated.
primary_models.dv: FreeSurfer 7.1.1 (ABCD 6.0 tabulated data) cortical thickness for the 34 Desikan-Killiany ROIs in each hemisphere plus whole-hemisphere 'All Cortical Gray Matter' thickness, z-scored (Table 2 column header: 'mean z-scored thickness'). One further in-text estimate uses right-hemisphere total cortical volume. Surface area, other volume and subcortical volume ROI results are not printed.

papers.extraction_flags: The single qualifying estimate is the adjusted RR 1.09 (1.00-1.19), p = 0.049, in Table 2. The IV is checking COVID-related information on social media "almost every hour or more" versus less often. It is not general social media time, so a coder should confirm it counts as a phone/SM modality under FT-IC2. The DV "always masking" was taken to mean the "all the time last week" response (62.3%), but the paper never states the cut explicitly. p0 = 0.623 is the weighted marginal rate for the whole sample; the rate in the unexposed group is not reported. Exposure prevalence is 9.1%, close to the 10% threshold, and the high base rate makes the RR-to-OR conversion sensitive to p0. The question wording, the response options and the included/excluded comparison are in an online Supplemental Appendix that is not bundled in the PDF. Site was adjusted for, but the paper does not say how it was modelled. The other information-source variables (internet/YouTube, TV, parent counseling) were excluded as non-phone/SM; they enter the model as mutual covariates.

primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Single wave: the December 2020 ABCD COVID-19 Rapid Response Research survey. IV (adolescent self-reported frequency of checking COVID-related information on social media in the past week) and DV (adolescent self-reported masking in the last week) were collected in the same survey. One observation per adolescent; no repeated measures. Sociodemographic confounders were taken from the baseline parent survey. All four information-source variables (social media, internet, television, parent counseling) enter the same adjusted model, so the social media ARR is adjusted for the other three.
primary_models.dv: Always masking: binary indicator derived from the adolescent item 'I wear a mask over my face or protective gear (e.g. gloves, things to cover my clothes)' in the last week. Response distribution (Table 1, weighted): have not done this 4.3%, some of the time 12.0%, most of the time 21.5%, all the time 62.3%. The outcome 'always masking' corresponds to 'all the time last week' (62.3%); the comparison category is the other three responses. The paper does not explicitly state the cut, but Table 2 is labelled 'Always masking' and the text equates it with wearing masks all the time.

primary_models.sample: ABCD COVID-19 Rapid Response Research Release, December 2020 survey. Analytic N = 4,106 adolescents aged 12-14 years (35% response rate among ABCD participants invited). 50.6% female, 49.4% male; 60.5% White, 16.7% Latino/Hispanic, 11.3% Black, 8.2% Asian, 2.1% Native American, 1.2% Other (39.5% racial/ethnic minorities). Household income <$75,000 47.7%, >=$75,000 52.3%. Parent highest education high school or less 12.8%, college or more 87.2%. Schooling in past week: online/school-at-home 65.2%, in person 15.9%, hybrid 13.3%, other 5.7%. Parent-reported child COVID-19 diagnosis 4.4%. Percentages in Table 1 are ABCD propensity-weighted. Included vs excluded participant characteristics are in the Supplemental Appendix (not bundled in this PDF); the authors note responders were more likely to be White, female and higher SES.

d_transformation.notes: p0 = 0.623 is the propensity-weighted proportion of the whole analytic sample reporting wearing a mask/protective gear 'all the time last week' (Table 1, p. 2). The outcome rate in the unexposed (less-than-hourly) group is not reported; because exposure prevalence is 9.1% (Table 1), the marginal rate is used as an approximation per guidelines §4a, but 9.1% is near the ~10% threshold and the base rate is high (62%), so the RR-to-OR conversion is sensitive to p0. The RR is also covariate-adjusted and weighted, while p0 is a crude weighted marginal rate. The resulting d is a binary-contrast effect and is not directly comparable to per-1-SD d's from continuous-IV papers. The IV is COVID-information checking on social media, not general social media time. Complete-stage check: whole PDF re-read; no unexposed-group masking rate, SE, or group n printed; marginal p0 approximation retained.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a). Alternative from raw B: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV, then the same formula.
d_transformation.notes: The paper prints standardized betas directly in Table 3 (p. 6), so d can be derived without SDs. No CIs or SEs are printed in the table, so d CIs cannot be computed from the table; Fig. 1 (p. 7) plots 95% CIs for M2 betas but these were not read off the figure. sd_iv for M1 is the grand (all-observation) SD from Table 2 (p. 5); sd_iv for M2 between-person terms is the participant-mean SD from Table 2; the within-person deviation SD is not reported (null). sd_dv is the grand SD from Table 2: steps 4578.02, sedentary 333.41, exercise 47.52, total sleep 95.39; sleep onset SD printed as '2 h, 14 m' and wake time as '2 h, 17 m', converted to 134 and 137 min. The paper does not state exactly how beta_std was standardized (e.g., grand vs. within SDs); recomputing B*SD_IV/SD_DV with the grand SDs reproduces the printed beta_std only approximately (e.g., app 6AM-7:59PM on exercise: -0.046*140.26/47.52 = -0.136 vs. printed -0.128), so the printed beta_std should be used. Effects are per-day associations from intensive longitudinal data and are not directly comparable to between-person cross-sectional d's from questionnaire-based papers. [complete pass 2026-10-01] Re-read the full 10-page PDF (no supplement file exists in docs/pdfs for this DOI). All 108 beta_std/p values re-verified against Table 3. primary_models.dv: Six Fitbit Charge-derived daily outcomes, each modeled separately: total daily steps (grand M = 7553.73, SD = 4578.02); minutes of sedentary activity (METs < 1.5; M = 973.01, SD = 333.41); minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise (METs >= 3.0; M = 31.73, SD = 47.52); total minutes of sleep between 5:00PM and 4:59PM the next day (M = 449.98, SD = 95.39); sleep onset, first minute recorded asleep each night, modeled as minutes delayed (grand M = 11:48PM, SD = 2 h 14 m; labeled 'Bedtime' in Table 3); wake time, first minute awake followed by at least 30 consecutive minutes awake, modeled as minutes delayed (grand M = 8:02AM, SD = 2 h 17 m). Physical-activity outcomes are same-day; sleep onset and total sleep are same-night; wake time is next morning. Days with < 599 min of valid waking wear, > 20% of steps excluded in QC, or < 30 s of recorded sleep were excluded. Grand means/SDs from Table 2 (p. 5).
primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects models fit with the nlme package in R 4.3.0, with individual-level random intercepts. A separate model was fit for every smartphone measure x outcome pair. Table 3 reports both the unstandardized beta (per additional minute of use) and the standardized beta; no CIs or SEs are printed in the table, though Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the within- and between-person standardized betas. Significance judged at P < .05 (Fig. 1 marks * P < .05); no multiple-comparison correction is reported across the 36 combined or 72 disaggregated tests. No interaction or stratified analyses by sex or other demographics. Sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement (not in this PDF) and summarized narratively on p. 5: adding race and socioeconomic status (all significant effects retained), adding time recorded awake to the physical activity models (11/15 retained), redefining late night as 9:00PM-4:59AM or 11:00PM-6:59AM, winsorizing outcomes at +/-3 SD (30/31 retained), and inverse-propensity weighting by proportion of complete days (25/31 retained). Standardized effects in all sensitivity models were within 0.10 SD of the primary effects.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up visit (ages 13-14), participants in the ABCD EARS/Fitbit wearables substudy who concurrently provided up to three weeks of passively sensed smartphone, sleep and physical activity data (data collection ended after 21 days of data or 42 elapsed days). N = 791 participants overall (Table 1): mean age 14.12 (SD 0.69); 369 male (46.6%), 422 female (53.4%); Asian 17 (2.1%), Black 75 (9.5%), Hispanic 144 (18.2%), White 471 (59.5%), another race 84 (10.6%); highest parent education: no HS diploma 15 (1.8%), HS/GED 40 (5.1%), some college 241 (30.5%), bachelor's 225 (28.4%), graduate/professional 270 (34.1%); iOS 486 (61.4%), Android 305 (38.6%). Keyboard measures come from all 791 participants (11,797 day-observations for daytime and evening, 10,159 for late night); application-use measures come only from Android users (302 participants, 6340 days; 5993 for late night). Fitbit outcomes: steps 791 participants / 6228 days; sedentary and exercise 791 / 6748 days; total sleep and sleep onset 604 / 5634 nights; wake time 604 / 5375 nights (Table 2). The paper reports 6748 days of concurrent smartphone and physical activity data and 5634 nights of concurrent smartphone and sleep data. Each model uses all pairwise-complete day-observations for that IV-DV pair; the exact day-level and participant-level N per model is not reported. Attrition and inclusion detail is in Supplementary Figure S1 (not in this PDF). The authors note the sample is more female and more non-Hispanic White and less low-income than the US population of 10-14 year olds.

primary_models.iv: Passively sensed smartphone use from the EARS app. Application use (Android only) is the minutes any application, third-party or native, was in the foreground each day, after removing system apps and apps meant to stay foregrounded during sleep (lock screens, alarm clocks). Keyboard use (Android and iOS) is the total minutes the keyboard was open and logging keystrokes (time between first and last keystroke of each session), with the same app exclusions; on Android it was recorded from the native keyboard, on iOS via an EARS keyboard overlay that participants were told to use exclusively. Each is split into three time windows: daytime/evening 6:00AM-7:59PM, 'night time' 8:00PM-9:59PM, and late night 10:00PM-5:59AM the next morning. Six IVs total, each entered in a separate model, in minutes. Table 2 descriptives: Smartphone application use, 6:00AM-7:59PM (min/day): grand M = 190.47 min, SD = 140.26; participant-mean M = 188.68, SD = 96.00; Smartphone application use, 8:00PM-9:59PM (min/day): grand M = 37.66 min, SD = 36.89; participant-mean M = 36.98, SD = 23.10; Smartphone application use, 10:00PM-5:59AM (min/night): grand M = 71.52 min, SD = 97.11; participant-mean M = 70.53, SD = 69.58; Keyboard use, 6:00AM-7:59PM (min/day): grand M = 11.68 min, SD = 21.28; participant-mean M = 9.89, SD = 14.62; Keyboard use, 8:00PM-9:59PM (min/day): grand M = 2.90 min, SD = 7.27; participant-mean M = 2.47, SD = 4.52; Keyboard use, 10:00PM-5:59AM (min/night): grand M = 4.04 min, SD = 12.25; participant-mean M = 3.33, SD = 7.68.
primary_models.design: Intensive longitudinal (daily diary-style) design within the ABCD Year-4 follow-up: up to three weeks of daily passive sensor data per participant. IV and DV are measured on the same day (activity outcomes), the same night (sleep onset, total sleep) or the next morning (wake time). Days are repeated measures nested within participants, handled by a participant random intercept. The combined effect uses raw daily minutes of use, so it does not separate within-person from between-person variation. No time trend or IV x time interaction.
primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of daily Fitbit sleep and physical activity outcomes on same-day passively sensed smartphone app or keyboard minutes (combined effect), adjusted for sex, age, day type, summer, Fitbit wear time

primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up visit (ages 13-14), participants in the ABCD EARS/Fitbit wearables substudy who concurrently provided up to three weeks of passively sensed smartphone, sleep and physical activity data (data collection ended after 21 days of data or 42 elapsed days). N = 791 participants overall (Table 1): mean age 14.12 (SD 0.69); 369 male (46.6%), 422 female (53.4%); Asian 17 (2.1%), Black 75 (9.5%), Hispanic 144 (18.2%), White 471 (59.5%), another race 84 (10.6%); highest parent education: no HS diploma 15 (1.8%), HS/GED 40 (5.1%), some college 241 (30.5%), bachelor's 225 (28.4%), graduate/professional 270 (34.1%); iOS 486 (61.4%), Android 305 (38.6%). Keyboard measures come from all 791 participants (11,797 day-observations for daytime and evening, 10,159 for late night); application-use measures come only from Android users (302 participants, 6340 days; 5993 for late night). Fitbit outcomes: steps 791 participants / 6228 days; sedentary and exercise 791 / 6748 days; total sleep and sleep onset 604 / 5634 nights; wake time 604 / 5375 nights (Table 2). The paper reports 6748 days of concurrent smartphone and physical activity data and 5634 nights of concurrent smartphone and sleep data. Each model uses all pairwise-complete day-observations for that IV-DV pair; the exact day-level and participant-level N per model is not reported. Attrition and inclusion detail is in Supplementary Figure S1 (not in this PDF). The authors note the sample is more female and more non-Hispanic White and less low-income than the US population of 10-14 year olds.
primary_models.dv: Same six Fitbit outcomes as M1.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 'Within-Person Effect' and 'Between-Person Effect' columns (p. 6); Fig. 1 (p. 7, standardized betas with 95% CIs); Results pp. 4-5; Abstract; Discussion p. 8.
primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects models fit with the nlme package in R 4.3.0, with individual-level random intercepts. A separate model was fit for every smartphone measure x outcome pair. Table 3 reports both the unstandardized beta (per additional minute of use) and the standardized beta; no CIs or SEs are printed in the table, though Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the within- and between-person standardized betas. Significance judged at P < .05 (Fig. 1 marks * P < .05); no multiple-comparison correction is reported across the 36 combined or 72 disaggregated tests. No interaction or stratified analyses by sex or other demographics. Sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement (not in this PDF) and summarized narratively on p. 5: adding race and socioeconomic status (all significant effects retained), adding time recorded awake to the physical activity models (11/15 retained), redefining late night as 9:00PM-4:59AM or 11:00PM-6:59AM, winsorizing outcomes at +/-3 SD (30/31 retained), and inverse-propensity weighting by proportion of complete days (25/31 retained). Standardized effects in all sensitivity models were within 0.10 SD of the primary effects. Fig. 1 marks a reference line at standardized beta = 0.2 described as a 'clinically significant effect size'.

primary_models.design: Same intensive longitudinal Year-4 data as M1. Each smartphone measure is decomposed into a between-person term (the participant's mean daily use over the study) and a within-person term (that day's use minus the participant's mean). Both terms enter the same model as fixed effects, so the within-person coefficient estimates the association of a day of above-usual use with that day's/night's outcome, net of stable individual differences in use. Repeated days nested in participants with a random intercept.
primary_models.iv: Same six smartphone measures as M1, each decomposed into two terms: between-person (participant mean minutes) and within-person (daily minutes minus participant mean). Participant-mean SDs from Table 2: app 6:00AM-7:59PM 96.00; app 8:00PM-9:59PM 23.10; app 10:00PM-5:59AM 69.58; keyboard 6:00AM-7:59PM 14.62; keyboard 8:00PM-9:59PM 4.52; keyboard 10:00PM-5:59AM 7.68. The SD of the within-person deviation is not reported.
primary_models.equation: Outcome[i,t] = b0 + b1*(PhoneUse[i,t] - mean_i(PhoneUse)) + b2*mean_i(PhoneUse) + b3*sex[i] + b4*age_c[i] + b5*weekend[t] + b6*school_night[t] + b7*summer[t] + b8*fitbit_wear[i,t] (+ b9*OS[i] in keyboard models) + u_i + e[i,t]; b1 = within-person effect, b2 = between-person effect; one model per PhoneUse measure x Outcome.
primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of daily Fitbit sleep and physical activity outcomes on within-person (person-mean-centered) and between-person (person-mean) smartphone app or keyboard minutes, same covariates as M1

papers.title: Adolescent smartphone use, sleep, and physical activity: daily associations between sensor-based measures in the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) study
papers.extraction_flags: 1) The authors interpret both the combined-effect models and the within/between decomposition (both appear in the Abstract), so I extracted two cards: M1 with 36 combined estimates and M2 with 72 within- and between-person estimates. A reviewer should decide whether both cards belong in the meta-matrix or only one; they share the same data. 2) Native metric is set to the standardized beta printed in Table 3. Each estimate's note gives the unstandardized B per minute. No CIs or SEs are printed in Table 3. Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the M2 betas, but I did not read values off the figure, so beta_lo and beta_hi are null. 3) The paper does not say how beta_std was standardized. Recomputing it from B and the grand SDs in Table 2 matches the printed values only approximately (e.g., -0.136 vs. -0.128), so use the printed beta_std. 4) The covariate set "varied by model" per the Table 3 note. The 'school night' covariate is listed in that note but not in the Methods, and the paper does not say which models include which covariates. OS was included only in the keyboard models. 5) The analytic N per model (days and participants) is not reported, since each model uses pairwise-complete days. App-use IVs are Android-only (302 participants); keyboard IVs cover 791. 6) The sleep-onset and wake-time SDs were printed as '2 h, 14 m' and '2 h, 17 m' and converted to 134 and 137 minutes. 7) I counted significance at P<.05 with no multiple-comparison correction, across 108 tests. 8) The hourly-binned models (Supplementary Fig. S1) and all sensitivity analyses are supplementary and not printed in the PDF, so they are excluded; reviewers may want to check the online supplement.json
papers.authors: Alexander JD, Nguyen-Louie TT, Gupta S, Cummins KM, Wade NE

d_transformation.notes: For M2, marginal sample rate approximates unexposed-group rate to within ~1% since exposure prevalence is 1.5-3.8%. Not directly comparable to per-1-SD-of-IV d's from papers like 394. [complete-stage] M1 d values/signs/sig flags re-verified against Tables 2-3 page images; several draft cells corrected (see verification_log). Group Ns, adjusted group means and SEs added per M1 estimate to allow CI computation (SE_d approx sqrt(1/n1+1/n0)). sd_dv from Table 1.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: >=2 hr group vs. <2 hr group difference / pooled SD. M2: log-OR scale via Chinn.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: passthrough (native is already d). M2: OR = RR * (1-p0) / (1 - RR*p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000). p0 = 0.155 (insufficient sleep marginal base rate); 0.275 (disturbed sleep).

primary_models.location_in_paper: Tables 2 (weekday IVs) and 3 (weekend IVs). Pre-registered on OSF (deviation: IVs dichotomized post-hoc due to skew).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of a single ABCD timepoint (baseline, Release 2.0). Both IV and DVs measured at same visit. One observation per child. Pre-registered hypotheses H1-H7; IVs were pre-registered as continuous but data skew forced dichotomization at the AAP <2 vs >=2 hr threshold.

primary_models.estimation: OLS. Software not specified; analyses pre-registered on OSF. No survey weights. No random intercept for family despite siblings/twins in sample; sensitivity check with vs. without them yielded similar findings. alpha = 0.001 (paper's MC correction). Race and ethnicity interactions with IV all p > 0.001; no stratified per-modality estimates reported.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 2.0 baseline (2016-2018), 21 U.S. sites. Analytic N varies 10,666-10,676 across cells (listwise). >=2 hr groups small (1.5-3.8% of sample): weekday texting 2.8%; weekend texting 3.8%; weekday SM 1.5%; weekend SM 2.2%; weekday video chat 2.1%; weekend video chat 3.2%. Mean age 9.91 (SD 0.62); 52% female; 53% White, 20% Hispanic/Latinx, 18% Black, 5% Asian, 2% Indigenous. Middle-upper class (mean parent ed 16.61 yr; mean income $103,309).
primary_models.iv: Six binary IVs (3 modalities x 2 day-types), each 0 (<2 hr) or 1 (>=2 hr). Instrument: 12-item ABCD screen-time questionnaire with continuous response options (none/<30m/30m/1h/2h/3h/4+h). Dichotomization at AAP <=2 hr recommendation; deviates from pre-reg (right-skew). beta_1 is a group difference, not per-hour slope. Cohen's d from adjusted group means and pooled SD.

primary_models.name: Logistic regression of binary clinical-threshold sleep outcomes on dichotomized phone/SM use (relative risk)
primary_models.equation: logit(P(bad_sleep_DV[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*phoneSM_IV[i] + b2..b8*controls. Estimator returns log-odds-ratio; paper converts to relative risk for Tables 4-5.
primary_models.dv: Two binary clinical-threshold outcomes: (1) Insufficient sleep = 7-8 hr or fewer per SDSC duration item (NSF recommends 9-11 hr for 9-11 year olds); sample base rate ~14-17% depending on day type. (2) Disturbed sleep = SDSC total sum >= 39 (clinical threshold for likely clinically significant sleep-wake disturbance; sample M=36.54); sample base rate ~25-30%.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The IV set goes beyond the Stage 2 pointer (talk/text). I also included bedtime social media, the phone-at-bedtime ringer categories (silent/vibrate, ringer on and outside the room, each vs turning the phone off), and being woken by phone calls, texts or emails (this item also covers emails). Please confirm the ringer and woken-by-phone items count as phone-specific under FT-IC2. 2) I excluded 'spend time in chat rooms' (ARR 1.27/1.08) and 'used phone or other device after waking' (mixed device and activities). A coder may want chat rooms back in. 3) Table 3 gives social media vs sleep disturbance as 1.06 (1.01, 1.11), but the Results text on p. 500 says 1.01-1.13. I used the table value. 4) The IV coding is unclear. Methods describe a 5-point Likert scale (1 never to 5 every night), Table 2 shows 4 categories (0, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights), and the exposures were 'treated as continuous'. So the per-unit contrast is ambiguous, and no SD is reported for any IV. 5) The covariates are inconsistent. Age is listed among confounders in Methods but is missing from the Table 3 footnote and the abstract. 6) p0 values are marginal rates (15.5%, 28.0%), not rates in the unexposed group, and exposure prevalence is over 10%, so the RR-to-OR conversion is approximate. 7) Each exposure seems to be modeled separately, but the paper does not say so. 8) The ABCD data release is not stated. p-values printed as '<.001' are stored as p null with p_label.

primary_models.iv: Items from the 9-item ABCD Screen Usage Around Bedtime questionnaire (adapted from Lemola et al. 2014 and Arora et al. 2014) plus four sleep-and-phone items adapted from a National Sleep Foundation poll, youth self-report. Qualifying items: (1) 'Talk on the phone or text' and (2) 'Spend time online on social media (eg, Facebook)', both asked as how often in the past week the youth did the activity while already in bed before going to sleep. Methods describe a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (never) to 5 (every night), while Table 2 shows four response categories (0 nights, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights); the authors state exposures were treated as continuous variables, so the ARR is per one-step increase on this frequency scale. Distribution (Table 2): talk/text 65.9% 0 nights, 19.6% 1-2, 7.9% 3-4, 6.6% 5-7; social media 69.4%, 16.5%, 7.5%, 6.6%. (3) 'What do you usually do with your phone when you are ready to go to sleep?' coded categorically with 'Turn the phone off' (54.9%) as referent versus 'Put the ringer on silent or vibrate' (18.3%), 'Leave the ringer on' (11.8%), and 'Put it outside of the room where I sleep' (14.9%). (4) 'In the past week, how often have you had phone calls, text messages or emails that wake you after trying to go to sleep?' (83.1% none/0, 11.0%, 3.6%, 2.3% across the four Table 2 columns), treated as continuous. No means or SDs are reported for any IV.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study Year 2 follow-up (data release not stated). N = 10,280 of the 11,878 baseline participants who had complete data for this analysis; same N for every Table 3 cell. Age at Year 2 mean 12.02 (SD 0.66), range given as 10-14. 48.8% female, 51.2% male. Race/ethnicity: 52.4% non-Latino/Hispanic White, 20.1% Latino/Hispanic, 17.3% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.5% Other. Household income 47.6% < $75,000. Parent education 20.3% high school or less. 73.3% assessed pre-COVID-19 (before March 13, 2020). 2.3% depressed mood. Descriptives are ACS-propensity-weighted (Table 1, p. 499).

primary_models.equation: log(P(sleep_problem[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*bedtime_phoneSM_IV[i] + b2*sex + b3..b7*race_ethnicity + b8*income + b9*parent_ed + b10*depressed_mood + b11*covid_period + site terms (+ possibly age) ; ARR = exp(b1). For the phone-at-bedtime item, b1 is replaced by three dummy coefficients versus 'turn the phone off'.
primary_models.iv_type_note: Mixed: talk_text, social_media and woken_by_phone are ordinal frequency items 'considered continuous variables' (Statistical analyses p. 499); ringer_silent, ringer_on, phone_outside are categorical dummies vs 'Turn the phone off' (Table 3). Per-estimate 'iv_type' overrides set on the categorical cells.
primary_models.dv: Two binary sleep outcomes. (1) Trouble falling or staying asleep, adolescent report: single KSADS DSM-5 item about problems falling or staying asleep in the past 2 weeks, rated 0 (not at all) to 4 (nearly every day), binarized into problem on at least several days vs rarely or never; 15.5% yes (Table 1). (2) Overall sleep disturbance, caregiver report: 26-item Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children total (items 1-5, past 6 months), dichotomized at the developers' cutoff of 39 (Table 1 footnote says score > 39); 28.0% yes.

d_transformation.notes: p0 values are marginal sample prevalences from Table 1 (15.5% and 28.0%), not unexposed-group rates; exposure prevalence here is well above 10% (e.g., about 34% any bedtime texting), so the marginal-rate approximation from guidelines section 4a is weaker than usual and the derived d values should be treated as approximate. No SD is reported for any IV; the per-step contrast depends on how the 4-category (Table 2) or 5-point (Methods text) frequency scale was coded, which the paper does not resolve. d values are therefore per-scale-step and not comparable to per-1-SD or per-hour d's from other papers. [complete stage] Full PDF re-read (6 pages, no supplement file): every RR and CI for the 12 included cells is printed in Table 3 and already filled; no SEs, test statistics, IV SDs or unexposed-group event rates are printed anywhere.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Talk/text, social media, and woken-by-phone items: per one-step increase on the past-week frequency scale (ordinal categories treated as continuous). Ringer items: category vs 'turn the phone off' referent.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR = RR * (1 - p0) / (1 - RR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000). p0 = 0.155 for trouble falling/staying asleep and 0.28 for overall sleep disturbance (marginal sample rates, Table 1 p. 499). Apply to RR_lo and RR_hi for the CI.
d_transformation.native_metric: RR (adjusted risk ratio from modified Poisson regression)

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The methods describe logistic regression for SDSC sleep disturbance, but the table footnotes say the output comes from "modified Poisson and linear regression" models. The columns are labeled OR, so I recorded the values as OR. 2) The paper does not say whether each bedtime item was fit in its own model or whether all items were entered together; "in addition to all variables listed" in the footnote is ambiguous. 3) No SDs are reported for the 1-5 Likert bedtime items or for MCTQ sleep duration, so the B models (M2, M3) cannot be converted to d. The ORs can be converted with the Chinn formula. 4) I included the item about being woken by "phone calls, text messages, or emails" as phone-qualifying even though emails could come from a non-phone device; please check that call. I excluded the night-waking "phone or other device ... play games/browse ..." item as a mixed composite (OR 1.25, B -0.25); coders may want to revisit it. 5) I extracted the sex-stratified Table 5 estimates as separate cards (M3 linear, M4 logistic) because the authors interpret the sex differences. If you prefer, strike them or treat them as interaction results. 6) The ABCD release is not stated, and the online Appendices A and B are not in the PDF. 7) The paper's description of the sleep-duration weights ("weekdays (7) and weekends (2)") is copied as written but looks like an error for 5/2. All 12 values were checked against the Table 4 and Table 5 text.
papers.title: Social epidemiology of bedtime screen use behaviors and sleep outcomes in early adolescence

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1-point increase on the five-point bedtime frequency Likert scale (1 = never to 5 = every night) for each item.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR models: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000). B models: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1) - not computable here because SD_IV and SD_DV are not reported.
d_transformation.notes: ORs (M1, M4) convert via Chinn without additional inputs. For B models (M2, M3), the paper reports no mean or SD for the bedtime Likert items (Table 2 gives only categorical frequencies: 0, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights) and no mean or SD for MCTQ sleep duration, so standardized d cannot be derived from the PDF; online supplement may contain them. Baseline prevalence of SDSC >= 39 is not reported (not needed for Chinn). Methods describe logistic regression for sleep disturbance, but table footnotes mention modified Poisson; columns are labeled OR. [complete-stage check 2026-10-01] Re-read full PDF (pp.562-571): all 12 estimates and CIs present and match Tables 4-5; no SEs/t printed; no SDs for Likert items or sleep duration; SDSC prevalence not printed; no supplement file available in docs/pdfs.

d_transformation.notes: OR converts directly via Chinn, so no SD or base rate is needed. The resulting d is per 1 hour/day, not per 1 SD. Baseline SDs from Table 1 (p. 10, propensity-weighted): texting 0.56, video chat 0.52, social networking 0.45 h/day; a 1 hour/day contrast is about 1.8-2.2 SDs of these right-skewed IVs, so a per-SD rescaling (ln(OR)*SD_IV) would give smaller values. Outcome base rate p0 = 0.0138 (1.38% at two-year follow-up, Table 1 and Results p. 4), so the outcome is rare and the OR approximates the RR. The Chinn conversion assumes an underlying logistic latent variable. Completion pass (2026-10-01): all ORs/CIs/exact p re-verified vs Table 2; no SEs printed; no supplementary file available.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 additional hour/day of the modality at baseline

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The analytic N conflicts inside the paper: the abstract and Results say 11,633, but the Table 1 title says 11,363. I used 11,633. 2) Age is listed as a confounder in Methods 2.4 but is missing from the Table 2 footnote, so it is unclear whether the final adjusted model includes age. 3) There is another inconsistency about baseline suicidal behaviors. Methods says participants missing baseline suicidal behaviors were excluded, the Table 2 footnote lists baseline suicidal behaviors as a covariate, and a sensitivity analysis that excluded baseline cases is described only as "unchanged", with no numbers printed. 4) The paper never says whether each modality was run as its own model or all were entered together. I assumed separate models, based on the one-row-per-modality layout next to a separate total-screen-time row. 5) The ORs are per 1 hour/day of each modality. The baseline SDs are 0.45-0.56 h/day, so one hour is about 2 SDs, and the derived d will not be on the per-SD scale used by some other papers. 6) Social networking was not significant in the adjusted model (OR 1.27, CI 0.97-1.66, p=0.076). It is extracted as a null estimate. 7) Table 1 has a copy-paste error in its title ("binge eating characteristics"). Values were checked against both the page images and pdftotext output: Table 2 adjusted ORs, CIs and p-values, and the Table 1 SDs.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) Eligibility: in this paper, age of smartphone ownership is used only to split the sample into 5 groups (8 & under, 9 & 10, 11 & 12, 13 & 14, No Phone) for multi-group models (M1 Table 3/4, M2 latent growth). It never enters a model as a regressor with its own coefficient, so in practice it works as a moderator, and FT-IC2 clarification 7 says moderators do not qualify. The only direct phone-trait numbers are the unadjusted bivariate r values in Table 1 (M3: 'Cellphone age' with youth/parent internalizing Y1-Y4) and three Wald chi-square tests comparing adjacent groups' informant effects. A human should confirm whether Stage-2 inclusion holds. 2) M1 is the analysis the authors use to interpret their findings, but it is not convertible to d. Only M3 converts (r to d), and M3 is unadjusted. It also treats the coded group variable (No Phone presumably = 5) as continuous, and the coding is not printed explicitly. 3) Table 3 errors in the No Phone column: the informant row (.03/.02/.064) and the time row (.06/.07/.401) duplicate the screen-time and puberty rows. The text reports b = -.04, SE = .06, p = .694 and b = -.09, SE = .05, p = .068. I extracted the table values and flagged them in notes. 4) The text gives SE = .17 for the 11 & 12 informant effect; Table 3 gives .03. 5) Table 4, 13 & 14 column: every printed z equals b, and Y4 z = .40 vs b = -.40, which looks like a typesetting error. Y1 b = .22, p = .039 contradicts the text's claim that 13 & 14 was significant only at Y4. 6) Per the text, beta1/beta2 in Table 3 come from the model before the interaction was added and beta3 from the interaction model. 7) M2 (post-hoc latent growth curve) values come from the Results text p. 5, which matches Figure 1. Covariates for that model are not reported. 8) The full-sample interaction CI [-.29, -.23] does not contain b = -.21 (excluded, not phone-specific). 9) There is no supplement in the PDF; Supplemental Table 1 and Figure 1 are online only and were not reviewed.

primary_models.design: Longitudinal, four annual waves (Year 1 to Year 4 follow-ups, mean ages 10.9, 12.0, 12.9, 14.1). Internalizing problems from both reporters (youth BPM and parent CBCL) at each wave are stacked as repeated observations nested within dyads; informant (youth = 0, parent = 1) and time are level-1 predictors and the time x informant product tests whether the parent-youth discrepancy changes over time. Age of smartphone ownership (parent-reported, earliest reported age used) does not enter as a predictor; it defines five groups (8 & under, 9 & 10, 11 & 12, 13 & 14, No Phone) for a multi-group model in which all parameters are estimated separately by group. The phone variable therefore functions as a grouping/moderating variable: the phone 'effect' is the between-group difference in the informant effect and in its change over time, tested with post-hoc Wald tests for adjacent groups. Per the Results (p. 6), beta1 and beta2 in Table 3 come from the model before the time x informant term was added; beta3 comes from the final model with the product term. Table 4 probes the informant effect at each year from the interaction model.
primary_models.native_metric: other:within-group unstandardized MLM coefficient (b); Wald chi-square for group contrasts
primary_models.name: Multi-group two-level model of parent- and youth-reported internalizing problems on time, informant, and time x informant, grouped by age of smartphone ownership, adjusted for screen time, puberty, sex, and parent education
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, complete parent-adolescent dyads. Wave Ns: baseline 11,876 (mean age 9.9), Year 1 11,219 (10.9), Year 2 10,972 (12.0), Year 3 10,335 (12.9), Year 4 4,754 (14.1; about half of the sample per ABCD's release schedule). Abstract and Participants: 52.0% White, 20.3% Hispanic, 15.0% Black, 2.1% Asian, 10.5% Other; 47.8% female. Parent reporters 85.3% biological mothers, 10.0% biological fathers, 2.3% adoptive, 1.0% custodial, 1.4% other. Smartphone ownership groups (Table 2): 8 & under n = 677, 9 & 10 n = 2,641, 11 & 12 n = 5,037, 13 & 14 n = 744, No Phone n = 376 (sum 9,475). Attrition about 15% by Year 3 for internalizing and 17.9% missing for smartphone age; boys and youth of less-educated parents were more likely to drop out. Missing data handled with FIML under MAR.
primary_models.dv: Internalizing problems, the six items shared by the parent-report CBCL and the youth-report BPM (3 anxious/depressed, 3 withdrawn/depressed items), each 0-2, sum range 0-12, measured Years 1-4. Parent alphas .756/.762/.776/.783; youth alphas .619/.615/.619/.616. Right skewed. Means/SDs in Table 1 (youth Y1-Y4: 1.74 (2.11), 1.81 (2.23), 2.02 (2.38), 2.27 (2.56); parent Y1-Y4: 1.49 (1.88), 1.43 (1.88), 1.46 (1.93), 1.48 (1.96)) and by group in Table 2. Columns of the estimate matrix are model parameters within each group: beta1 time, beta2 informant (parent minus youth difference averaged over waves), beta3 time x informant, and the probed informant effect at each year.
primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.3, maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR), FIML for missing data (MAR). ABCD propensity weights (ACS-calibrated) applied in all models. Random vs fixed effects compared in the full sample with the Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square difference test (chi2_SB(2) = 8753.51, p < .001), so random effects retained. Group differences in the informant effect tested with post-hoc Wald tests for adjacent groups (9 & 10 vs 11 & 12, 11 & 12 vs 13 & 14, 13 & 14 vs No Phone; 8 & under vs 9 & 10 not reported as significant). Interaction probed by computing the informant effect at each year (Table 4, Figure 2). Alpha = .05; no multiple-comparison correction reported. No sex interaction tested. A full-sample (not grouped) version was also run (time b = 0.04, informant b = -0.47, time x informant b = -0.21).
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 (p. 7) for beta1, beta2, beta3 by group; Table 4 (p. 8) for probes of the informant effect at each year; Figure 2 (p. 7); Results pp. 6-8; interpreted in Discussion pp. 8-9.

primary_models.name: Post-hoc multi-group latent growth curve model of youth- and parent-reported internalizing problems, grouped by age of smartphone ownership
primary_models.dv: Six-item internalizing problems score (0-12), youth-report (BPM) and parent-report (CBCL), Years 1-4.
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, four annual waves (Years 1-4). Separate linear latent growth trajectories for youth-reported and parent-reported internalizing problems, estimated separately in each of the five smartphone-ownership groups (multi-group). As in M1, smartphone ownership age is the grouping variable, not a regressor; the phone contrast is the difference in slopes across groups, which the paper does not formally test.
primary_models.estimation: Described as post-hoc. Presumably Mplus 8.3 with MLR and ABCD propensity weights as for all models, but estimator details for this analysis are not given separately. No formal between-group test of slopes reported. Alpha = .05. Figure 1 also shows full-sample slopes (youth beta = .26***, parent beta = -.03), not extracted.
