d_transformation.conversion_formula: M3 only: d = 2r / sqrt(1 - r^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009). M1 and M2: no conversion.
d_transformation.native_metric: M1: other (within-group unstandardized b, Wald chi-square); M2: other (within-group latent growth slope); M3: r
d_transformation.contrast_type: M3: per unit of the coded ownership-age variable expressed as a correlation (higher code = later or no smartphone ownership); sign is negative for youth-report internalizing, so later ownership goes with fewer youth-reported problems. M1/M2: smartphone age is a grouping variable; estimates are within-group parameters (parent vs youth difference, change per year), not effects of phone ownership.
d_transformation.notes: M3 correlations are directly convertible; SD_IV (0.85) and SD_DV per wave/reporter are from Table 1 (p. 5) but are not needed for the r-to-d conversion. M3 is unadjusted and treats a five-category variable (with No Phone coded as the highest value) as continuous, so the derived d is a rough association, not the authors' focal estimate. M1 is the analysis the authors use to interpret the smartphone finding, but it is a multi-group model in which smartphone age only defines groups; the parameters are the informant (parent minus youth) effect and its change over time within each group, in raw internalizing-score units (0-12). A between-group phone contrast exists only as Wald chi-square tests (df = 1) with no effect size, so no Cohen's d for smartphone ownership can be derived from M1 or M2 without the raw between-group differences and their SEs, which are not reported. M2 slopes are within-group change over time, likewise not a phone effect. [complete pass 2026-10-01] Added se/se_scale to all Table 3 and M2 cells, z to Table 4 probes, chi2_df/n/sign to Wald tests, pooled per-wave sd_dv (Table 2) for Table 4 informant probes, iv_type on each model. No supplement PDF in docs/pdfs (online supplement holds only item list and distributions per text p.3).

d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of within-person social EMU (or within-person family conflict) at wave t, on the within-person outcome at wave t+1; for the random-intercept rows, the between-person standardized association
d_transformation.notes: Standardized betas are printed in the Results text (pp. 1030-1032) and match Figures 3-4 except girls FC->social EMU T1-T2 (text -.07, figure -.06) and the girls random-intercept association (text .24, figure .22). No CI is printed for beta, so no d CI from the native metric; a d CI could only be approximated from the b CIs with SDs. sd_dv values on the dv_axis are full-sample observed SDs from Table 1 (p. 1031; family conflict T2 1.88, T3 1.83, T4 1.94; social EMU T2 1.16, T3 1.66, T4 2.07), not the SDs of the within-person latent components and not sex-specific, so B-based conversion would be approximate; sd_iv left null because it depends on the lag (Table 1: social EMU T1 0.82, T2 1.16, T3 1.66; family conflict T1 1.95, T2 1.88, T3 1.83). Several printed b values are internally inconsistent (girls T1->T2 social EMU -> FC b = -0.59 with SE .02 and CI [-0.94, -0.25]; boys FC T3 -> social EMU T4 b = -0.04 with positive beta and CI), so beta is the safer basis for d. Random-intercept rows are nondirectional between-person associations, not effects of one variable on the other. Completion pass: per-estimate sd_iv added from Table 1 (lag-matched observed SDs); printed SE of b added as 'se'. Sex-specific SDs are not reported. Fig 4 girls -.04 label near e1 is the T1 residual covariance, not a cross-lag.
d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (standardized RI-CLPM path coefficient); unstandardized b with 95% CI also recorded in B/B_lo/B_hi
d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (beta_std treated as approximate r; guidelines section 4a, standardized SEM path). Alternative from b: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV, then same r -> d.

papers.title: Youth electronic media use and family conflict: Bidirectional associations across early adolescence

primary_models.dv: Family conflict: youth report on the 9-item Conflict subscale of the Family Environment Scale (True/False, summed, range 0-9) at T1-T4; alpha = .68, .67, .64, .68. Table 1 full-sample: T1 M = 2.04, SD = 1.95; T2 M = 1.91, SD = 1.88; T3 M = 1.92, SD = 1.83; T4 M = 2.10, SD = 1.94. Outcome is within-person family conflict at wave t+1. For the reverse-direction paths the DV is within-person social EMU at wave t+1 (descriptives as above).
primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.3, full information maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR). Model selection by Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square difference tests across M1 (all constrained over time) to M4 (all free), then gender multigroup models M5-M8; for social EMU, M8 (all parameters free over time and across gender) was selected (Supplemental Table 4). Fit: CFI = .99, TLI = .97, RMSEA = .04, SRMR = .02, chi2(20) = 195.91, p < .001 (Figure 3/4 notes print CFI = .991, TLI = .966, RMSEA = .038, SRMR = .015). Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction applied (p-adj reported). Gender differences tested via multigroup comparison and reported as separate boys/girls estimates. Sensitivity analysis adding youth internalizing/externalizing problems and parents' screen-use behavior as covariates on the random intercepts is described narratively as similar (p. 1033); its path estimates are not printed. Paper reports both unstandardized b (with SE and 95% CI) and standardized beta (no CI).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal four-wave panel: ABCD baseline (T1, age ~9.9), 1-year (T2), 2-year (T3), and 3-year (T4) follow-ups. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (Hamaker et al., 2015) separating stable between-person components (random intercepts for social EMU and family conflict, allowed to correlate) from within-person deviations at each wave. Within-person part has autoregressive paths, same-wave residual covariances, and lag-1 cross-lagged paths in both directions (social EMU at t -> family conflict at t+1, and family conflict at t -> social EMU at t+1) for T1-T2, T2-T3, and T3-T4. The selected model (M8) frees all autoregressive and cross-lagged parameters across time and across gender (boys and girls estimated as separate groups), so each lag and each sex has its own estimate. Social media/texting is the IV for the EMU -> conflict paths and the DV for the conflict -> EMU paths.
primary_models.name: Multigroup (boys vs girls) random-intercept cross-lagged panel model of within-person social EMU (social media + texting) and family conflict across four annual waves, adjusted for family income

primary_models.equation: Within-person part, per group g (boys, girls): FC_w[t+1] = a_F[t,g]*FC_w[t] + c_EF[t,g]*SEMU_w[t] + e_F[t+1]; SEMU_w[t+1] = a_E[t,g]*SEMU_w[t] + c_FE[t,g]*FC_w[t] + e_E[t+1], for t = T1,T2,T3, with cov(e_F[t], e_E[t]) free. Observed: FC[i,t] = mu_F[t] + RI_FC[i] + FC_w[i,t]; SEMU[i,t] = mu_E[t] + RI_SEMU[i] + SEMU_w[i,t]; cov(RI_FC, RI_SEMU) free; RI_FC and RI_SEMU regressed on income. Focal effects: c_EF (social EMU -> later family conflict) and c_FE (family conflict -> later social EMU); cov(RI_FC, RI_SEMU) is the between-person association.

papers.extraction_flags:
There is one model card (M1): the gender-multigroup RI-CLPM M8 for social EMU (social media + texting) and family conflict, adjusted for income. It has 12 cross-lagged estimates (both directions x 3 lags x boys/girls) and 2 between-person random-intercept associations. All values come from the Results text (pp. 1030-1032). I checked each one against Figures 3 and 4. I recorded native beta_std and also kept b with its 95% CI in B/B_lo/B_hi, because the paper prints no CI for beta.

Printed values a human should check:
(1) Girls social EMU T1->FC T2: b = -0.59 with SE = .02 and CI [-0.94, -0.25]. The SE does not fit the CI.
(2) Boys FC T3->social EMU T4: b = -0.04, but beta = .03 and the CI [-0.00, 0.07] is positive. The figure shows .03, so the sign on b is probably a typo.
(3) Girls FC T1->social EMU T2: the text says beta = -.07, the figure says -.06.
(4) The girls random-intercept sentence says 'total EMU' even though it is in the social EMU paragraph. Its beta is .24 in the text and .22 in Figure 4.
(5) The girls T2->T3 b CI is asymmetric.

Other issues:
- sd_dv values are full-sample observed SDs from Table 1. They are not within-person or sex-specific SDs.
- Group-specific Ns are not reported. T3 N is printed as '100,972'.
- The ABCD release is not stated.
- Supplemental Tables 1-5 are not in the PDF.
- Texting is defined as 'on a phone, tablet, or computer'. I counted it as qualifying under the activity-defined clarification 5.
- I excluded the sensitivity-model coefficients for parents' screen behavior -> youth social media intercept (girls beta = -.05, p = .049; boys beta = -.12, p < .001), because they are covariate effects the authors do not interpret further. A coder may disagree.

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 SD of social media time (minutes/day), within a given assessment (simple slope), on TIB in hours, bedtime in hours, or sleep onset latency in minutes.
d_transformation.native_metric: M1: unstandardized simple slope B (DV raw units per 1 SD of social media time) plus LRT chi-square for main effects; M2: LRT chi-square only
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1 simple slopes: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV with SD_IV = 1 (predictor standardized), so beta_std = B / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). Requires SD_DV, which is not reported. LRT chi-square cells and M2: no conversion defined in guidelines section 4a.
d_transformation.notes: The main text gives no SDs for time in bed, bedtime or sleep onset latency, and no SD for social media time (not needed for the slope because predictors were standardized). Figure 1 shows means with CIs only. Supplementary Tables S2-S5 (web only, not in this PDF) may contain descriptive statistics or model coefficients that would allow conversion of the M1 simple slopes; if SD_DV can be located there, M1 simple slopes become transformable. The LRT chi-square statistics (main effects and M2 awakenings) are omnibus model-comparison tests that are not convertible without the coefficient and its SE. No CIs or SEs are printed for any slope, so a d CI could not be computed even with SD_DV. Completion pass (2026-10-01): re-read all 19 PDF pages; confirmed no SDs, SEs, CIs or coefficient tables are printed. LRT chi-square main effects recorded as other:chi2 (df=1) but test N not printed. Supplement (PMC web) not bundled in docs/pdfs.

iv_axis.label: Social media time (main effect, LRT)

primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed models in R lme4 (Bates et al., 2015). Random terms for participant ID and collection site. Continuous predictors standardized. Sleep variables winsorized at 1st/99th percentiles. Significance of terms assessed with likelihood ratio tests (chi-square and p reported); interactions probed with simple slope analysis (R package 'interactions'). No CIs or SEs for the slopes are printed in the main text. No survey weights and no multiple-comparison correction reported; alpha appears to be .05. Sex x social media interactions were tested and reported as non-significant for TIB and bedtime. An additional cross-sectional comparison of 12-year-olds (May 2020 vs pre-pandemic) addresses pandemic vs developmental effects but does not involve social media as a predictor of sleep.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 3.0 (Year 2 follow-up) plus ABCD COVID-19 Survey first and second data releases. N = 5,027 adolescents (2,424 girls, 2,603 boys) who completed the Year 2 visit and at least one COVID-19 survey; per-assessment and per-outcome Ns not reported in the main text (selection pipeline in Figure S1). Pre-pandemic age 10-13 years (mean 11.94); pandemic-survey age 11-14 years. Table 1: female 48.2%, male 51.8%; White 77.5%, Black 9.6%, Asian 4.6%, multi-racial/multi-ethnic 1.1%, Other 5.8%, unknown 1.1%; Hispanic/Latino 17.8%, not Hispanic 81.0%, unknown 1.1%; parental education <high school 6.7%, HS/GED 1.3%, some college 22.7%, bachelor's 29.0%, postgraduate 40.1%. Analytic sample was less likely to be Black or Latino and had higher parental education than the full ABCD cohort.
primary_models.equation: Sleep[i,t] = b0 + b1..b6*assessment[t] + b7*age[i] + b8*school[i,t] + b9*SM[i,t] + b10*VG[i,t] + b11*sex[i] + race[i] + ethnicity[i] + parent_ed[i] + age x assessment + sex x assessment + sex x SM + sex x VG + b(6 terms)*assessment x SM + assessment x VG + u_participant(i) + u_site(i) + e[i,t]. Focal estimates are the simple slopes of SM at each assessment level (b9 plus the relevant assessment x SM term), in DV units per 1 SD of social media time.
primary_models.dv: Three continuous sleep outcomes from items of the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (youth version), harmonized across timepoints: (1) time in bed (TIB), hours, computed from reported bedtime and wake-up time; (2) bedtime, clock time from the item 'I go to bed at...' (responses 7 PM to 6 AM), modeled in hours; (3) sleep onset latency, minutes, from 'I need __ minutes to fall asleep' (0 minutes to 4 hours, pseudo-continuous). All sleep variables winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Means and SDs are not printed in the main text; Figure 1A-C plots means by sex and assessment.
primary_models.iv: Time spent on social media platforms (minutes per day), from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey at Year 2 (typical hours/day excluding school-related activity, weekday and weekend asked separately and combined as a weighted average) and from the same items in the COVID-19 surveys (past week, no weekday/weekend split). Pseudo-continuous response scale from 0 minutes to 9 hours or more. Continuous predictors were standardized before entry, so slopes are per 1 SD of social media time. Social media and single-player video game time were the two screen variables retained out of six because they had the lowest intercorrelation (Spearman rho = 0.13, Table S1). No mean or SD of social media time is printed in the main text; p. 9 reports that 92% (pre-pandemic) and 72% (pandemic average) used social media less than 1 hour per day, 2% vs 12% used it 2-6 hours, and 0.5% vs 2% used it more than 6 hours; Figure 2A plots means by sex and assessment.

primary_models.name: Linear mixed model of continuous sleep outcomes (time in bed, bedtime, sleep onset latency) on standardized social media time, with assessment x social media interaction, adjusted for video game time, age, sex, school, race, ethnicity and parental education
primary_models.design: Longitudinal repeated-measures design with seven assessments: one pre-pandemic assessment (ABCD Year 2 follow-up, 2018-2020) and six ABCD COVID-19 Rapid Response Research surveys (May 2020, June 2020, August 2020, October 2020, December 2020, March 2021). Social media time and sleep are both measured at each assessment and enter concurrently (time-varying predictor, same-assessment outcome), so each slope is a within-assessment association rather than a prospective one. Assessment is a 7-level factor; an assessment x social media interaction was included and probed with simple slopes at each assessment. Pre-pandemic sleep items referred to typical sleep with school/free days harmonized; pandemic items referred to the past week without weekday/weekend distinction.

primary_models.sample: Same as M1: N = 5,027 ABCD participants (Release 3.0 Year 2 plus COVID-19 surveys), ages 10-13 pre-pandemic and 11-14 during the pandemic; per-model N not reported.
primary_models.equation: log(E[Awakenings[i,t]]) = b0 + assessment[t] + b*age[i] + school[i,t] + b_SM*SM[i,t] + VG[i,t] + sex[i] + race[i] + ethnicity[i] + parent_ed[i] + age x assessment + sex x assessment + sex x SM + sex x VG + assessment x SM + assessment x VG + u_participant(i) + u_site(i)
primary_models.dv: Number of awakenings, from the MCTQ item 'After falling asleep, I wake up __ times during the night' (0 to 10), treated as discrete non-negative count data; winsorized at 1st/99th percentiles. No descriptive statistics in main text; Figure 1D plots means by sex and assessment.

covariates.detail: Assessment (7 levels), standardized pre-pandemic age, school, single-player video game time, sex, race, ethnicity, parental education, age x assessment, sex x assessment, sex x screen time and assessment x screen time interactions; participant ID and site random terms

primary_models.iv: Time spent on social media platforms (minutes per day), standardized; identical to M1.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. The PDF does not include Supplementary Tables S1-S9. The full LMM/GLMM coefficients (Tables S2-S5) are only in the web supplement. Because of that, the extraction relies on the in-text likelihood ratio chi-squares and simple slopes. Someone should get the supplement and check for social media coefficients, SEs and SDs of the sleep outcomes.

2. The seven simple slopes for social media and time in bed (p. 7: -0.24, -0.08, -0.07, 0.05, -0.15, -0.13, -0.12) are the same numbers as the age and time-in-bed slopes printed just above them. The only difference is the sign of the August value, which is printed as -0.05 for age and +0.05 for social media. This looks like a copy error in the paper. The August +0.05 also contradicts the text saying social media was linked to shorter time in bed. The bedtime slopes for social media and age are different from each other, so they look fine. A human should verify against Table S2 / Figure S4.

3. d is marked not transformable. The slopes are in raw sleep units (hours or minutes) per 1 SD of social media time, since predictors were standardized. The paper gives no SD for any sleep outcome and no CI or SE for any slope. Sleep onset latency and awakenings have only likelihood ratio chi-squares, with no coefficient. If the supplement gives SDs for the outcomes, the M1 slopes could be converted, so the status might change to partial.

4. The design is concurrent: social media and sleep are measured at the same assessment across 7 timepoints. It is not a prospective design. The model names were built from the methods text, because the full term list is only in the supplement. Results on p. 8 also mention an age x video game interaction that the methods do not list.

5. p-values printed as 'p < .01' are entered as p = null with p_label '<.01'. Page numbers in locations use the manuscript's printed page numbers. Texting and video chat were collected but dropped from all models because of multicollinearity, so no estimates for them can be extracted.

Phone/SM is the DV here: SMAQ and MPIQ regressed on six parent-reported media parenting practices. Parenting practices count as individual-trait under FT-IC2, but problematic-use scales are themselves the phone/SM variable, so a reviewer may want to confirm this pairing is in scope. Table 3 is printed rotated, and I read it from a re-rotated render. I checked all 12 values against that render and against the results text on pp. 405-406. Per-outcome analytic Ns are not reported. SMAQ was asked of n=6916 and MPIQ of n=8310, while the parenting SDs in Table 1 come from the full N=10,048 sample, so the standardization behind the derived d is approximate. Exact p-values are printed only for the two non-significant control-behavior cells; the rest are '<0.001'. Appendix A, which compares included and excluded participants, is not in the PDF. The total screen time column is excluded because it is a mixed composite, and the VGAQ column is excluded because it measures generic gaming.json

primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD Year 3 follow-up visit (2019-2022). primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 5.0, Year 3 follow-up. N = 10,048 adolescents with media parenting practices and any screen use (screen time or problematic screen use) data were included in any part of the analysis; 1,827 were excluded due to missing outcome data (comparison in Appendix A, not bundled in the PDF). The SMAQ was asked only of adolescents reporting at least one social media account (n = 6916) and the MPIQ only of those reporting mobile phone use (n = 8310), so the per-outcome analytic Ns are at most these values; exact per-model Ns are not reported. Mean age 12.47 (SD 0.77) years; 48.3% female, 51.7% male; 5.5% Asian, 15.6% Black, 19.9% Latino, 3.1% Native American, 54.4% White, 1.5% Other (45.6% racial/ethnic minorities). Household income: 16.2% <$25,000, 19.9% $25-50k, 17.9% $50-75k, 14.0% $75-100k, 24.2% $100-200k, 7.7% >=$200,000. Parent highest education: 17.8% less than high school, 82.2% college or more (Table 1, propensity weighted).
primary_models.iv: Six media parenting practice categories from a 14-item parent-report questionnaire (adapted from Tang et al. 2018), each item rated on a 4-point Likert scale from 1 'Strongly Disagree' to 4 'Strongly Agree'; items were summed and averaged into a mean score per category: parental screen time modeling (2 items; 'I try to limit how much I use a screen-based device when I am with my child' reverse coded), mealtime screen use (2 items), bedroom screen use (3 items), use of screens to control behavior (2 items: reward and punishment), parental monitoring of screen time (2 items), and limiting screen time (3 items). Weighted means (SD) in Table 1: modeling 3.05 (0.63), mealtime 1.86 (0.94), bedroom 1.82 (0.89), control behavior 2.54 (0.89), monitoring 2.75 (0.95), limiting 3.14 (0.72). Coefficients are per 1-point increase in the category mean score.
primary_models.equation: ProblematicUse[i] = b0 + b1*ParentingPractice_k[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*race/ethnicity + b5*parent_education + b6*household_income + b7*site + b8*COVID_period + e[i], fitted separately for each of the 6 parenting practice categories k and each outcome (SMAQ total, MPIQ total), with ABCD propensity weights.

papers.extraction_flags: 1. The qualifying IV is 'Socializing', which combines texting, social networking sites and video chat. It counts as a phone/SM-only composite under FT-IC2 Step 2, but the texting item says 'cell phone, tablet, or computer'. 2. M1 (the latent change score SEM) is the anchor model. A coder should decide whether to keep M2 (the Table 1 correlations, which are descriptive and Holm-corrected but have no exact p-values or N), M3 (the post hoc sibling mixed models, where the paper prints 'r' for the baseline result and 'beta' for the change result and does not state the scaling) and M4 (the mediation indirect effect, which is not convertible). 3. The Socializing<->cogPGS covariance (-0.04) was read from the Figure 1 labels. No p-value is printed; I marked it significant only because the figure does not label it 'n.s.' 4. The follow-up N is inconsistent: 5374 in Methods (p. 8) versus 5169 in the Introduction (p. 2). 5. No raw SD for Socializing is reported, but the SEM coefficients are fully standardized, so the d conversion does not need it. No CIs or SEs are given for the M1 paths. 6. A Socializing-only model is in the online Supplementary Information, which is not in this PDF. 7. Figure 1 draws the baseline-intelligence/change link as a double-headed arrow, but the gender section calls it an 'effect'. The M1 equation treats it as a covariance.json

primary_models.design: Longitudinal two-wave design. Screen time (Watching, Socializing, Gaming), cogPGS and SES are exogenous variables measured at baseline (ages 9-10). Intelligence is a latent factor measured at baseline and at the 2-year follow-up (ages 11-12) from the same five cognitive tasks with loadings and intercepts constrained equal across waves (strong invariance). The model estimates two outcomes simultaneously: the baseline latent intelligence (a cross-sectional association with baseline Socializing) and the latent change in intelligence from baseline to 2-year follow-up (a prospective association, with baseline intelligence also predicting change). Screen time is measured only at baseline; no repeated measurement of the IV and no time x IV interaction.
primary_models.name: Strong measurement-invariant latent change score SEM of baseline intelligence and 2-year change in intelligence on Socializing screen time (texting + social networking + video chat), adjusted for Watching, Gaming, cogPGS and SES

primary_models.dv: Latent general intelligence factor from five cognitive tasks (NIH Toolbox Picture Vocabulary, Flanker, Oral Reading Recognition; Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test; Little Man Task), each residualized for age, site and 20 genetic PCs. Two latent DVs: baseline intelligence (ages 9-10) and latent change in intelligence from baseline to 2-year follow-up (ages 11-12). Standardized loadings at baseline: Vocab 0.63, Flanker 0.28, Reading 0.70, RAVLT 0.41, LMT 0.36 (Fig. 1). Latent intelligence increased by beta = 0.24 (p < 0.001; 3.64 IQ points) over two years. Also reported in Figure 1: the covariance of Socializing with cogPGS (a genetic, individual-trait variable).
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 3.0. Baseline N = 9855 (M age = 9.90 years, SD = 0.62; 4686 females); 2-year follow-up N = 5374 (M age = 11.92, SD = 0.63; 2512 females) per Methods p. 8, but the Introduction (p. 2) says 5169 were followed up; the smaller follow-up N reflects the partial release, and missing follow-up data are handled by FIML. Inclusion required demographics (age, gender, SES), cognitive tasks, SNP genotypes and screen time. One participant per family retained at random (siblings/twins dropped). Children missing more than one of the three SES components excluded (n = 45). Race/ethnicity breakdown not reported; authors state the sample is representative of the U.S. on sex, race, ethnicity, SES and urbanicity.
primary_models.equation: Measurement: Task_k,t = lambda_k * INT_t + tau_k + e_k,t (k = 5 tasks, t = baseline, follow-up; lambda and tau equal across t; residual covariances of same task across waves). Change: INT_follow-up = 1*INT_baseline + 1*dINT. Structural: INT_baseline = a1*Watching + a2*Socializing + a3*Gaming + a4*cogPGS + a5*SES + z1; dINT = b1*Watching + b2*Socializing + b3*Gaming + b4*cogPGS + b5*SES + z2; exogenous covariances among Watching, Socializing, Gaming, cogPGS, SES; residual covariance between INT_baseline and dINT (-0.05, n.s.; drawn as a double-headed arrow in Fig. 1, although the gender section describes it as an effect of baseline intelligence on change). All observed variables are residuals from regressions on age, site and 20 genetic PCs. Focal: a2 and b2.

primary_models.estimation: R 4.0.3, lavaan 0.6-9 (also semTools). Full-information maximum likelihood with robust ML (Yuan-Bentler scaled test statistic). Fit: RMSEA = 0.023, CFI = 0.975. Covariates handled by prior residualization (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell argument) rather than in the SEM. No random effects; one child per family. No survey weights. No multiple-comparison correction stated for SEM paths; alpha 0.05 implied. Standardized betas reported, no CIs or SEs. Gender moderation tested by multigroup SEM (free vs constrained, chi-square difference = 1093, p < 0.001) with planned contrasts: Socializing -> baseline intelligence not different by gender (chi-square difference = 0.84, p = 0.357); Socializing -> change not different (chi-square difference = 0.94, p = 0.331); gender-specific Socializing betas not reported. Post hoc sensitivity analyses (SES replaced by parental education; Watching split into TV vs online video) did not report Socializing estimates. Separate Socializing-only models are said to be in the Supplementary Information (not in this PDF).

primary_models.estimation: lme4::lmer in R, restricted maximum likelihood. Random intercept for site; per-child random intercept and random slope on time. No weights. Quadratic over linear age model chosen by AIC/BIC (eTable 1) and likelihood ratio test. Bonferroni correction across 3 DM types x 3 brain regions x (overall + sex) = 18 tests, significance p < 0.05/18 = 0.0027 (Table 2 caption; text says p < 0.003); p values in Table 2 are uncorrected. Separate models fit for each DM type (social media, video games, TV/videos); social media not mutually adjusted for the other DM types. Sex x DM x time three-way interactions tested (Eq. 2; eTable 4), all non-significant, so no sex-stratified estimates. Three-way DM x time x SES interactions non-significant (no numbers in main text). Sensitivity analyses: excluding preterm (<37 weeks), birth weight <2500 g or ADHD (n = 3979; eTable 7) and restricting to children with MRI at all three visits (n = 1462; eTable 8) reported narratively as remaining significant; and excluding texting/video chat from the social media composite (beta = -0.02, p = 0.002, text p. 6). primary_models.design: Longitudinal, three MRI waves: baseline (T0, age ~9.9), 2-year follow-up (T2) and 4-year follow-up (T4). The outcome enters as repeated measures (not averaged) with random intercepts and random slopes on time per child. The IV is time-invariant: average self-reported social media hours/day across all annual visits (T0-T4). The focal estimates are the interactions of average social media usage with the linear and quadratic (orthogonal polynomial) time terms, i.e. whether brain developmental trajectories differ by social media use; the social media main effect is also reported.
primary_models.equation: Y_ij = b0 + b1*cogPGS_i + b2*Poly(Time,2)_ij + b3*Sex_i + b4*AgeAtBaseline_i + b5*SMUsage_i + b6*SES_i + b7*Ancestry(20 PCs)_i + b8*SMUsage_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij + b9*SMUsage_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij*SES_i + b10*SMUsage_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij*cogPGS_i + (1|site) + u0_i + u1_i*Poly(Time,2)_ij + e_ij. Focal terms: b5 (main effect), b8 split into SMUsage x Time and SMUsage x Time^2.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 5.0, data collected September 2016 to January 2022. Of 11,875 children, 6469 met inclusion criteria at T0 (age mean 9.9, SD 0.6; boys n = 3369, 52.1%; girls 3100), 4610 at T2 (age 12.0, SD 0.7; boys 2487, 53.9%) and 1697 at T4 (age 13.4, SD 0.6; boys 949, 55.9%); 1462 had usable MRI at all three time points. Exclusions: born <28 weeks or birth weight <1200 g, not proficient in English, neurological problems, seizure history, MRI contraindication, missing SES, genetic, DM usage or neuroimaging data, failed MRI QC or incidental findings; one child randomly selected per family. Race/ethnicity breakdown not reported.
primary_models.iv: Average estimated hours/day using social media, from the child-reported Youth Screen Time Survey, defined as the sum of texting on a cell phone, tablet or computer (item 4), visiting social networking sites such as Facebook, Twitter, Instagram (item 5) and video chat such as Skype, FaceTime (item 6). Weekday and weekend hours combined as [(weekday*5)+(weekend*2)]/7. T0/T1 categorical responses (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4); T2-T4 continuous responses recoded to the same categories (top code 4). The IV is the average across all annual visits, entered as a continuous variable. Table 1: average over four years 1.35 h/day (SD 0.95) overall, 1.12 (0.87) boys, 1.60 (0.99) girls; T0 0.49 (1.06), T1 0.84 (1.49), T2 1.22 (1.33), T3 1.87 (1.45), T4 2.50 (1.45).

d_transformation.notes: The paper never says whether variables were standardized. Raw brain volumes (cerebellum ~150 x 10^3 mm^3, Fig. 1) are incompatible with time coefficients of 0.04-0.12 and SEs of 0.001-0.02, which suggests the outcomes were standardized; SES and cogPGS are explicitly z-scored, but social media hours apparently entered in hours/day. SD_IV for the average social media variable is 0.95 h/day (Table 1, p. 3, 'Average estimated time spent over four years on Using social media'); SD at T0 is 1.06 (Table 1). SD_DV is not reported anywhere in the PDF. The M1 main-effect beta and the M2 betas can be converted to an approximate d under the beta_std assumption. The M1 interaction coefficients with Poly(Time,2) (orthogonal polynomial terms) are slope-difference parameters and do not map onto a between-person Cohen's d; they should be displayed in native metric only. No CIs are reported (SEs only for M1; neither SE nor CI for M2 in the PDF), so d CIs cannot be produced. [Completion pass] Printed Table 2 SEs now stored in each M1 estimate's 'se' field; whole PDF re-read (14 pages, no supplement file available); no CIs, SD_DV or M2 SEs printed anywhere.
d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (assumed; paper labels coefficients only as 'beta')
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1 main effect and M2: per 1 unit (h/day) of social media use, or per 1 SD if the IV was standardized (not stated). M1 interaction terms: difference in the linear or quadratic orthogonal-polynomial time slope per unit of average social media use.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Treat beta as approximate r: d = 2*beta / sqrt(1 - beta^2). If beta proves to be unstandardized, beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV first (SD_DV not reported).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) Standardization: the paper labels coefficients only as "beta" and never says whether variables were standardized. Raw volumes of about 150x10^3 mm^3 don't fit coefficients of 0.01-0.12, so the outcomes look standardized, but this is an assumption. I coded native_metric as beta_std. 2) The focal M1 estimates are social media x Poly(Time,2) interaction slopes (orthogonal polynomial). They don't convert cleanly to a between-person d; only the main effect and the M2 betas are roughly convertible. SD_DV is not reported anywhere. SD_IV = 0.95 for average social media use (Table 1); T0 SD = 1.06. 3) Composite: the social media IV is texting (cell phone/tablet/computer) + social networking sites + video chat. That qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2 and clarification 5. 4) The supplement (eTables 1-8) is not bundled in the PDF. M2 estimates (beta -0.01, p 0.10, eTable 5; beta -0.03, p 0.16, eTable 6) are from the text only, with no SE or CI, and their analytic N is unknown. The abstract anchors on the beta -0.03. Please check the online supplement. 5) The SNS-only sensitivity estimate (beta -0.02, p 0.002, text p. 6) does not name which model term it is. I inferred it is the Time^2 term for cerebellum and flagged this in its note. 6) The significance threshold is Bonferroni p<0.0027 (Table 2 caption), while the text says p<0.003. CSA x Time^2 has p = 0.004, so I coded it sig=false. 7) Coders may want to decide whether M2 (the abstract-cited accumulated-effect estimate) should be the primary anchor rather than the M1 interactions.

papers.extraction_flags: 1. Fig. 3 shows only significant results (p < 0.05), so the matrix holds only the 13 significant cells and pooled estimates would lean toward non-null findings. 2. The covariates in the LMMs are unclear. Methods say only that the Table 1 demographics "were considered as potential covariates", plus a family random effect. 3. Total-EARS (all smartphone app time) and Game-EARS (smartphone gaming apps) are included as passively sensed phone or app time, and as mobile gaming for Game-EARS. Please confirm these count under FT-IC2. Self-reported total and gaming rows are excluded. 4. The Methods never describe the Fitbit sleep outcomes and give no N for them. 5. The SM-time vs SMAQ/VGAQ betas (text p. 3, e.g. SR 12-mos SMAQ beta = 0.15) are excluded under FT-IC2 clarification 1, which treats them as SM-to-SM associations. The reporting-bias multinomial logistic models (Table 3, picture vocabulary OR = 0.96) are excluded as measurement-concordance analyses. Please check both decisions. 6. It is not stated whether the CBCL scores are raw or T-scores. sd_dv is null, which does not matter here because the betas are already standardized. 7. The supplementary tables (4-7) are not bundled with the PDF. Values were read from the high-resolution Fig. 3 image and cross-checked against the Results text and Abstract where these report them.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up. Of 4,754 youth at Year 4, 1,483 agreed to install EARS, and EARS-logged app data were available only for 495 Android users (Apple blocked app scraping). Analytic sample N = 495; CBCL available for n = 492; NIH Toolbox cognition missing for at most 20; paired EARS vs self-report comparisons used n = 395 for social media and gaming and n = 376 for total time (Table 2). N for the Fitbit sleep outcomes is not reported. Seven participants with family income still missing after LOCF imputation were excluded from relevant analyses. Sample (Table 1): age 14.01 (SD 0.70) years; 288 male (58.18%), 207 female (41.82%); White 281 (56.77%), Black 54 (10.91%), Hispanic 97 (19.60%), Other 63 (12.73%); family income >=$100k 202 (40.81%), $50-100k 154 (31.11%), <$50k 132 (26.67%), missing 7 (1.41%); parents married 338 (68.28%). Compared with excluded Year-4 participants, the EARS sample had more boys, was slightly younger, and had lower parental education and income.

primary_models.equation: z(Outcome)[i] = b0 + b1*z(SMA_measure)[i] + (demographic covariates from Table 1, as applicable) + u_family(i) + e[i], fitted separately for each SMA measure (EARS / SR 3-wks / SR 12-mos x total / social media / gaming) and each outcome; b1 is the standardized estimate in Fig. 3.
primary_models.name: Linear mixed model (family random effect, standardized betas) of CBCL, NIH Toolbox cognition and Fitbit sleep outcomes on EARS-logged and self-reported social media / smartphone app time
primary_models.iv: Screen media activity (SMA) time in hours per day, entered as a standardized predictor. EARS measures: foreground app usage time passively logged on the youth's Android smartphone over 3 weeks, averaged over days with at least one upload; system apps excluded. EARS social media = summed time in apps classified as social media by Google Play (Snapchat recoded from communication to social media); EARS gaming = summed time in apps classified as games (some entertainment apps such as Google Play Games, Xbox, PlayStation App and Steam recoded as games); EARS total = summed time across all non-system apps. Self-report measures: youth-reported social media hours on a typical day over the past 12 months from the ABCD Screen Time Questionnaire (SR 12-mos), and post-sensing survey social media hours for the 3-week sensing period (SR 3-wks). Descriptives in the paired subsample (Table 2): EARS social media 1.64 (SD 1.93) h, SR 3-wks social media 1.63 (1.93) h, SR 12-mos social media 1.44 (1.97) h (n = 395); EARS gaming 0.52 (0.73) h (n = 395); EARS total 4.89 (2.87) h (n = 376). Per self-report, 94.26% of social media time occurred on smartphones.
primary_models.dv: Six outcomes, each modelled separately: CBCL internalizing and externalizing problems (parent report; internalizing = withdrawn/depressed, anxious/depressed, somatic complaints; externalizing = rule-breaking and aggressive behavior; the paper does not say whether raw or T-scores were used); NIH Toolbox picture vocabulary and picture sequencing memory (Year-4 cognition, higher = better); Fitbit average sleep duration and sleep duration variability (Fitbit measures are not described in Methods). All estimates are standardized.

primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed models in R using lme4, with family as a random effect. Standardized estimates reported. Two-sided tests, alpha = 0.05. No multiple-comparison correction reported despite many SMA-measure x outcome tests. Missing family income, parental education and marital status imputed by last observation carried forward from earlier waves; no imputation for cognition or self-reported SMA. Fig. 3 prints only associations with p < 0.05; non-significant combinations are not printed. No interaction or stratified analyses for these models. A pubertal-stage sensitivity analysis is reported only for the reporting-bias models.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. All measures come from the ABCD Year-4 follow-up visit. EARS passive sensing ran for 3 weeks around that visit; the self-report measures are the Year-4 ABCD Screen Time Questionnaire (typical day over the past 12 months) and a post-sensing survey covering the 3-week sensing period. CBCL, NIH Toolbox and Fitbit outcomes are from the same follow-up. One observation per youth; no repeated measures and no time interactions. Each SMA measure (EARS, SR 3-week, SR 12-month) and each category (total, social media, gaming) was entered in a separate model against each outcome.

excluded_models.why: Fig. 3 prints only associations with p < 0.05. Estimates for the remaining combinations (e.g., EARS social media with internalizing, any phone/SM measure with picture sequencing memory other than EARS gaming) are not reported anywhere in the main text, so they cannot be extracted. The matrix therefore contains only significant cells.
excluded_models.model: Non-significant SMA measure x outcome combinations from the same linear mixed models

excluded_models.why: Self-reported total screen time bundles TV/video and other non-phone activities, and self-reported gaming is not restricted to phones (only 33.47% of reported gaming was on smartphones). Fail FT-IC2 Step 2.
excluded_models.model: Self-reported total screen time and self-reported gaming as IVs (SR 12-mos / SR 3-wks Total and Game rows)

excluded_models.why: Per 2L-criteria FT-IC2 clarification 1, SMAQ and VGAQ are themselves smartphone/SM (or gaming) use scales, so these are SM-use-to-SM-use associations without an individual-trait variable on the other side. Recorded here for reviewer judgment.

excluded_models.location: Results p. 3 (text only): SMAQ EARS beta = 0.06 (0.01-0.11), SR 3-wks 0.08 (0.03-0.14), SR 12-mos 0.15 (0.10-0.20); VGAQ SR 12-mos 0.05 (0.01-0.10); also Abstract

excluded_models.why: The DV is a self-report vs EARS discrepancy category, not a measure of phone/SM use amount; this is a measurement-concordance analysis (FT-IC2 clarification 6). Under-reporting at 0.5 h cutoff: picture vocabulary OR = 0.96 [0.93-0.99], p = 0.010; at 1 h: OR = 0.96 [0.93-0.99], p = 0.007. Over-reporting: OR = 0.98 [0.95-1.01] and 0.98 [0.95-1.02]. Flagged for reviewer in case the team counts reporting bias as a phone/SM variable.

excluded_models.why: Discrepancy measure, not phone/SM use; unadjusted Pearson correlations (r = -0.21, p < 0.001; r = -0.06, p = 0.177).

d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of the phone/SM time measure (h/day), in SD units of the outcome
d_transformation.notes: Fig. 3 caption states 'Beta estimates were standardized', so no SD_IV/SD_DV is needed for conversion. SD_IV values in iv_axis are from Table 2 (p. 4, paired subsamples n = 395 / 376) and are for reference only; outcome SDs are not reported (sd_dv null). The betas are adjusted for family clustering, but the covariate set is not stated explicitly. Only significant cells are reported, so any pooled estimate built from this paper is biased toward non-null results. Completion pass (2026-10-01): all 13 Fig. 3 cells re-verified against the printed forest-plot table (estimate, 95% CI, p); every CI is printed. Outcome SDs (CBCL, NIH Toolbox, Fitbit) are not printed anywhere in the PDF, and no SE/t/df is printed; neither is needed for standardized betas. iv_type set to continuous.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Treat beta_std as approximate r: d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2), applied to each CI endpoint for the d CI.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. Missing supplement. The PDF is the 10-page main article only. All per-exposure ExWAS coefficients and CIs are in Supplementary Table S1, which was not available. In the main text they appear only as a forest plot (Fig. 2B). The only qualifying number printed in the text is public (vs private) social media account, B = 2.13 (Discussion p. 6), with no CI. The other 30 qualifying cells are B = null on purpose: I did not read values off the plot. To fill them, get Table S1 from the online supplement at 10.1038/s44277-024-00006-9.

2. Sample label conflict. The Methods and Results headings say the ExWAS ran in the training subsample (n = 5082). The Fig. 2 caption says "testing subsample". I followed the Methods; please check.

3. Units and coding of exposures are not given in the main text. SD_IV and per-model N are not reported. SD_DV is set to 10 because BPM scores are normed T-scores, but BPM T-scores are floor-truncated, so the observed SD may differ.

4. Six non-significant exposures (Table S1 numbers 10, 17, 23, 24, 25, 26) are not named in the main text. Some are probably phone/SM null results and should be added once Table S1 is available.

5. Eligibility calls a coder should check:
- Included: "Night chatroom use" (platform not specified), "Connectedness via phone", "Parent suspects secret account" (parent report) and "Follower/Following count".
- Excluded as gaming: "Screentime Video Games [20]", although Fig. 2A puts it in the App-type domain, so it may be app-based.
- Excluded: cyberbullying, per FT-IC2 clarification 3.
- Excluded: the headline exposomic risk score (Table 2, and the suicide-attempt ORs in Table S3). It is a weighted composite that includes cyberbullying and video-game items, so it fails FT-IC2 Step 2.

6. Spot-checked against the page images: Table 1 training demographics, Table 2 Model-4 (1.78, 1.58-1.98, t = 17.41, n = 4004), the text values 2.13 and 3.57, and the suicide ORs 1.76 [1.39-2.23] and 2.76 [1.88-4.05].

d_transformation.native_metric: B (unstandardized LME coefficient, BPM T-score points per unit of exposure)
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per one unit of each exposure as coded in Table S1: yes vs no for binary items (e.g., public vs private account), per unit of time or count for continuous items. Units are not given in the main text.
d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 10 by construction for BPM T-scores (normed), but BPM T-scores are floor-truncated in community samples so the observed SD may differ; the paper reports no BPM descriptives. SD_IV is not reported for any exposure in the main text, and exposure units/coding are only in the Supplement. Only one qualifying coefficient is printed as a number in the main text (public social media account, B = 2.13, Discussion p. 6, no CI); this is binary, so d is computable with SD_DV = 10. All other 30 qualifying coefficients and all CIs are in Fig. 2B (graphic only) and Supplementary Table S1, which is not in the PDF. With Table S1, the binary items become convertible; continuous items still need SD_IV. [complete-stage 2026-10-01] Re-read entire PDF (10 pp.) and searched docs/pdfs for a '_supplement' file for this DOI (none). No additional per-exposure estimates, CIs, SEs, exact p-values, t-statistics, or exposure SDs are printed; Fig. 2B is an unlabelled forest plot. Model iv_type set to continuous with per-estimate iv_type='binary' overrides for public account, secret accounts, parent-suspects-secret-account, and top-app TikTok (prevalences reported in Discussion p.6). SD_DV = 10 (T-score convention) retained. [complete-stage 2026-10-01] Supplement (docx) is now bundled and was read in full. Its Table S1 is a variable list, not a coefficient table: no per-exposure B/CI/SE/p are printed anywhere, so 30 of 31 cells remain without a value and the one printed B (public account 2.13) has no CI input. Table S1 does give coding/units: '[n] Screentime <App>' items (#12-22) are actually number of accounts on that app (0-10), not time; #2,#3,#5,#6,#7,#8 are hours; #28-33 are 1-6 frequency scales; #34-36 are 1-4 nights/week; #39 is 1-7 agreement; #40-41 counts (>5000 removed). The public/private item (#38) is listed as '1=Public; 0=Private, Reverse coded for analysis'. The 6 non-significant exposures are #10 parent follows child on SM, #17 Pinterest accounts, #23-26 most-used app Instagram/Snapchat/YouTube/Multiplayer chat (not bolded in Table S1); no estimates printed for these either. No exposure SDs printed (sd_iv unavailable).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Binary exposures: d = B / SD_DV (adjusted mean difference over SD 10). Continuous exposures: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1).

primary_models.equation: BPM_T[i] = b0 + b1*exposure_k[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*Black + b5*White + b6*Hispanic + u_site + u_family(site) + e[i], estimated separately for each exposure k = 1..41
primary_models.dv: Brief Problem Monitor (BPM) Total Problems T-score, youth self-report, age- and sex-normed; reflects internalizing, externalizing, and attentional problems. Measured at the 2-year follow-up. No descriptive statistics for BPM T-scores reported in the main text.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Both exposures and outcome come from the ABCD 2-year follow-up visit (2019-2020, mean age about 12). One observation per child. Each of 41 retained digital exposures was entered as the sole exposure in its own LME model; there is no time structure and no exposure-by-time interaction. The ABCD sample was first split into matched training and testing subsamples (ABCD Reproducible Matched Samples); the ExWAS was run in the training subsample and its coefficients were used as weights to build the digital exposomic risk score applied in the testing subsample.
primary_models.estimation: R, lme4::lmer linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for family nested within study site. Missing exposure data imputed with missForest (random forest) within each subsample. Collinear exposures (Pearson r > 0.9) removed with caret::findCorrelation. FDR correction across the 41 comparisons; exposures with FDR-corrected p < 0.05 and coefficient > 0 treated as risk factors, < 0 as protective; 35 of 41 survived. Sensitivity: ExWAS rerun with list-wise deletion instead of imputation yielded 31 significant variables (Table S1, not in PDF); per-variable sensitivity estimates not in main text. No interaction tests at the ExWAS level. No survey weights reported.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 4.0, participants who completed the 2-year follow-up including screentime and social media assessment (N = 10,147). ExWAS run in the training subsample, n = 5082 (testing subsample n = 5065). Training subsample (Table 1, p. 4): age M = 12.01 (SD 0.66); 2446 (48.13%) female; SGM identity 406 (7.99%); race White 3901 (76.76%), Black 985 (19.38%), American Indian/Alaska Native 169 (3.33%), Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander 34 (0.67%), Asian 313 (6.16%), other 317 (6.24%), mixed 608 (11.96%); Hispanic ethnicity 1014 (19.95%); non-social screentime 24.88 (SD 13.97) hours/week. Missing exposure data were imputed with missForest separately within each subsample; outcome values were not imputed. The per-model analytic N for the ExWAS is not reported in the main text.

Interpreted in Discussion pp. 6-7.
primary_models.iv: Each of 41 digital and social media exposure variables, one per model, drawn from the ABCD Cyber Bullying Questionnaire and the Youth and Parent Screen Time Surveys (youth and parent report). Of 52 candidate variables, 7 were dropped for <1% endorsement and 4 for collinearity (|r| > 0.9); extreme values on continuous variables (e.g., number of followers) were removed. Exposures span five domains: screentime (minutes/hours per day by weekend/weekday), parental monitoring of social media (e.g., parent suspects secret accounts), apps used (yes/no per platform, platform-specific screentime, most-used app), overuse/addictive patterns of use (e.g., 'I use social media apps so much that it has had a bad effect on my schoolwork or job'), and peer interaction (e.g., connectedness via phone). Exact coding and units per variable are in Supplementary Table S1 and the Supplement, not the main text. Of the 35 FDR-significant exposures, 31 are phone/SM-specific and are extracted here; cyberbullying and three video-game screentime items are not. No descriptive statistics for the exposures are given in the main text, apart from 48% reporting a public account and 16% reporting TikTok as most-used app.

(2) Problematic social media use score (Year 2): Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), six items modeled after the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale (mood modification, salience, relapse, conflict, tolerance), administered to youth reporting at least one social media account; M = 5.9, SD = 6.6 (Table 1). papers.extraction_flags:
1) How I grouped the models. M1 puts two separate regressions on one card, Table 2 Model 1 (social media time) and Model 2 (problematic social media use), because they use the same covariates. M2 is Table 2 Model 3, with both variables entered together. M3 is the GSEM mediation in Table 3. A coder may prefer to split Model 1 and Model 2 into separate cards, or to drop M2 and M3 as mediation scaffolding. The abstract's headline estimate is Model 1, RR 1.31.

2) The paper labels problematic social media use (SMAQ) as the "mediator variable". In Table 2 Model 2 it is the main predictor of sipping, so I kept it. Confirm this is acceptable under FT-IC2, which says a variable does not qualify if it appears only as a mediator.

3) The SMAQ score comes only from youth with at least one social media account. The paper does not say how youth without an account were scored. Table 1 gives M 5.9, SD 6.6, which looks like a summed score, though the text says item averages were used.

4) Converting RR to d uses p0 = 0.087, the overall Year 3 sipping rate for the whole sample (Table 1). It is not an unexposed-group rate, because both social media variables are continuous. The contrast is per 1 hour/day or per 1 SMAQ point, not per SD.

5) The Model 2 row is printed as 1.03 (1.03, 1.05), so the point estimate equals the lower bound, likely from rounding.

6) In the GSEM mediation (M3), the scale of B is not reported: no link function is given, and B = 0.03 does not match ln(1.21). So it is not convertible to d. The abstract gives the proportion-mediated p as 0.002, but Table 3 prints 0.001.

7) The authors call the outcome "new-onset" sipping, but participants who sipped at Year 1 were adjusted for, not excluded. The Results text also says "sipping alcohol (Year 2, Model 1)", which looks like a typo for Year 3.

8) Study site is listed as an adjustment variable, but the paper does not say whether it was entered as a fixed effect or a clustering term.

primary_models.iv: Baseline socializing screen time, one of three screen-time types the authors derived from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (TV shows/movies, video games, socializing). Socializing is defined as texting, video chatting (e.g., Skype, FaceTime) and social media (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter) (p. 3; Supplementary S2), so it is built only from phone/SM items and qualifies under FT-IC2 as a phone/SM-exclusive composite. Daily screen time was computed as [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)] / 7 hours (Supplementary S2). The paper does not state the coding of the subtype explicitly; given that total screen time was entered as continuous hours/day, socializing is most likely continuous hours/day, so B would be per 1 hour/day. No mean or SD for socializing time is reported anywhere in the paper or supplement (Table 1 gives only total daily screen time, 3.7 h, SD 2.9).
primary_models.estimation: Weighted multivariable linear regression in Stata 18, using American Community Survey-based propensity weights and study sites as clusters in the survey procedures (Supplementary S1, S5). Missing covariate data handled by multiple imputation by chained equations, 10 imputed datasets pooled (Supplementary S4). Regression assumptions reported as tested and met. alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. Sex-stratified estimates reported alongside the overall model; no formal sex x socializing interaction test reported. Complete-case sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Tables 8-13) cover total screen time and the joint categories only, not the subtypes.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (data release not stated). N = 7,445 participants with complete baseline screen time, sleep disturbance and sleep duration and year-2 BMI and WC (Methods p. 3; Table 1 p. 17); Supplementary Table 1 gives the included group as N = 7,455 and the excluded group as N = 4,516. COVID-19 reduced year-2 anthropometric collection. Implausible anthropometrics excluded (BMI z <= -4 or >= 8 SD; WC z < -4 or > 4 SD). Missing covariates imputed (puberty 16.3%, income 7.6%, baseline BMI percentile 0.4%, parent education 0.2%, physical activity 0.1%; Supplementary S4). 3,511 females (47.3%) and 3,934 males; mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6). Weighted race/ethnicity: 5.9% Asian, 16.6% Black, 16.2% Latino/Hispanic, 3.5% Native American, 56.5% White, 1.3% Other; 57.0% household income < $75,000; 85.3% parent with college education or more (Table 1, p. 17). The sex-stratified columns use the female (n = 3,511) and male (n = 3,934) subsamples.

primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Socializing screen time is measured once at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10). The outcome is a single follow-up value at the year-2 visit (BMI percentile in one model, WC percentile in the other), with the baseline percentile of the same measure entered as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with year-2 adiposity net of baseline adiposity. No repeated measures. Screen time x sleep interaction terms were tested for the main total-screen-time models and reported as nonsignificant (p. 4); no interaction tests are reported for the subtype models. The subtype models are reported for the whole sample and separately for females and males.
primary_models.dv: Two continuous year-2 outcomes, modeled separately: (1) BMI percentile, computed from the mean of three measured weights and heights against CDC age- and sex-specific references; (2) waist circumference percentile, the mean of two WC measurements (inches, nearest 0.1) converted to percentiles using NHANES III reference data via the R package childsds (Supplementary S2). The footnotes of Supplementary Tables 6 and 7 state that the dependent variable is BMI percentile and WC percentile, and Supplementary S3 says baseline BMI and WC percentiles were the adjustment covariates. The main text and Table 1 instead describe BMI (kg/m^2; year-2 mean 20.6, SD 4.9) and WC (year-2 mean 28.8, SD 4.9), but those raw-unit descriptives do not appear to be the modeled scale. Year-2 percentile SDs are not reported; baseline percentile SDs for the included sample are BMI percentile 61.8 (SD 30.3) and WC percentile 61.1 (SD 29.0) (Supplementary Table 1).
primary_models.name: Weighted multivariable linear regression of year-2 BMI percentile and WC percentile on baseline socializing screen time (texting + video chat + social media), adjusted for baseline BMI/WC percentile, puberty and sociodemographics, overall and stratified by sex
primary_models.equation: Y2_pct[i] = b0 + b1*socializing_hours[i] + b2*baseline_pct[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*income + b15*parent_ed + b16*physical_activity + b17..*study_site + b..*pubertal_status + e[i], where Y2_pct is year-2 BMI percentile or year-2 WC percentile (separate models) and b1 is the focal estimate. Sex term omitted in the female and male models. The supplement does not say whether TV/movies and video games (or the sleep variables, which the S6/S7 footnote mentions) enter the same model as socializing.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Supplementary Table 6 (BMI) and Supplementary Table 7 (WC) in the separate supplementary appendix (docs/pdfs/10.1089_chi.2025.0022_supplement.docx; not bundled in the 20-page author-manuscript PDF). Subtype analysis described in Statistical Analysis (p. 4); referred to in Results (p. 6) as 'consistent with the main findings'. The Discussion (p. 6) singles out TV/movies and video games as 'particularly associated' and does not discuss socializing.

papers.extraction_flags:
Things a human should verify:

(1) Outcome scale. The S6/S7 footnotes and Supplementary S2/S3 say the DV is BMI percentile and WC percentile, with baseline percentiles as covariates. The main text and Table 1 describe raw BMI (kg/m2) and WC. I treated the DV as percentile and dropped the earlier draft's raw-unit SD_DV of 4.9. In its place I entered the baseline percentile SDs for the included sample from Supplementary Table 1 (BMI 30.3, WC 29.0), as proxies for the overall columns only. The sex-specific SD_DVs are null.

(2) SD_IV. No mean or SD for socializing time is reported anywhere, so d cannot be computed and transformable is false.

(3) IV coding. That socializing is in hours/day is my inference, not stated by the authors.

(4) Model contents. The paper does not say whether socializing was modeled alone or together with TV/movies and video games. The S6/S7 footnote also lists the sleep variables as IVs, which may be copied boilerplate.

(5) Supplement error. The Video games row of S7 is identical to the one in S6, which looks like a copy-paste error. It does not affect the socializing rows.

(6) Sample size. N is 7,445 in the main text but 7,455 in Supplementary Table 1.

(7) Interpretation. The authors never interpret socializing directly. They say subtype results were "consistent with the main findings" and highlight TV/movies and video games. The male BMI cell is the only significant one (B = 0.77, p = 0.001).

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 unit of baseline socializing screen time, presumably 1 hour/day (coding of the subtype not stated explicitly)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1)
d_transformation.notes: Not convertible because SD_IV is missing: neither the main text nor the supplement reports a mean or SD for socializing screen time (Table 1, p. 17 gives only total daily screen time, 3.7 h, SD 2.9, which cannot stand in for the subtype). On SD_DV: the Supplementary Table 6/7 footnotes and Supplementary S2/S3 indicate the modeled outcomes are BMI percentile and WC percentile, not raw BMI (kg/m^2) or WC. I therefore did not use the Table 1 year-2 raw-unit SDs (BMI 4.9, WC 4.9). Year-2 percentile SDs are not reported; as the closest available values I entered the baseline percentile SDs for the included sample from Supplementary Table 1 (BMI percentile SD 30.3; WC percentile SD 29.0) for the overall columns only, and left the sex-specific SDs null. If an SD for socializing hours becomes available (e.g., from ABCD baseline data for this sample), the overall cells could be converted with these proxy SD_DVs. [complete pass] Re-read full PDF (pp.1-20) and supplement docx (S1-S5, Supp Tables 1-13): still no socializing mean/SD and no sex-specific percentile SDs; every native B/CI/p for M1 is already filled.

SD_IV = 1.5 h/day; SD_DV = 2.2 (positive expectancies) and 2.1 (negative expectancies), weighted Table 1 descriptives for the N = 8292 analytic sample (p. 4). M1 B is on the log-odds scale because the gsem outcome equation is binomial logit (Statistical analysis, p. 3); it is not an OR and should not be run through the linear B formula. A per-1-SD log-odds contrast would multiply by 1.5. M2 values are read from Figure 1 labels with no CI, so only point d can be derived, and the mediator equation's link function is not stated. M3 indirect effects mix a linear and a logit equation and are kept in native units as non-convertible. Year 4 nicotine prevalence (5.4%, weighted marginal) is given as p0 but is not the non-user rate. Completion pass: SEs from Table 2 added to M1 (0.029, 0.027; logit scale) and M3 (0.003, 0.001). M2 a-path CIs/SEs confirmed not printed.
d_transformation.native_metric: M1: unstandardized logit coefficient (log-odds); M2: unstandardized B (mediator equation, presumably linear); M3: indirect effect on the logit scale
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: ln(OR) = B, so d = B * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to B and each CI bound. M2: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1). M3: not converted (mediation indirect effect).
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1 and M3: per 1 hour/day of Year 2 social media time. M2: per 1 hour/day, converted to per 1 SD of social media time via SD_IV.

primary_models.estimation: Stata 18, generalized structural equation modeling (gsem); outcome equation binomial with logit link. Indirect effects and SEs by the delta method; proportion mediated = indirect / (indirect + direct). Sampling weights calibrated to the American Community Survey applied. Study site entered as a covariate; no random effects or family clustering described. Two-sided alpha = .05. No multiple-comparison correction. No interaction or stratified analyses reported. No sensitivity analyses reported. Coefficients are unstandardized log-odds (B); ORs are not printed.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study, Years 2-4 (release not stated in the paper). N = 8292 after excluding participants with missing data on social media use, nicotine variables, or sociodemographic factors (exclusion flowchart in Appendix A, not bundled in the PDF). Mean age 12.0 years (SD 0.7) at Year 2; 48.7% female, 51.3% male; 56.7% White, 19.0% Latino/Hispanic, 14.4% Black, 5.3% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.3% Other (43.3% racial/ethnic minorities). Parent education: 10.5% high school or less, 89.5% college or more. Weighted descriptives (Table 1, p. 4).
primary_models.dv: Past-year nicotine experimentation at Year 4, binary (yes/no). From the youth-administered modified Timeline Follow-Back question asking whether the child had ever tried a puff of a nicotine product (cigarette, e-cigarette, or smokeless tobacco) since the last visit. Weighted prevalence 5.4% at Year 4 (0.9% at Year 2) (Table 1).
primary_models.equation: logit(P(nicotine_Y4[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*SM_hours_Y2[i] + b2*expectancy_Y3[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race/ethnicity + b10..b14*income + b15*parent_ed + b16*CBCL_depression + b17*nicotine_Y2 + b18*expectancy_Y2 + site terms; fit jointly with the mediator equation expectancy_Y3[i] = a0 + a1*SM_hours_Y2[i] + covariates + e[i]. Focal estimate b1 (direct effect). Run separately with expectancy = positive and expectancy = negative.
primary_models.iv: Year 2 youth-reported social media time in hours per day. Adolescents reported usual daily time on social media separately for weekdays and weekends; the daily average is ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2]) / 7. Continuous, per 1 hour/day. Weighted M = 0.7, SD = 1.5 h/day (Table 1).

papers.extraction_flags:
The paper is 7 pages and the supporting appendices are not in the PDF.

1. The M1 direct effects (0.138 and 0.153) are unstandardized log-odds from a binomial-logit gsem outcome equation. They are not linear B. I coded them as other:logit_B, the same way as sibling paper 107 (same authors and design, with a cannabis outcome). They should be converted with d = B*sqrt(3)/pi, per 1 hour/day.
2. The two direct effects come from the positive-expectancy and negative-expectancy mediation models. The authors interpret both, and neither is clearly the anchor. No total effect is printed.
3. The M2 a-path values (0.07* and 0.003) are read off the Figure 1 labels. There is no CI, SE or exact p, and the link function for the mediator equation is not stated.
4. p0 = 0.054 is the weighted whole-sample prevalence at Year 4, not the rate among non-users.
5. Study site is entered as a covariate, not a random effect, as far as the text says.
6. The ABCD release is not stated.
7. Including the a-path (social media time to smoking expectancies) as a qualifying analysis assumes expectancies count as an individual-trait construct (substance-related cognition). The coder should confirm this.

d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 66.14 min/day from Table 1 (p. 828, 'All (n = 10650)' column; printed with two decimals while other rows use one). The pooled within-group SD is not reported, so the total-sample SD is used; with exposure prevalence of 4-13% the difference should be small. SD_IV is not needed for this contrast. The authors themselves report Cohen's d of 0.09-0.10 for Table 2 total screen time results, not for social media. The DV is right-skewed (43% report zero social media), so d based on SD of a skewed outcome should be read with caution. This d (group difference / SD) is not directly comparable to per-1-SD-of-IV d values from continuous-IV papers. [complete-stage] Verified all B and CIs against Table 3 p.830; iv_type set binary; exposed/unexposed group sizes from Table 1 added as n1/n0. Group-specific SDs of social media minutes by parental problem status are not printed (Table S3 online only).

primary_models.iv: Presence of a clinically significant parental psychological problem from the Adult Self-Report (ASR, 123 items, 0/1/2 response), completed by the main caregiver. Three broadband scales are used: externalising, internalising and total problems. Raw scores were converted to gender-normed T-scores and dichotomised at T >= 65 (clinically significant problem = 1) vs T < 65 (= 0). Prevalence: externalising 8.8%, internalising 13.4%, total 4.2% (Table 1, p. 828).
primary_models.estimation: Multilevel general linear model with a random intercept for study site; coefficients are raw (unstandardised) minutes/day. Analyses conducted in RStudio 1.1.463. No survey weights reported. No multiple-comparison correction; significance flagged at p < 0.05 and p < 0.01. Table 3 column headers for the non-TV activities are printed as 'OR', but the table title and footnotes identify these as multilevel general linear model coefficients in minutes per day (the same as the TV 'Coeff.' column). Gender interaction terms (parental problem x child gender) were tested; results reported in Table S2 (not bundled in the PDF). A second step (Model 2) additionally adjusted for family conflict (extracted as M2). An additional logistic regression on any vs no social media use found no association (p-values 0.201 to 0.786; ORs not printed).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit (2016-2018). Parent-reported psychopathology (IV) and child-reported screen time (DV) measured at the same visit. One observation per child. Phone/SM is the DV here: the predictor is a binary indicator of clinically significant parental psychological problems and the outcome is the child's daily minutes of social media. Each parental problem scale (externalising, internalising, total) is entered as the predictor in a separate model, with the reference group being children whose parent does not have that problem.
primary_models.equation: SM_minutes[i,site] = b0 + b1*ParentProblem[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*ethnicity + b5*family_income + b6*main_caregiver + b7*child_psych_problem + u_site + e[i], fitted separately with ParentProblem = externalising, internalising, or total problems (each coded 1 = T >= 65 vs 0 = T < 65). b1 is the adjusted difference in daily social media minutes between children of parents with vs without the problem.
primary_models.sample: ABCD baseline data released in 2019 (NDA DOI 10.15154/1524631), N = 11,875 enrolled; 10,650 participants with complete data on study variables. 5112 girls and 5538 boys, mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6). Child-identified ethnicity: Black n = 1480, Asian n = 215, White n = 5843, Hispanic n = 1746, Multiracial n = 1366. Main caregiver was the mother for 85% and father/other for 15%. 16.7% of children had a psychological problem (CBCL). Parental problem prevalence (Table 1): externalising 935 (8.8%), internalising 1425 (13.4%), total problems 446 (4.2%).
primary_models.name: Multilevel general linear model of child social media minutes/day on presence of parental psychological problem, basic adjustments (Model 1)
primary_models.dv: Child-reported daily minutes of social media use from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey. The social media item covers visiting social networking sites such as Twitter or Instagram; the paper's methods list texting and video chat as separate questionnaire activities, and the paper does not state explicitly whether they were folded into the 'social media' category. Responses on a 7-point scale (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, >=4 h) for a typical weekday and weekend day; daily minutes computed as (weekday minutes x 5 + weekend minutes x 2)/7. Mean 30.8 (SD 66.14) min/day in the full sample; girls 35.7 (69.9), boys 26.2 (62.1) (Table 1, p. 828). 43% of children reported no social media use.

papers.title: Parental psychological problems were associated with higher screen time and the use of mature-rated media in children
papers.extraction_flags: 1) Which specification to anchor on is unclear. The abstract quotes Model 1 numbers (basic adjustments), and the text says nothing changed after adding family conflict (Model 2). I extracted both as M1 and M2. A coder should strike whichever one the review does not want. 2) Phone/SM is the DV here: parental ASR problem (binary, T >= 65) predicts the child's social media minutes per day. 3) In Table 3, the Video/youtube, Video games and Social media columns are headed 'OR', but the title and the scale of the values show they are linear-model coefficients in minutes per day. I coded them as B. 4) No p-values are printed for the social media cells. They have no asterisk, so I set them to p null and sig false. 5) Paper-wide social media prevalence is 43% non-users and Table 1's SD is printed as '66.14', with two decimals where every other row has one. Please check the SD_DV, which comes from Table 1. Since the pooled within-group SD is not reported, d = B/66.14 is an approximation, and the outcome is highly skewed. 6) The paper does not say clearly whether the 'social media' category includes texting and video chat or only social networking sites. 7) The logistic model for any vs no social media use gives only a p-value range, with no ORs. The supplementary Tables S2-S4 are not in the PDF, so these are listed under excluded models.json
papers.authors: Pulkki-Råback L, Barnes JD, Elovainio M, Hakulinen C, Sourander A, Tremblay MS, Guerrero MD

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The stage2_reason gives the wrong pairings. F(1,9662)=6.79 is not in the paper. Social media→FCF is F(1,9,664)=6.79, p<.01. Texting→FCF is F(1,9,669)=0.10, p=.75, which is not significant. Video chat→FCF is F(1,9,670)=27.18, p<.001. The texting F(1,9,666)=7.99 and video chat F(1,9,666)=6.81 figures are for sleep length, not FCF. I extracted both outcomes (FCF and parent-reported sleep length), since sleep is also an individual-trait outcome. 2) The paper reports only F statistics and p values: no coefficients, SEs or CIs, and no signs. Direction comes from the authors' wording ('small negative', and 'small positive' for video chat→sleep). The sign for texting→FCF is unknown. 3) The §4a rules have no F-to-d conversion. A point d is possible via d=2*sqrt(F)/sqrt(df) using approximate mixed-model df, but no CI is possible, so I marked it partial. 4) The models have no covariates beyond site and family random effects, so they are essentially unadjusted. The family random effect is odd because only one child per family was kept. 5) It is unclear whether each activity type was tested in a separate model or all were entered together. The differing error df suggest separate models. 6) Sleep length is a 5-category ordinal SDSC item with no SD reported, and its coding in the LME is not stated. 7) Figures S5/S6 and Table S1 are in an online supplement that is not in the PDF, so they were not checked. 8) The headline ML/VI and Table 2 analyses use mixed STQ totals that include TV and gaming, so they are excluded.

primary_models.location_in_paper: Method, Follow-Up Analyses (p. 2042); Results, Follow-Up Analyses (p. 2044, in-text F statistics; also plotted in Figure S5, not included in the PDF). FCF findings interpreted in Discussion p. 2046 and p. 2047.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional, ABCD baseline visit only. Screen media time and both outcomes (age-corrected NIH Toolbox fluid cognition composite; parent-reported sleep amount) measured at the same baseline assessment. One observation per child (one child randomly kept per family). These LMEs are post hoc follow-ups to a stacked machine-learning ensemble in which the weekday Screen Time Questionnaire total was among the 15 most important predictors of FCF; the follow-up decomposes weekday screen time by activity type. The text says activity type was 'entered as fixed effects'; the error df differ by activity type (e.g., 9,664 for social media vs 9,670 for video chat in the FCF models), which suggests each activity was tested in its own model with its own listwise N, but this is not stated explicitly. Direction of the screen-sleep relation is not stated as causal; screen activity is treated as the fixed-effect predictor in both sets of models.

primary_models.iv: Youth-reported Screen Time Questionnaire (STQ) hours on a typical weekday for each activity type, with response options none, < 30 min, 30 min, then 1-hr increments up to 4+ hr (range 0.00 to 4.00 hr per item). Qualifying items: social network sites, M = 0.11 hr (SD 0.42); text and instant messages, M = 0.22 hr (SD 0.56); video chat, M = 0.18 hr (SD 0.50) (Table 1, pp. 2040-2041). Non-phone items modeled the same way (TV shows/movies, R-rated movies, Internet videos, video games, mature-rated games) are excluded. Units of the fixed effect are presumably hours/day, but no slope is reported, only the F test.
primary_models.equation: Y[i] = b0 + b1*weekday_screen_activity_k[i] + u_site + u_family + e[i], where Y is FCF or sleep length and k is one of the STQ weekday activity types (social media, texting, video chat for this extraction). Focal effect b1 is tested with an F(1, df) statistic; b1 itself is not reported.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 2.0.1, complete baseline sample N = 11,877. Excluded participants without the FCF composite, then randomly selected one child per family where multiple siblings were assessed, leaving N = 9,718 (mean age 9.89, SD 0.62, range 9.00 to 10.92). Male 5,125 (52.8%), female 4,590 (47.2%). White 4,937 (50.9%), Black or African American 1,459 (15.0%), Hispanic 2,066 (21.3%), Asian 225 (2.3%), Other/mixed 1,019 (10.5%). Twins 856 (8.8%). Income < $50,000 30.4%, $50,000-$100,000 41.3%, > $100,000 28.3% (Table 1, pp. 2039-2041). Model-specific N not printed; error df range from 9,662 to 9,670, implying roughly 9,660-9,690 children per model depending on random-effect df.
primary_models.dv: (1) Age-corrected fluid cognitive functioning (FCF) composite from the NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery (Dimensional Change Card Sort, Flanker, Picture Sequence Memory, List Sorting Working Memory, Pattern Comparison Processing Speed), normed standard score; sample M = 95.57, SD = 17.48 (Results p. 2043). (2) Sleep length: parent-reported Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children item 'How many hours of sleep does your child get on most nights?', five ordered categories (< 5, 5-7, 7-8, 8-9, 9-11 hr; Table 1 p. 2040 gives counts only, no mean or SD). How this ordinal item was coded in the LME is not stated.
primary_models.estimation: R 3.5.1 (RStudio), package lme4 (Bates et al., 2014). Linear mixed-effects models with ABCD site and family ID as random effects. Only F(1, df) and p are reported; no coefficients, standard errors, or confidence intervals. Spearman correlations among screen types (Figure S6) were also computed. No multiple-comparison correction is described for the follow-up LMEs (FDR was applied only to the Table 2 univariate Spearman correlations). The authors state that, given the large sample, the analysis focused on effect sizes rather than significance, but no effect sizes are printed. No sex or other interaction tests and no stratified results. The parent machine-learning model (stacked elastic net, SVR, conditional inference forest, kNN with repeated nested cross-validation) is described separately and does not include per-modality phone/SM predictors.
