d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 hour/day of weekday activity (implied by STQ coding; slope not reported). The F-based d is a test-statistic conversion and does not depend on the IV unit.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Not one of the §4a conversions. A point d can be approximated from a 1-df F test as t = sqrt(F), d = 2*t/sqrt(df_error) (equivalently r = sqrt(F/(F+df_error)), d = 2r/sqrt(1-r^2)), with the sign taken from the authors' prose description (negative for social media and video chat with FCF; negative for social media and texting with sleep; positive for video chat with sleep; unknown for texting with FCF).
d_transformation.notes: No regression coefficients, SEs, or CIs are reported, so the §4a B-to-d route cannot be used even though SD_IV (Table 1, pp. 2040-2041: social network sites 0.42, texting 0.56, video chat 0.50) and SD_FCF (17.48, Results p. 2043) are available. Only F(1, df) and p are printed (p. 2044). A point d is recoverable from F and the error df, but no CI on d is possible, the sign depends on narrative wording, and the error df come from mixed models with site and family random effects (approximate df). Sleep length is an ordinal five-category item with no SD reported. The models carry no fixed-effect covariates, so these are essentially unadjusted associations apart from site/family clustering. [complete pass] Error df and direction (sign) were added to each estimate so the F(1,df) can be converted. SD_IV (Table 1) and SD_FCF = 17.48 (p. 2043) were confirmed. The sleep-length SD is not printed. The supplement (Appendix S1: Table S1, Figs S3-S6) is not bundled in docs/pdfs.

papers.extraction_flags: The PDF is the 5-page short communication only. Appendices A and B are online supporting information that was not available, so the per-modality sensitivity estimates for BMI and BMI z-score were not extracted. Site is listed as a covariate, but the paper does not say whether it is a fixed effect or a random effect. Age is not among the covariates; this is presumably because BMI percentile is already age- and sex-specific. SD_DV is the raw SD of follow-up BMI percentile (30.5), but the model adjusts for baseline BMI percentile, so the derived d values will be very small and are not comparable to cross-sectional d values. The SDs in Table 1 are propensity-weighted. The social networking estimate was not significant (p=0.075). Texting and video chat were significant.

primary_models.dv: BMI percentile at 1-year follow-up. BMI computed from the average of two to three research-staff measurements of height and weight (kg/m^2) and converted to sex- and age-specific percentiles using CDC growth curves. Table 1: follow-up BMI percentile mean 63.5 (SD 30.5); baseline BMI percentile mean 62.1 (SD 30.7).
primary_models.estimation: Multiple linear regression in Stata 15.1 (analysis performed in 2020). ABCD pre-constructed propensity weights based on the American Community Survey were applied. Single imputation by Gaussian normal regression for missing covariates. Site entered as a covariate; no family clustering, but a sensitivity analysis including only one sibling per family gave similar findings (numbers not printed). Significance at p < 0.05 (bold in Table 2); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification of screen time by sex was tested and was not present (p for interaction > 0.05); no stratified estimates reported. Appendices A and B (online supporting information, not in this PDF) repeat the analyses with BMI and BMI z-score as outcomes.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, right-hand columns 'BMI percentile at follow-up, fully adjusted' (Model 2) (p. 4); reported in Results p. 3 and Abstract; interpreted in Discussion pp. 3-4.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort with two waves. Screen time exposures measured at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10); the outcome, BMI percentile, measured once at the 1-year follow-up (2017-2019, ages 10-11). Baseline BMI percentile is entered as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with follow-up BMI percentile net of baseline BMI percentile. Single follow-up outcome, not repeated measures; no time interaction. Each screen modality was examined in a separate regression model (Table 2 note: 14 regression models in total across the 7 exposures x 2 adjustment levels).
primary_models.name: Weighted multiple linear regression of 1-year follow-up BMI percentile on baseline phone/SM hours per day (texting, video chat, social networking), fully adjusted including baseline BMI percentile

d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 3), baseline screen time hours per day for the analytic N = 11,066: texting 0.56, video chat 0.52, social networking 0.45. SD_DV = 30.5, the SD of BMI percentile at 1-year follow-up in Table 1 (p. 3). Table 1 values are propensity-weighted. Because baseline BMI percentile is a covariate, B reflects association with follow-up BMI percentile net of baseline; standardizing by the raw follow-up SD (not a residual/change SD) yields a very small d and is not directly comparable to cross-sectional estimates. IVs are heavily floor-skewed (means under 15 min/day). papers.extraction_flags: 1) The native metric is an adjusted prevalence ratio (PR) from modified Poisson regression. It is coded as "RR". 2) The stage2_reason gives p<.001 for video chat and texting predicting ODD. Table 3 actually prints p=0.003 for video chat and p=0.002 for texting, and the file uses the table values. 3) Age is listed as a confounder in the Methods (p. 5) but is missing from the confounder footnotes of Tables 2 and 3, so it is unclear whether age is in the final models. Site appears as an adjustment variable, not a random effect. 4) p0 uses the marginal one-year prevalences from Table 1 (CD 1.9%, ODD 6.3%), not an unexposed-group rate, because the IV is continuous. SD_IV comes from the propensity-weighted Table 1: texting 0.6, video chat 0.5, social media 0.4. These SDs differ from paper 394's ABCD descriptives. 5) Each modality was modeled separately, so the estimates are not mutually adjusted for the other modalities. The analysis uses all N=11,875 after imputation (outcome imputed for n=793). Baseline cases were not excluded even though the Discussion calls the outcome "new-onset". 6) Supplementary Tables S1 to S3 are not in the PDF. They hold assumption checks, the share of each modality with zero use, and confounder estimates, and were not reviewed. 7) The two "<0.001" p-values are stored as p=null with p_label "<0.001". All 6 PRs/CIs/p-values and the 3 SDs were checked against the pdftotext output of Tables 1 to 3.

primary_models.iv: Baseline child-reported hours per day of three phone/SM modalities, each in its own model: texting, video chatting (e.g. Skype, Facetime), and social media (e.g. Facebook, Instagram, Twitter; labeled 'Social networking' in Tables 2-3). Instrument: ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, typical weekday and weekend hours, combined as a weighted average [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)]/7 and entered as a continuous variable. Prevalence ratios are per 1 hour/day. Table 1 baseline means (SD): texting 0.2 (0.6), video chat 0.2 (0.5), social media 0.1 (0.4) hours/day. The Discussion notes that 80% of the sample reported zero social media use at baseline.
primary_models.name: Modified Poisson regression (robust SE) of KSADS-5 conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder at 1-year follow-up on baseline texting, video chat, and social media hours/day, adjusted for sociodemographics, baseline symptoms, baseline MDD, and family psychopathology history
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort with a single follow-up outcome. Each screen time modality is measured at baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10) and the binary disorder outcome is measured once at the one-year follow-up (2017-2019, ages 10-11). One observation per child; no repeated measures and no time interaction. Each modality was entered in its own model (one modality per model; Tables 2 and 3 each summarize fourteen models across unadjusted and adjusted versions), so the phone/SM estimates are not mutually adjusted for the other screen modalities. Baseline symptoms of the respective disorder are entered as a covariate; the outcome itself was not restricted to children free of the disorder at baseline, although the Discussion describes the finding as 'new-onset' disorder.

primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, adjusted columns (conduct disorder; manuscript p. 20) and Table 3, adjusted columns (oppositional defiant disorder; manuscript p. 21); Results p. 6; interpreted in Abstract and Discussion pp. 6-9.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study release 3.0, baseline and one-year follow-up, 21 U.S. sites. Analytic N = 11,875 (full baseline cohort). Missing data were imputed with Gaussian normal regression imputation rather than excluded: baseline screen time missing n=63, outcome missing n=793, covariate data missing N=1,016. Table 1 (propensity-weighted): mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.8% female, 51.2% male; 52.2% White, 20.0% Latino/Hispanic, 17.3% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.9% Other; 79.7% of parents with college education or more; 66.7% married/partnered. At one-year follow-up 1.9% met criteria for conduct disorder (1.1% of girls, 2.8% of boys) and 6.3% for oppositional defiant disorder (4.7% of girls, 7.9% of boys).
primary_models.dv: Two binary outcomes at one-year follow-up, modeled separately: conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder, each derived from the parent/caregiver-completed KSADS-5 computerized interview scored to DSM-5 criteria. Prevalence at follow-up (Table 1): conduct disorder 1.9%, oppositional defiant disorder 6.3%.
primary_models.estimation: Stata 15.1. Modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors (Zou 2004) to estimate prevalence ratios. Propensity weights applied to yield nationally representative estimates based on the American Community Survey. Missing exposure, outcome, and covariate data imputed with Gaussian normal regression imputation. Alpha 0.05 (bold in tables indicates p<0.05); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification by sex tested; sex did not modify any screen time association with either disorder (all p>0.05), and no sex-stratified estimates are printed. Sensitivity analyses using logistic regression and using complete cases yielded similar findings (logistic slightly stronger), data not shown. Statistical assumption checks are in supplementary Table S1 (not included in this PDF).

primary_models.equation: log(Pr(Disorder_1yr[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*PhoneSM_hours_baseline[i] + b2..b6*race_ethnicity + b7*sex + b8..b12*income + b13*parent_education + b14*marital_status + b_site*site[i] + b15*baseline_disorder_symptoms + b16*baseline_MDD + b17*family_history_psychopathology (+ age per Methods); Poisson working likelihood with robust (sandwich) SEs. PR = exp(b1) per 1 hour/day. Disorder is conduct disorder or oppositional defiant disorder; PhoneSM is texting, video chat, or social media, one per model.

papers.authors: Nagata JM, Chu J, Ganson KT, Murray SB, Iyer P, Gabriel KP, Garber AK, Bibbins-Domingo K, Baker FC

d_transformation.native_metric: RR (adjusted prevalence ratio from modified Poisson regression)
d_transformation.notes: p0 values are the marginal sample prevalences at one-year follow-up from Table 1 (manuscript p. 19: conduct disorder 1.9%, ODD 6.3%), not the rate in an unexposed group; with a continuous IV there is no unexposed group, and because both outcomes are rare the PR/OR distinction is small. SD_IV values are from Table 1 (manuscript p. 18; propensity-weighted, full N=11,875): texting 0.6, video chat 0.5, social media 0.4 hours/day. The IVs are heavily right-skewed with floor effects (80% report zero social media), so per-hour and per-SD contrasts may both be unrepresentative. Binary DVs, so sd_dv is null. Not directly comparable to per-1-SD d values from linear models or to group-contrast d values (e.g. paper 156). [complete-stage 2026-10-01] Whole PDF (23 pp) re-read; no supplement bundled. All 6 PRs, CIs and p-values verified against table images; SD_IV (Table 1 p.18) and p0 (Table 1 p.19) confirmed. No additional numbers (SE, z) are printed.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR = PR * (1 - p0) / (1 - PR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the point estimate and each CI bound. p0 = 0.019 for conduct disorder and 0.063 for oppositional defiant disorder (marginal one-year follow-up prevalence). To express per 1 SD of the IV rather than per 1 hour/day, ln(PR) could first be multiplied by SD_IV (ln(PR_SD) = SD_IV * ln(PR)) before the PR -> OR step.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 hour/day of the baseline modality (continuous IV); optionally rescaled to per 1 SD using Table 1 SDs

papers.extraction_flags:
Each gives 4 social media paths: the slope-slope covariance, i_sm -> s_cog, i_cog -> s_sm and the intercept-intercept covariance. That makes 12 estimates.

Things to check:
(1) The native metric is the standardized beta column. The 95% CI in Table 3 is on the unstandardized Est. scale, so beta CIs are null. I kept Est., SE and CI in each estimate's note. This means the d values will have no CIs.
(2) The covariance rows are latent correlations between growth factors, not directional effects. Please decide whether to convert them to d with the r -> d formula, or to keep only the directional paths.
(3) Table 3 is inconsistent with itself in two places. For i_sm -> s_cryst, SE = 0.12 is printed next to CI [-0.15, -0.07] and p < .001. For i_cryst <-> i_sm, the CI [-0.33, 0.01] includes 0 but p = .024.
(4) For i_flanker <-> i_sm, beta = +.06, but the zero-order correlation is negative and the Discussion says the two were negatively linked at baseline.
(5) The analytic N per model is not printed (FIML). Y2 N is printed as '100,972', which is probably a typo for about 10,972. The listwise sensitivity N is 4289 and is reported only as narrative.
(6) Race appears as a covariate in the Table 3 note but not in the Covariates section.
(7) Social media hours were log-transformed. It is unclear whether the SMU M/SD in Table 1 are raw or log values; this does not matter for converting the standardized betas.
(8) For p < .001 I set p to null and kept p_label as '<.001'.

primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.3. Full-information maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR) for non-normality of social media hours; data assumed MAR with race and parent education included as auxiliary covariates. Fit benchmarks RMSEA < .06, SRMR < .08, CFI > .95, TLI > .95; reported fit CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.97-0.98, SRMR = 0.01-0.02, RMSEA = 0.03-0.04. No random effect or clustering for site or family reported, and no survey weights. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR applied to cross-construct associations (p-adjusted column in Table 3). Alpha .05. No sex or other interaction tests. Sensitivity analysis re-estimated each model with listwise deletion (N = 4289); described narratively (slope-slope findings similar; crystallized i-i association and pattern intercept-slope associations no longer significant) with no numbers printed. Mplus syntax at https://osf.io/5d9s8/.

primary_models.iv: Social media hours (Y0, Y2, Y4), youth self-report of weekday and weekend hours on the item asking how many hours they visit social networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram; responses in hours (Y0 1-4, Y2/Y4 1-23) plus minutes (0, 15, 30, 45). Mean daily hours = weighted average of weekday (5/7) and weekend (2/7). Positively skewed, so log-transformed before modeling. Table 1 reports SMU Y0 M = .12, SD = .42; Y2 M = .68, SD = 1.32; Y4 M = 1.71, SD = 2.05 (the table does not state whether these are raw or log-transformed values). In the growth model the focal social media terms are the latent intercept (i_sm, baseline level) and latent linear slope (s_sm, rate of change per year). Social media is the predictor in the i_sm -> s_cog path, the outcome in the i_cog -> s_sm path, and a correlate in the covariance paths.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3, Models 5 (crystallized), 6 (Flanker) and 7 (Pattern Comparison) (p. 8); results text pp. 7-8; interpreted in Discussion p. 9. Univariate growth models in Table 2 (p. 7); descriptives in Table 1 (p. 6).
primary_models.equation: For each domain cog in {cryst, flanker, pattern}: SM[i,t] = i_sm[i] + s_sm[i]*time_t + e_sm[i,t]; COG[i,t] = i_cog[i] + s_cog[i]*time_t + e_cog[i,t], time_t = 0, 2, 4 years. i_sm = a1 + g1*X + u1; i_cog = a2 + g2*X + u2; s_sm = a3 + b1*i_cog + g3*X + u3; s_cog = a4 + b2*i_sm + g4*X + u4; Cov(u1,u2) = intercept-intercept covariance; Cov(u3,u4) = slope-slope covariance. X = sex, race, parent education, Y0 TV hours, Y0 streaming hours, Y0 video game hours. Focal terms: Cov(u3,u4) (s_cog <-> s_sm), b2 (i_sm -> s_cog), b1 (i_cog -> s_sm), Cov(u1,u2) (i_cog <-> i_sm).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, three ABCD waves: baseline (Y0, mean age 9.9), 2-year follow-up (Y2, mean age 12.0) and 4-year follow-up (Y4, mean age 14.1). Social media hours and cognitive performance are both measured at all three waves. For each cognitive domain a separate bivariate parallel-process latent growth curve model estimates an intercept and a linear slope for social media hours and for the cognitive score (slope loadings rescaled to assessment timing, 0/2/4 years). Intercept-intercept and slope-slope covariances are freely estimated, and each slope is regressed on the other construct's intercept (i_sm -> s_cog and i_cog -> s_sm), so social media appears both as predictor and as outcome within the same model. Three separate models were run (crystallized, Flanker, Pattern Comparison) with identical specification.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a, SEM path coefficients, standardized).
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 SD of the latent predictor (for i_sm -> s_cog and i_cog -> s_sm); for the covariance rows the standardized value is a latent correlation between growth factors (slope-slope or intercept-intercept).

d_transformation.notes: Standardized coefficients taken from the beta column of Table 3 (p. 8); the conversion needs no SD_IV or SD_DV, so sd_iv and sd_dv are left null. No CI is printed on the standardized scale (the 95% CI column is on the unstandardized Est. scale), so d CIs cannot be derived; unstandardized Est., SE and CI are kept in each estimate's note. The d values describe associations between latent growth factors (levels and rates of change), not per-hour associations between observed social media time and cognitive score, so they are not directly comparable to per-SD observed-variable d's from regression papers. Social media hours were log-transformed. Table 3 contains internal inconsistencies (i_sm -> s_cryst SE 0.12 with CI [-0.15, -0.07] and p < .001; i_cryst <-> i_sm CI [-0.33, 0.01] with p = .024). Unstandardized Est/SE/95% CI and BH-adjusted p from Table 3 added as structured fields est_unstd, se_unstd, ci_unstd_lo, ci_unstd_hi, p_adjusted_label on every estimate. Guidelines §4a give no conversion for chi-squared Wald/ANOVA test statistics from mixed models; a chi-squared(1) could in principle be converted via r = sqrt(chi2 / N) and d = 2r / sqrt(1 - r^2), but df are not reported and the statistics come from multi-predictor mixed models (partial effects), so this would not be valid without further information.

papers.title: Neural Sensitivity to Social Media Use: Implications for Sleep Duration in Adolescents

primary_models.iv: Self-reported daily social media use at Year 2 from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Questionnaire: typical daily hours on social media separately for school days and weekend days (excluding school-related activities), combined as ([weekday x 5] + [weekend x 2]) / 7 and winsorized at the 99th percentile; non-users kept at zero. Continuous predictors were standardized (mean = 0, SD = 1) before entry, so the IV is in SD units. Descriptives for Year 2 SM are not reported; Year 4 distribution reported (p. 5): 26.3% (n = 523) no SM use, 19.7% (n = 391) 1-59.9 min/day, 20.4% (n = 405) 60-119 min/day, 33.6% (n = 666) more than 120 min/day. Moderators: Year 2 mean bilateral beta-weights for large reward vs neutral anticipation in the MID task (Destrieux parcellation) for 12 ROIs including nucleus accumbens, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, insula, caudate, precuneus, putamen, thalamus proper, hippocampus, and inferior, middle and superior frontal gyri.
primary_models.estimation: lmer (lme4) linear mixed-effects models in R (analyses carried out in R and Python 3.5), with family ID and MRI scanner manufacturer as random terms. Continuous predictors standardized. Propensity weights calibrating ABCD to the American Community Survey were employed (p. 3); how they were applied in the models is not described. Effects are reported as chi-squared statistics with FDR-corrected p-values (correction applied within each set of 12 models; significance at corrected p < 0.05). No coefficients, standard errors, CIs or degrees of freedom are printed in the main text; full results are in Supplementary Table S1, which is not in the PDF. The authors prioritized interpretation of models with highest average R^2. A separate 10-fold cross-validated R^2 comparison across the three model sets was run without random terms (Friedman test, Holm-corrected Wilcoxon post hoc, alpha = 0.01). The SM main-effect chi-squared is reported once (7.76) without saying which of the 12 ROI models it comes from.
primary_models.design: Prospective two-wave design. Predictors (social media use, MID-task ROI activation, and the Year 2 measure of the outcome) measured at the Year 2 follow-up; outcome (sleep duration) measured at the Year 4 follow-up. One Year 4 outcome per participant, not repeated measures. This is the first of three sets of prospective models; within the set, each of 12 ROIs is entered separately, giving 12 models, each testing the direct effects of social media use and ROI activation and their interaction (SM x ROI) on Year 4 sleep duration.

primary_models.estimation: glmmTMB zero-inflated mixed model in R, with family ID and scanner manufacturer as random terms; continuous predictors standardized. The text attributes the log(x + 1) transform and glmmTMB to 'the first set of models' even though SM is the outcome only in the third set; the description reads as applying to the SM-outcome models. Which component (conditional vs zero-inflation) the chi-squared tests refer to is not stated. FDR-corrected p-values within the set of 12 models. Propensity weights mentioned (p. 3) without details of their use. No coefficients, SEs or CIs printed; full output in Supplementary Table S2 (not in the PDF). papers.extraction_flags:
The main text reports only chi-squared statistics with FDR-corrected p-values. It gives no coefficients, SEs, CIs, df, or SDs for social media use or sleep, so none of the estimates can be converted to d. Supplementary Tables S1–S3 should hold the full model output, but they are not in the PDF; someone needs to get them. If they report standardized betas, M1 might become transformable, and the SM -> brain activation model (Set 2, Table S3), which is currently excluded for having no printed numbers, could be added.

1) The main effects of SM on sleep (χ²=7.76) and of sleep on SM (χ²=6.72) are each reported once. The paper fits 12 models per set, one per brain region, and does not say which of these models the numbers come from.

2) I included the SM × ROI interaction chi-squares as phone/SM estimates in M1. In M2 I included the effects of insula and middle frontal gyrus activation on SM, with SM as the DV. Please check that both choices meet the eligibility criteria.

3) The abstract says the sleep -> SM effect was moderated by insula and middle frontal gyrus activation. The results text instead reports these as main effects of brain activation on SM and gives no interaction statistics.

4) The methods say the log(x+1) transform and the zero-inflated glmmTMB model were used for the "first set" of models, but SM is the outcome only in the third set. It is also not stated whether the chi-squares come from the conditional component or the zero-inflation component.

5) The propensity weights are mentioned, but the paper does not say how they were applied in the models.

1) The PDF is a 24-page author manuscript with no figures and no supplement. Figures 1-3 and Tables S1-S2 (the exact edge weights and bootstrap CIs) are missing, so every edge value comes from the Results text on pp. 9-10. No CIs or p-values exist for M1 edges; sig=true is inferred from retention after stepup pruning (alpha=.05) plus at least 50% bootstrap inclusion. 2) I added an irritability-to-social-media cell with value null and sig=false, inferred because the text never reports that edge and the Discussion calls social media "unidirectional." Please verify against Table S2/Figure 3. 3) M2 (sex comparison, Figure S4) gives online chat to irritability as 0.37 in males and 0.14 in females. Both are positive and much larger than the pooled adjusted -0.03, which may be an error in the paper or a different model (unadjusted?). The p=.047 tests the sex difference, not the edge vs. zero. Decide whether M2 should be kept as a primary model. 4) Online chat is a texting + video chat composite. It qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2, but texting and video chat are never broken out separately. 5) The journal name is not printed in the PDF. I filled in Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology from the DOI/ISSN prefix 1044-5463, so confirm it. 6) The cross-sectional GGM phone/SM edges are implied to be zero but not printed (excluded). The internalizing/externalizing temporal network (Figure S6) gives only a 0.02-0.04 range (excluded). 7) Edge weights cannot be converted to Cohen's d, so this paper goes to the later review level.json

primary_models.design: Longitudinal three-wave panel (baseline, Year 1, Year 2). All variables measured at every wave. The temporal network gives lagged within-person associations from one wave to the next (t to t+1), averaged over the two lag intervals, controlling for all variables at the previous wave, estimated as partial correlations. Bidirectional by construction: each screen node predicts later irritability and irritability predicts later screen nodes in the same model. The panel GVAR also estimates contemporaneous and between-person networks, but the authors interpret only the temporal edges. No wave-specific lagged estimates.
primary_models.iv: Youth self-report ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, typical hours per day on weekdays and weekends, 7-point scale recoded to hours: none (0), <30 min (0.25), 30 min (0.5), 1 h (1), 2 h (2), 3 h (3), 4+ h (4). Weighted daily average = [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)]/7; Year 2 items were rephrased slightly and recoded for consistency. Continuous. Social media (SNS) is a single modality item (e.g., Instagram). Online chat is a composite the authors formed because of low engagement: texting + video chatting (e.g., FaceTime), so it is built exclusively from phone/SM items (FT-IC2 Step 2 met). Table 2 M (SD), hours/day: SNS baseline 0.09 (0.34), Year 1 0.18 (0.50), Year 2 0.41 (0.78); Chat baseline 0.31 (0.58), Year 1 0.49 (0.77), Year 2 0.60 (0.90). Variables showing significant trends (video, videogame, online chat, social media, irritability, co-occurring symptoms) were detrended before GVAR estimation. Because the model is bidirectional, social media and online chat are both predictors (wave t) and outcomes (wave t+1); the irritability-to-chat edge treats chat as the DV.

Where the text gives CIs for other factors, they don't quite match a symmetric ± (games vs SM: 0.83 ± 0.07 in the figure, 0.76-0.89 in the text). No p-values are printed. primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 2.0.1, baseline, 21 U.S. sites. Of 11,875 enrolled, N=9,254 with complete data on all relevant measures (listwise). Ages 9-10. 8,308 youth endorsed at least one recreational activity and 946 did not. Table 1 reports demographics by group only (no-activity vs activity): age M 9.8 (SD 0.6) vs 9.9 (0.6); male 50.4% vs 52.1%; White 29.7% vs 59.3%, Black 31.3% vs 10.7%, Hispanic 26.2% vs 17.6%, Asian 1.4% vs 2.2%, Other 11.4% vs 10.3%; household income <$50K 64.6% vs 22.9%, $50-100K 25.7% vs 29.0%, >$100K 9.7% vs 48.2%; married/living together 59.3% vs 79.5%; parent age M 37.2 (7.1) vs 40.5 (6.6). Whole-sample demographics not reported.
primary_models.estimation: Generalized linear mixed model with logistic link, R package glmmTMB, parameters estimated by restricted maximum likelihood. Random intercepts for research site and siblings nested within site. No weighting reported. No multiple-comparison correction reported; significance appears to be judged at p < .05. Base vs full model compared with ANOVA F-test and BIC (full model R^2 = 0.35 vs base R^2 = 0.34, BIC = 5146.9, deltaBIC = 52.8, LRT = 84.2; the full model did not significantly improve on the base model). No interaction or stratified tests. Unadjusted group comparisons (ANOVA/chi-square, tableone) reported separately in Suppl. Table 1. Same GLMM structure repeated for five specific activities (soccer, music, swimming, baseball, art).
primary_models.dv: Any recreational activity involvement (binary yes/no), parent report on the Sports and Activities Involvement Questionnaire, 29 activities (sports, music, art, hobbies). Dichotomized because data were positively skewed with little gradation. 89.8% of parents endorsed at least one activity (8,308 of 9,254).
primary_models.iv: Latent group factor scores from GFA (R package 'GFA'). The SMA group comprised 12 youth-report items: hours per day (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4 h) on weekdays and weekends for TV shows/movies, videos, video games, messaging on a cell phone/tablet/computer, social networking sites, and video chat. GFA was repeated 10 times with different seeds; GFs whose posterior component means correlated >=0.7 across chains and that appeared in >=70% of replicates were retained, and their scores averaged across replicates. Two of the six SMA-related GFs carry phone/SM-specific labels in Fig. 5: 'Texting' and 'Weekday social SMA'. Their item loadings are shown only in supplementary figures not in this PDF, so the extent to which they load on non-phone items cannot be verified here. ORs are per 1 SD increase in the GF score (Results p. 6). Descriptive statistics for GF scores not reported.

primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit (data collected 2016-2017). IV and DV measured at the same visit, one observation per child. Two-stage approach: first, Group Factor Analysis (GFA) on four variable groups (12 SMA items, psychopathology, cognition, social environment) yields 15 robust latent group factors (GFs); second, the averaged GF scores enter a logistic GLMM as simultaneous predictors of recreational activity involvement. A base model (sociodemographics only) was compared with the full model (sociodemographics plus all 15 GFs). No interaction terms.

primary_models.iv: Two phone/SM exposures entered together. (1) Social media time: youth-reported hours and minutes on a typical weekday and weekend day visiting social media apps (e.g., Snapchat, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, TikTok), ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey; weighted daily average = (weekday x 5 + weekend x 2)/7, in hours per day. Table 1: M = 0.71, SD = 1.62 hours/day (N = 9,008). (2) Problematic social media use: Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), six items modeled on the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale (mood modification, salience, relapse, conflict, tolerance, withdrawal), averaged into a mean score; asked only of youth with at least one social media account. Cronbach's alpha = 0.82, test-retest r = 0.83 (cited). Table 1: M = 1.84, SD = 0.90 (n = 5,642). The item response range is not stated in the paper; Fig. 1 plots the SMAQ mean score on a 0-6 axis. Variance inflation factors in Model 3: social media time 1.19, SMAQ 1.17.
primary_models.equation: AlcExp_k[i] = b0 + b1*SM_time[i] + b2*SMAQ[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..*sexual_minority + b..*race_ethnicity + b*income + b*parent_ed + b*parent_marital + b..*site + e[i], fit separately for k = positive and k = negative expectancies; b1 and b2 are the focal estimates.

primary_models.dv: Alcohol expectancies, youth self-report, Alcohol Expectancy Questionnaire-Adolescent, Brief (AEQ-AB), 7 items on a 5-point Likert agree/disagree scale (range 1-5; higher = stronger expectancy). Positive expectancies = mean of items 1, 2, 4 and 6 (e.g., 'Alcohol makes a person feel stronger and more powerful'); Table 1: M = 2.99, SD = 0.61. Negative expectancies = mean of items 3, 5 and 7 (e.g., 'Alcohol can hurt how well a person gets along with others'); Table 1: M = 2.80, SD = 0.78. Each outcome is modeled separately; both are continuous.

primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. All variables (social media time, SMAQ, alcohol expectancies, covariates) taken from the ABCD Year 2 follow-up assessment (2018-2020). One observation per adolescent. Each of the two outcomes (positive and negative expectancies) is fit in a separate regression; Model 3 enters social media time and SMAQ score simultaneously so each estimate is adjusted for the other exposure. d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1); CI endpoints converted the same way.

SD_IV: social media time 1.62 h/day (computed on N = 9,008); SMAQ 0.90 (computed on the n = 5,642 subset with a social media account). SD_DV: positive expectancies 0.61, negative expectancies 0.78, both computed on N = 9,008, whereas Model 3 is presumably fit on the n = 5,642 subset; SDs in that subset are not reported, so the sample-level SDs are an approximation. Social media time is heavily right-skewed (M 0.71, SD 1.62). papers.extraction_flags: The paper never states the analytic N for Model 3. The SMAQ was only given to youth with a social media account (n=5,642), so Model 3 is presumably fit on that subset, but the outcome SDs (0.61 and 0.78) and the social media time SD (1.62) in Table 1 come from the full N=9,008. That makes the SD-based d conversion approximate. The SMAQ item response range is not stated: Fig. 1 plots it on a 0-6 axis, and the mean is 1.84 with SD 0.90. The abstract's covariate list leaves out age, but the Methods and the Table 2 footnote include it. Study site is treated as a covariate, not a random effect. Alpha is 0.01. Model 1, which uses social media time only, showed a significant negative-expectancy association (B=0.018, p=0.007). I excluded it as scaffolding because the authors anchor their conclusions on Model 3, so a coder should confirm that choice. Table 1's caption says 'Year 2 assessment 2016-2018', which conflicts with the 2018-2020 dates given in the text. Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 are not bundled in the PDF.

primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort with repeated outcome measurement. Baseline phone/SM exposure (and baseline CBCL t-score for the DV scale) predicts follow-up CBCL at Y1 and Y2 (2018-2020, overlapping COVID). Both follow-up scores enter long-format as separate rows; the model treats them as repeated measures. No wave-by-IV interaction, so beta_1 pools across the two-year follow-up window.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0. Baseline 2016-2018, 21 U.S. sites. N=9,538 with complete data on baseline screen time, baseline covariates, and Y1+Y2 CBCL. Excluded N=2,337 (19.7%) for missing data. Same N for all 18 IV x DV estimates. Mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.8% female; 52.4% NH White, 20.1% Latino, 17.3% NH Black, 5.5% NH Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.5% Other.

primary_models.estimation: Software: Stata 18.0 mixed procedure. Estimation: maximum likelihood. Weights: ACS propensity weights (nationwide-representative). Random intercept for study site. alpha = 0.05. Multiple-comparison correction: NONE reported (with 18 tests, ~1 false positive expected). Sex interactions all p > 0.05. Race/ethnicity interactions significant for some outcomes but stratified estimates in Table 3 are total-screen-time only. Sensitivity in Appendix B refits adding sleep and physical activity; per-modality numbers not printed.

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted multiple linear regression of year-3 CBCL anxiety and depression t-scores on social media trajectory group (GBTM), adjusted for demographics with a trajectory group x alcohol/e-cigarette use interaction
primary_models.dv: Two continuous parent-reported outcomes at the year-3 follow-up: CBCL DSM-5-oriented anxiety t-score and CBCL DSM-5-oriented depression t-score (ABCD-provided t-scores, range 50-97, higher = more symptoms). Sample means and SDs of the t-scores are not reported. The authors note the t-scores were right-skewed.
primary_models.design: Longitudinal two-stage design. Stage 1: group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) of self-reported social media hours/week across four ABCD waves (baseline, Y1, Y2, Y3; ages 9-10 to 12-13) assigns each participant to one of five latent trajectory groups. Stage 2: the trajectory group enters as a categorical IV in a linear regression predicting CBCL anxiety and depression t-scores measured once, at the year-3 follow-up. The DV is a single follow-up outcome, not repeated measures. Because the trajectory spans baseline through Y3, the IV window overlaps the wave at which the DV is measured. No baseline CBCL score is adjusted for. Two separate regressions are run, one per DV (anxiety, depression), with the same specification.
primary_models.estimation: Two-stage. GBTM in Stata 17; regression in R 4.3.3. Ordinary multiple linear regression with complex survey weights applied to adjust for sampling design and attrition. No random effects for site or family are reported. alpha = 0.05 implied by bolded p-values. No multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification by alcohol/e-cigarette use tested through the interaction terms (for anxiety only 3*Unknown reached p < .05, p = 0.049, printed unbolded; for depression only 3*Unknown, p = 0.013; the authors conclude no moderation). Sex interactions were not tested (listed as future work). No sensitivity analyses reported. GBTM fit indices for 2-6 class solutions are in Supplementary Table 1, which is not bundled in the PDF. Trajectory group is treated as known in stage 2 (classification uncertainty not propagated).
primary_models.iv: Social media trajectory group membership from GBTM (5 groups; Group 1 Persistent Low Use is the reference). Social media use was self-reported by the youth in hours per weekday and weekend day, standardized across follow-ups to make it comparable with the screen time variable, and aggregated to hours/week. GBTM fit 2-6 group solutions and chose the 5-group solution by BIC, polynomial order, entropy (> 0.8), posterior probability (> 0.7), and group size (> 2.5%). Group descriptions (Results p. 4, Fig. 1b): Group 1 Persistent Low Use (42.6%), less than 1 h/week, order 2; Group 2 Gradual Increase to Moderate Use (43.9%), reaching about 7 h/week, order 3; Group 3 Sharp Increase to High Use (7.2%), peaking at 25 h/week, order 3; Group 4 Moderate Increase to High Use (2.4%), peaking at 19 h/week, order 2; Group 5 Fluctuating High Use (3.9%), reaching 20 h/week, order 3. The authors note the social media item coding changed between the Y1 and Y2 follow-ups. Each coefficient is the adjusted difference in t-score between a group and Group 1.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 5.1, data through the year-3 follow-up (2016-2022), 21 U.S. sites. Analytic N = 9,474 participants with screen time data at one or more of the four time points, alcohol/e-cigarette data, and year-3 anxiety/depression data (Table 4 header n = 9,474). Social media trajectory group sizes (Table 2): Group 1 Persistent Low Use n = 4,255; Group 2 Gradual Increase to Moderate Use n = 3,970; Group 3 Sharp Increase to High Use n = 678; Group 4 Moderate Increase to High Use n = 226; Group 5 Fluctuating High Use n = 345. 52% male; median baseline age 9.92 (9.33, 10.42); 55% non-Hispanic White, 12% non-Hispanic Black, 20% Hispanic, 2.1% non-Hispanic Asian, 10% non-Hispanic Other. Household income <$50K 24%, $50K-<$99K 27%, $100K+ 42%, unknown 7.3%. Alcohol/e-cigarette use: yes 1.5%, unknown 0.4%.
primary_models.equation: CBCL_DV_Y3[i] = b0 + b1*SMgroup2[i] + b2*SMgroup3[i] + b3*SMgroup4[i] + b4*SMgroup5[i] + b5*SU_yes + b6*SU_unknown + b7*female + b8*age + b9..b12*race_ethnicity + b13..b15*income + b16..b20*parent_ed + b21..b24*(SMgroup2..5 x SU_yes) + b25..b28*(SMgroup2..5 x SU_unknown) + e[i]; fit separately for DV = anxiety and DV = depression. Focal effects are b1-b4 (each group vs Group 1 Persistent Low Use).
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 4 (p. 8), Trajectory Group rows 2-5; trajectories described in Results p. 4 and Fig. 1b; interpreted in Abstract, Discussion pp. 5-6 and Conclusions p. 9. Described by the authors as an exploratory (secondary exposure) analysis.

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The Table 4 footnote calls the coefficients a "standardized regression coefficient". But the Results text describes them as t-score points, and their size fits t-score units, so I coded them as unstandardized B. A human should confirm this. 2) The IV is social media trajectory group membership from GBTM, compared against the Persistent Low Use group. That makes d a group-difference d (B/10) using the CBCL norm SD of 10. The paper reports no sample SD for the year-3 t-scores. Those scores are floored at 50 and right-skewed, so the real SD is probably below 10 and d may be understated. 3) The model includes group x substance-use interactions, so the group main effects apply only to the no-substance-use stratum, which is 98% of the sample. 4) The trajectory window runs from baseline to Y3 and overlaps the Y3 outcome, and baseline CBCL is not adjusted for. 5) The authors call the social media analysis exploratory, and the coding of the social media item changed between Y1 and Y2. 6) Group 4 n is 266 in the Results text but 226 in Table 2. 226 sums to N = 9,474, so I used 226. 7) Two p-values print as '< 0.001', and I stored 0.001 as the bound. 8) Supplementary Table 1 (GBTM fit indices) is not included in the PDF. The total screen time trajectory model (Table 3) is excluded because it bundles TV and gaming.json

d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 10 is the CBCL t-score norming SD; the paper does not report the sample SD of the year-3 anxiety or depression t-scores (Tables 1-2 give no outcome descriptives). Because ABCD CBCL DSM-5 t-scores are floored at 50 and right-skewed, the actual sample SD is likely below 10, so d computed with SD = 10 may understate the standardized difference. SD_IV is not applicable (categorical group contrast), so sd_iv is null; d is a group-difference d, not a per-1-SD or per-hour slope, and is not directly comparable with per-SD d's from continuous-IV papers. Group main effects are conditional on the no-substance-use stratum because the model includes group x substance use interactions; since 98% of the sample is in that stratum the difference from a marginal effect is expected to be small. Table 4 footnote labels the coefficients as 'standardized regression coefficient', but the Results text describes the interaction estimates as t-score points (e.g., '9.84-point higher depression t-score') and the magnitudes match t-score units, so they were coded as unstandardized B.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Dichotomous contrast (group k vs reference group) on a continuous DV: d = (adjusted M_k - M_1) / SD_pooled = B / SD_DV, with SD_DV = 10 (CBCL t-score norm). CI endpoints converted the same way.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Membership in social media trajectory group k (2, 3, 4, or 5) versus the Persistent Low Use group (Group 1), among participants with no alcohol/e-cigarette use (reference level of the moderator)
d_transformation.native_metric: B (unstandardized adjusted mean difference in t-score points, group k vs Group 1)

papers.extraction_flags:
It has three cards, all from one Mplus negative binomial SEM:
- M1: 8 direct effects of social media on the 8 CBCL raw scales. The metric is IRR, and B with its CI is stored alongside.
- M2: the social media -> sleep duration path. The metric is B.
- M3: 8 indirect effects of social media through sleep, none significant.

Please check:
(1) The IV units are unclear. The Methods say screen-time behaviors were binned into 4 groups (<1, 1-1.99, 2-2.99, >=3 h), but the Results read coefficients as per one hour. The SD_IV of 1.15 h/day comes from Table 1 and may be on the wrong scale for converting M2.
(2) Table 2 prints the CIs on the B (log) scale only. No IRR CI is printed, so IRR_lo and IRR_hi are null.
(3) In Table 2, the CI for social media -> aggressive behavior is printed as (.029, .053), which excludes its own B of .06. This looks like a typo in the paper. I copied it as printed.
(4) The paper does not state the distribution of the sleep-duration path. I assumed it is linear, yet Table 2 still prints an 'IRR' of .968 for it.
(5) Social media is a composite of texting, social networking sites, and video chat. All three are phone/SM items, so it qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. There are no per-item estimates.
(6) The CBCL outcomes are raw counts, not T-scores. SD_DV values come from Table 1, which uses the full baseline sample. Converting IRR to d via Chinn is only a rough approximation for negative binomial outcomes.
(7) The ABCD release number is not stated, and the TYPE=COMPLEX cluster variable is not named.
(8) Supplement Additional file 1 was not bundled in the PDF.

I checked every social media number against the PDF text layer (Tables 2 and 3) and all of them match.

primary_models.iv: Child self-reported social media time from the Youth Screen Time Survey (14 items). Social media is a composite of three items collapsed by the authors because of low use: texting, visiting social networking sites (e.g., Twitter, Instagram), and video chat (e.g., FaceTime); all three components are phone/SM items, so the composite qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. Each item asked hours on a typical weekday and weekend day on a 7-point scale (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, >=4 h); daily time = (weekday hours x 5 + weekend hours x 2)/7. The Methods state ST behaviors were then categorized into four groups (<1 h, 1-1.99 h, 2-2.99 h, >=3 h) for analysis, yet the Results interpret coefficients as 'every one hour increase'; the exact coding entering the model is therefore ambiguous. Table 1 (p. 4): social media M = .54 h/day (SD 1.15); text .22 (.54), social networking sites .12 (.42), video chat .19 (.49).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional, ABCD baseline only. IV, mediator (sleep duration), and DVs all measured at the same visit; one observation per child. The direct effect of social media on each CBCL syndrome comes from a single multivariate path model in which all six screen-time variables predict sleep duration and all eight CBCL scales, and sleep duration predicts all eight CBCL scales.
primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.2 single structural equation model with negative binomial distribution for the eight CBCL count outcomes (overdispersion), maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR), TYPE = COMPLEX to account for non-independence of observations (clustering variable not named; presumably site or family). Multiple imputation for <1% missing data. Mediation via MODEL INDIRECT, with bootstrapping (B = 5000) for 95% CIs run without TYPE = COMPLEX because Mplus 8.2 does not allow both. IRRs are exponentiated B. Significance at p <= .05 with CI excluding zero (bold in tables). No multiple-comparison correction. No interaction or stratified analyses. No sensitivity analyses reported. Covariate associations are in Additional file 1 (not bundled in the PDF).
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2 (pp. 5-6), Social media rows; Fig. 1 (p. 7); interpreted in Results p. 3 and Discussion pp. 3-7
primary_models.equation: log E[CBCL_k] = b0k + b1k*SocialMedia + b2k*TV/movies + b3k*Videos + b4k*VideoGames + b5k*MatureVideoGames + b6k*RratedMovies + b7k*SleepDuration + b8k*sex + b9k*ethnicity + b10k*parent_ed + b11k*income + b12k*BMI + b13k*PA, CBCL_k ~ negative binomial, k = 1..8 syndrome scales, estimated jointly with the sleep-duration equation (M2). Focal term: b1k (direct effect); IRR = exp(b1k).

primary_models.estimation: Mplus 8.2 single structural equation model with negative binomial distribution for the eight CBCL count outcomes (overdispersion), maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR), TYPE = COMPLEX to account for non-independence of observations (clustering variable not named; presumably site or family). Multiple imputation for <1% missing data. Mediation via MODEL INDIRECT, with bootstrapping (B = 5000) for 95% CIs run without TYPE = COMPLEX because Mplus 8.2 does not allow both. IRRs are exponentiated B. Significance at p <= .05 with CI excluding zero (bold in tables). No multiple-comparison correction. No interaction or stratified analyses. No sensitivity analyses reported. Covariate associations are in Additional file 1 (not bundled in the PDF).
primary_models.dv: Sleep duration, one parent-reported item from the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children ('How many hours of sleep does your child get on most nights?'), in hours. Table 1 (n = 11,869): M = 9.00 h, SD 1.11. The paper does not state the distribution or link for this equation; it presumably is a linear (Gaussian) path, but Table 2 still prints an 'IRR' (exp(B)) for it.
primary_models.iv: Child self-reported social media time from the Youth Screen Time Survey (14 items). Social media is a composite of three items collapsed by the authors because of low use: texting, visiting social networking sites (e.g., Twitter, Instagram), and video chat (e.g., FaceTime); all three components are phone/SM items, so the composite qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. Each item asked hours on a typical weekday and weekend day on a 7-point scale (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, >=4 h); daily time = (weekday hours x 5 + weekend hours x 2)/7. The Methods state ST behaviors were then categorized into four groups (<1 h, 1-1.99 h, 2-2.99 h, >=3 h) for analysis, yet the Results interpret coefficients as 'every one hour increase'; the exact coding entering the model is therefore ambiguous. Table 1 (p. 4): social media M = .54 h/day (SD 1.15); text .22 (.54), social networking sites .12 (.42), video chat .19 (.49).

primary_models.equation: Indirect_k = a1 * b7k, where a1 is the social media -> sleep duration path (M2) and b7k the sleep duration -> CBCL_k path (negative binomial, log link). IRR = exp(indirect B).

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per one unit of the social media variable, which the authors describe as one hour/day; the Methods also state ST was categorized into four groups (<1 h, 1-1.99 h, 2-2.99 h, >=3 h), so one unit may be one category step.
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV = 1.15 h/day for social media and SD_DV = 1.11 h for sleep duration and CBCL raw-score SDs are from Table 1 (p. 4), full baseline sample (n = 11,769 for social media, 11,869 for sleep, 11,864 for CBCL). CBCL scales are raw scores, not T-scores, so SD_DV is not 10. The M2 conversion assumes the IV is in hours/day; if the model used the 4-category coding, SD_IV in hours is the wrong scale. The IRR->d approximation for negative binomial count outcomes is rough and ignores overdispersion. The aggressive behavior CI (.029, .053) printed in Table 2 excludes its own point estimate (.06), so its d CI should be treated with caution. M3 indirect effects are products of paths across a linear and a log-link equation with no standardized metric reported; not convertible to d. Completion pass (2026-10-01): all printed values verified against Tables 1-3; iv_type set to continuous for M1-M3; no SEs printed anywhere in the paper; IRR-scale CIs not printed (log-scale B CIs are).
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M1: IRR treated as OR at first approximation, d = ln(IRR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), with ln(IRR) = B; CI on d from the printed B CI endpoints, d_lo/hi = B_lo/hi * sqrt(3)/pi. M2: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV, d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2). M3: not converted.

primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal, two waves. All behaviors (including socializing) and covariates measured at ABCD baseline (2017-2018); outcome is BMI z-score at the one-year follow-up (2018-2019), a single follow-up value per child, with baseline BMI z-score as a covariate. Not repeated measures. Isotemporal substitution: for each sex, five linear regressions are fit, each dropping one behavior while keeping the other four plus total time, so each coefficient is the association of adding 30 min of the row behavior while removing 30 min of the dropped (column) behavior. Socializing is the qualifying phone/SM variable and appears both as the behavior added (row) and the behavior displaced (column). Phone/SM is the IV.

primary_models.iv: Baseline socializing screen time, defined as the sum of youth-reported texting, video chatting, and using social networking sites from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (weekday and weekend items; response options none, <30 min coded 0.5 h, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4+ h coded 4.8 h). Usual daily hours = weekday*0.71 + weekend*0.29, converted to minutes/day, then divided by 30 so one unit = 30 min/day. Weighted mean (SE) socializing: females 31.5 (2.0) min/day, males 22.3 (1.9) min/day (Table 1); overall 26.8 (1.9) min/day; 4,623 participants reported 0 min/day. Each estimate is a 30-min substitution: either 30 more min of socializing replacing 30 min of streaming, gaming, physical activity, or sleep, or 30 more min of one of those behaviors replacing 30 min of socializing. Other behaviors: streaming (TV shows/movies + videos e.g. YouTube), gaming (video games), physical activity (YRBSS days active >=60 min x 60 / 7), sleep (caregiver SDSC single item, category midpoints in minutes). SD of socializing not reported (only SE of mean).

primary_models.equation: For sex s and dropped (displaced) behavior R: BMIz_FU[i] = b0 + sum over k != R of b_k*(time_k[i]/30) + b_T*(total_time[i]/30) + b_age*age + b_race*race/ethnicity dummies + b_SES*income-to-needs dummies + b_int*internalizing + b_bmi*BMIz_baseline + e[i], where k ranges over {socializing, streaming, gaming, physical activity, sleep}. b_k is the association with adding 30 min/day of behavior k while removing 30 min/day of behavior R. Focal cells: k = socializing (R = each other behavior) and R = socializing (k = each other behavior).
primary_models.name: Sex-stratified isotemporal substitution survey linear regression of one-year follow-up BMI z-score on 30-min reallocations involving baseline socializing (texting + video chat + social networking), adjusted for baseline BMI z-score
primary_models.dv: BMI z-score at one-year follow-up, computed from staff-measured height and weight (triplicate) using the CDC 2000 Growth Chart SAS program (age- and sex-specific). Weighted mean (SE): females 0.49 (0.05), males 0.55 (0.05) (Table 1). Analyzed separately in females and males. Sample SD not reported.

primary_models.estimation: Linear regression with complex survey design in SAS v9.4 SURVEY procedures; study site specified as the cluster variable and ABCD sample weights applied to approximate the American Community Survey. Model formulation informed by a DAG (Supplemental Fig. 1, not bundled in this PDF). All analyses stratified by sex; no formal sex interaction test reported. Significance flagged *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001; exact p-values not printed. No multiple-comparison correction reported. Sensitivity analysis including participants whose reported time summed to > 24 h/day said to give qualitatively similar results (data not shown).
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0 (September 2021); baseline 2017-2018 and one-year follow-up 2018-2019, both pre-COVID. Of 11,876 enrolled, 156 were dropped for missing baseline exposure or covariate data (85 BMI z-score, 39 socializing, 7 gaming, 9 streaming, 10 physical activity, 4 internalizing, 2 race/ethnicity), 777 for missing follow-up BMI z-score, 78 for BMI z-score < -3 at baseline or follow-up, and 321 for > 13 h/day screen time (reports summing to > 24 h/day), giving an isotemporal substitution analytic N = 10,544 (Fig. 1). Analyses stratified by caregiver-reported sex assigned at birth: females n = 5,058 (48.9% weighted), males n = 5,486. Weighted mean (SE) baseline age 9.9 (0.03) in females and 10.0 (0.03) in males. Race/ethnicity, females / males, n (weighted %): Asian 120 (4.0%) / 107 (3.3%); Black 693 (12.3%) / 679 (11.0%); Hispanic 996 (23.0%) / 1,095 (23.5%); Other/Multiracial 534 (6.9%) / 565 (6.7%); White 2,715 (53.8%) / 3,040 (55.5%). Overall 45.4% non-White. Income-to-needs ratio range 0.1-15.4; 972 'not reported'.

primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal, two waves; same timing as M1 (baseline behaviors and covariates, BMI z-score at one-year follow-up as a single outcome, baseline BMI z-score as covariate). Secondary analysis. The 24-h day is treated as a six-part composition (socializing, streaming, gaming, physical activity, sleep, and 'other activities' = 1,440 min minus the sum of the five). Proportions are isometric log-ratio (ILR) transformed using sequential binary partitioning; separate regressions are fit with each behavior rotated into the first position, and only ILR 1 of each rotation is reported (12 models total, 6 per sex). The socializing estimate is the association of a greater proportion of time in socializing relative to the remaining behaviors (at their geometric mean) with follow-up BMI z-score. Phone/SM is the IV.

primary_models.iv: Baseline proportion of the 1,440-min day spent socializing (texting + video chatting + social networking sites; same instrument and scoring as M1), expressed as ILR 1 with socializing as the first component, i.e. the log-ratio of socializing to the geometric mean of the other five components. The authors illustrate that a 1% (14.4 min/day) increase in socializing relative to the remaining day in a male with baseline BMI z-score 0.50 corresponds to a predicted follow-up BMI z-score of 0.55.

primary_models.equation: For sex s, with socializing rotated first: BMIz_FU[i] = b0 + b1*ILR1[i] + b2*ILR2[i] + ... + b5*ILR5[i] + b_age*age + b_race*race/ethnicity + b_SES*income-to-needs + b_int*internalizing + b_bmi*BMIz_baseline + e[i], where ILR1 = sqrt(5/6) * ln( socializing / geometric_mean(streaming, gaming, physical activity, sleep, other activities) ). Only b1 is reported. (The sqrt(5/6) scaling follows standard sequential binary partitioning; the paper does not print the ILR formula.)
primary_models.dv: BMI z-score at one-year follow-up (CDC 2000 growth charts), analyzed separately by sex. Means for this subsample not reported by sex; overall included follow-up BMI z-score 0.57 (0.05) (Table 3).
primary_models.name: Sex-stratified compositional data analysis (ILR survey linear regression) of one-year follow-up BMI z-score on the baseline proportion of the day spent socializing relative to the remaining behaviors, adjusted for baseline BMI z-score
primary_models.estimation: Survey-weighted linear regression in R using the 'survey' package, with the same ABCD design features (site cluster, sample weights) as M1. Significance defined a priori as a 95% CI not crossing zero; no p-values printed; no multiple-comparison correction. Sex-stratified; no formal sex interaction test reported. Sensitivity analysis without 30-s replacement for zero physical activity reported as qualitatively similar in Supplemental Table 1 (not bundled in this PDF).
primary_models.sample: Subset of the M1 sample: 5,380 excluded for 0 min/day of socializing (n = 4,623), gaming (n = 746), or streaming (n = 11), leaving N = 5,164 (females n = 2,542, males n = 2,622). 50.4% female (weighted), baseline age 10.0 (0.03) years, 47.7% non-White. Included vs excluded differed in age, sex, race/ethnicity, all screen time forms, sleep, and BMI z-score (Table 3); included participants had socializing 46.8 (2.0) vs 6.2 (0.7) min/day. Zero minutes of physical activity (n = 574) replaced with 30 s using multiplicative replacement. Compositional means: socializing 2.4% of the day in females and 2.1% in males (Table 4).

d_transformation.native_metric: B (unstandardized isotemporal substitution coefficient, M1) + other: ILR regression coefficient (M2)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: None applied. Would require beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein 2009 eq 7.1), but no SDs are reported and the M1 contrast is a fixed-total-time substitution rather than a one-unit change in a single IV. M2 ILR coefficients are on a log-ratio scale with no reported SD of the ILR coordinate.
d_transformation.notes: Table 1 (p. 7) reports weighted means with standard errors, not SDs, for socializing (females 31.5 (2.0), males 22.3 (1.9) min/day) and follow-up BMI z-score (females 0.49 (0.05), males 0.55 (0.05)); SDs of the IV and DV in the analytic sample are not reported anywhere in the PDF. BMI z-score has reference-population SD 1 by construction, but the sample SD is not reported and the IV SD is still missing. Isotemporal substitution coefficients are conditional on total time and on the displaced behavior, so even with SDs a per-SD d would have no single-IV interpretation. CoDA ILR coefficients are not convertible without the SD of the ILR coordinate. Exact p-values are not printed for either model (M1 uses asterisks; M2 uses CI excluding 0). [complete-stage check] Re-read the whole PDF. No SDs, SEs of coefficients, or exact p are printed anywhere. SE*sqrt(n) applied to the Table 1 survey SEs gives implausible SDs (BMI z about 3.6), so it was not used. No supplement is bundled. [Complete pass 2026-10-01] Bundled supplement docx now checked: contains only Supplemental Fig. 1 (DAG) and Supplemental Table 1 (CoDA sensitivity without 30-s PA assignment, N=4,590; socializing F -0.01 [-0.02, 0.02], M 0.06 [0.02, 0.09]). No SEs, exact p-values, or SDs anywhere; transformability unchanged.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: adding 30 min/day of one behavior while removing 30 min/day of another (socializing added or displaced), total time fixed. M2: one-unit increase in ILR 1 (log-ratio of socializing to the geometric mean of the remaining five components).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) The qualifying IV is the 'socializing' composite (texting + video chat + social networking sites). Under §5 it counts as phone/SM-only, so it was extracted as the IV. 2) M1 is an isotemporal substitution model. For each sex I extracted all 8 cells that involve socializing in Table 2: the 4 cells in the ↑Socializing row, where socializing is added, and the 4 in the ↓Socializing column, where socializing is displaced. Each cell comes from a different drop-one regression. The authors anchor their claims on the column cells (PA replaces socializing in females; gaming and sleep replace socializing in males). Coders should decide whether to keep both directions. 3) For both models, Table 1 gives only weighted mean (SE), not SD, so sd_iv and sd_dv are null and d_transformable is false. BMI z has a reference SD of 1, but the sample SD is not reported. 4) No exact p-values are printed. M1 uses asterisks, which I recorded in p_label. M2 counts as significant when the CI excludes 0. 5) In Table 2, the females ↑Streaming/↓Socializing estimate is printed as '.003'; I recorded it as 0.003. 6) In the M2 equation, the sqrt(5/6) ILR scaling is my standard-SBP reconstruction; the paper does not print it. 7) Supplemental Table 1 and Supplemental Fig. 1 (the CoDA sensitivity analysis and the DAG) are not in the bundled PDF. 8) M2 drops the 4,623 participants with zero socializing, so it is a selected subsample (N = 5,164).

primary_models.dv: Parent/caregiver-reported CBCL DSM-oriented Affective (depression) Problems scale, 13 items scored 0-2, analyzed as a continuous sum score (scale range 0-26) at Year 5. Analytic sample M = 1.9, SD = 2.9, observed range 0-23 (Table 1). Residuals were right-skewed with many zeros.

primary_models.name: Multivariable linear regression of parent-reported CBCL depression symptoms on lifetime dating app use, adjusted for sociodemographics and site
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 6.0, Year 5 follow-up, adolescents aged 13-16 years. Of those enrolled, 3,305 were missing depression symptom data, 51 missing dating app data and 162 missing sociodemographic data, giving 8,444 complete cases (Appendix A). Missing data were handled with multiple imputation by chained equations (predictive mean matching, MAR assumption), imputing dating app use and depression symptoms from covariate information; final analytic N = 11,530. Mean age 15.0 years (SD 0.6, range 13.3-16.7); 47.9% female, 52.1% male; 52.7% White, 19.9% Black, 17.0% Latino/Hispanic, 6.1% Asian, 3.5% Native American, 0.9% Other (47.3% racial and ethnic minorities). Household income: 12.7% <=$24,999, 12.6% $25,000-49,999, 11.2% $50,000-74,999, 11.4% $75,000-99,999, 33.3% $100,000-199,999, 18.8% >=$200,000. Parent education: 14.7% high school or less, 85.3% college or more (Table 1, post-imputation).

primary_models.estimation: Multivariable linear regression reported as standardized beta coefficients, pooled across multiply imputed datasets (MICE with predictive mean matching). Heteroskedasticity-robust (cluster-robust) standard errors clustered at the family level to address heteroskedasticity and non-normality of residuals. Software not reported. No survey weights (baseline weights judged inappropriate for Year 5). Two-sided alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. No interaction or stratified analyses. Precision/stability checks and leave-one-site-out analyses reported narratively as stable (no numbers printed). Sensitivity model with additional covariates in Appendix D (see excluded_models). The unadjusted model in Table 2 is reported for comparison.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of a single ABCD wave (Year 5 follow-up, 2021-2023). Dating app use and depression symptoms measured at the same visit. One observation per adolescent; no repeated measures and no time interactions.
primary_models.iv: Lifetime dating app use from the adolescent item "Have you ever used a dating app?" (yes, no, don't know what that is), entered as a three-level categorical variable with "never used" as reference. Distribution after imputation: never used 98.8%, used 0.9%, don't know what it is 0.3% (Table 1). No information on recency, frequency, platform, or time spent was used; current use (4 participants) and weekly time on dating apps (0.4% >0 min) were judged too rare to analyze.

papers.title: Dating app use and depression symptoms in adolescents
papers.extraction_flags: 1) The paper calls its coefficients "standardized beta" but never says which variables were standardized. A fully standardized beta of 0.42 is implausible for a binary IV with 0.9% prevalence, so the value is probably standardized on Y only (d-like) or in raw score points. The r-to-d rule in guidelines 4a gives d of about 0.93, while passing the value through gives d of about 0.42. A human needs to choose before converting. 2) The PDF has only the 6 main-text pages. Appendices A-E are online-only, so the M2 values (youth-reported internalizing, Appendix E: 0.66, 0.34-0.99, p<0.001) and the Appendix D sensitivity values (0.44, 0.03-0.85, p=0.035) come from the Results text and could not be checked against the appendix tables. M2's covariates and N are assumed to match M1. 3) The 'don't know what a dating app is' vs never-used estimate (0.04, -0.33 to 0.41, p=0.817) is included in M1 with a note. It is not a use contrast, so coders may want to strike it. 4) N=11,530 is after multiple imputation of the exposure and the outcome; there are 8,444 complete cases. 5) SD_IV is not reported (binary exposure). SD_DV is 2.9 (Table 1).json

d_transformation.contrast_type: Ever used a dating app vs. never used (binary group contrast)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Coefficients are treated as Y-standardized mean differences for a binary IV (ever used vs never used dating apps), i.e. already on the Cohen's d scale: d = beta. Not passed through r -> d.
d_transformation.notes: Paper labels them 'standardized betas' without saying which variables were standardized. With a binary IV at 0.9% prevalence a fully standardized beta of 0.42-0.66 is impossible, so they are read as Y-standardized group differences (SD units of the outcome) and used directly as d. Coders should confirm against Appendix E. The paper labels coefficients as standardized betas from linear regression but does not say whether X, Y, or both were standardized. With a binary IV at 0.9% prevalence, a fully standardized beta of 0.42 would be implausibly large, so the value most likely reflects Y-standardized units (i.e., a mean difference of about 0.42 SD of the depression score, d-like) or possibly raw score points. SD_DV for CBCL depression sum score = 2.9 (Table 1, p. 3). SD_IV not reported (binary indicator, 0.9% used, Table 1). Applying r-to-d to 0.42 gives a very different d than passthrough, so the human coder should decide which interpretation applies before conversion. M2 SD_DV not available (Appendix E not in PDF). [complete stage] Verified against full PDF: M1 cluster-robust SEs 0.17 (used) and 0.19 (don't know) added as 'se'; CIs already printed. No supplement file bundled; M2 sd_dv remains unavailable.

papers.extraction_flags:
The qualifying estimates are missing from the PDF. All of the texting, social media and video chat coefficients are in Supplementary Tables S6-S31: S6-S18 cover weekday use and S19-S31 cover weekend use, with one table per outcome, each split by sex. PLOS ONE publishes these as separate DOCX files, and they are not bundled in the 23-page PDF. Pages 18-21 list only their titles. I did not download them, because downloading a file needs explicit permission.

I set up two model cards. M1 covers weekday use (N=11,727) and M2 covers weekend use (N=11,672). Each card has the full specification, 6 IV slots (3 modalities x 2 sexes) and 13 DV slots, but the estimates are empty (n_estimates = 0). A human needs to get S6-S31, for example from journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0256591, and fill in about 156 cells (2 day types x 2 sexes x 3 modalities x 13 outcomes).

Things to check against the supplement:
(1) Whether each screen type was its own regression or all types were entered together in one regression per outcome. The PDF does not say.
(2) Whether the supplement tables report standardized beta, t, p, SE and partial r, like Tables 3 and 5. I assumed beta_std is the native metric.
(3) Race/ethnicity (coded 1-5) and SES (coded 1-10) look like they were entered as single numeric predictors, because Tables 2 and 4 show one coefficient each. The paper does not confirm this.
(4) These per-type analyses are labelled secondary and tested at alpha .05 with no correction.

SD_IV for each modality, day type and sex comes from Table 1 (p. 8). I spot-checked all 12 against the table. SD_DV for the CBCL outcomes is set to 10 by construction, but the in-sample SDs are about 5-11. That does not matter for conversion, because beta_std converts directly once the values are in. d_transformable is false only because no values are available yet. It becomes true once the supplement is entered.

The ABCD release number is not stated; the paper cites only NDA DOI 10.15154/1519271. The headline total-screen-time models in Tables 2-5 were excluded because total screen time includes TV, videos and gaming.

primary_models.estimation: IBM SPSS Statistics Version 26. Ordinary least squares multiple linear regression, run separately by sex. Output reported as standardized beta, t statistic, p-value, standard error and partial correlation (format of main-text Tables 3 and 5; the supplementary tables are described as including effect sizes). No survey weights, no site or family random effects, no clustering adjustment (siblings/twins retained). Per-type-of-screen-time regressions are labelled secondary tests and evaluated at alpha = .05 with no multiple-comparison correction (the Bonferroni alpha of .004 applies only to the 13 primary total-screen-time regressions). Sex moderation was tested only for total screen time (sex x ST interaction, Tables 2/4); no sex x modality interaction is reported. The paper does not state whether each screen type was entered in its own regression or all types were entered jointly in one regression per outcome; the table titles ('regressed on various types of ... screen time') and Stage 2 notes suggest separate regressions per type, which needs checking against the supplement. No sensitivity analyses reported. The authors state that the analyses assume normality and that variables are only approximately normal.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit. The study is split into Part 1 (weekday screen time) and Part 2 (weekend screen time), each with its own exclusions and analytic sample; this card is Part 1 (weekday). Screen time and all outcomes come from the same baseline visit. One observation per child, no repeated measures.
primary_models.iv: Child-reported hours per typical weekday day spent on texting (on cellphone, tablet, or computer), visiting social media sites, and video chat, from the 14-item youth Screen Time Questionnaire (recreational, not schoolwork). Each item response runs from '0 h' to '4+ h' and is analyzed in hours. One modality per IV slot; analyses run separately for males and females. Descriptives (Table 1, Part 1): see iv_axis meta. Very low means and floor effects at age 9-10, as the authors note in the Limitations (p. 17).

primary_models.estimation: IBM SPSS Statistics Version 26. Ordinary least squares multiple linear regression, run separately by sex. Output reported as standardized beta, t statistic, p-value, standard error and partial correlation (format of main-text Tables 3 and 5; the supplementary tables are described as including effect sizes). No survey weights, no site or family random effects, no clustering adjustment (siblings/twins retained). Per-type-of-screen-time regressions are labelled secondary tests and evaluated at alpha = .05 with no multiple-comparison correction (the Bonferroni alpha of .004 applies only to the 13 primary total-screen-time regressions). Sex moderation was tested only for total screen time (sex x ST interaction, Tables 2/4); no sex x modality interaction is reported. The paper does not state whether each screen type was entered in its own regression or all types were entered jointly in one regression per outcome; the table titles ('regressed on various types of ... screen time') and Stage 2 notes suggest separate regressions per type, which needs checking against the supplement. No sensitivity analyses reported. The authors state that the analyses assume normality and that variables are only approximately normal.

papers.extraction_flags: The PDF at the items.json path is already the 19-page NIH author manuscript (modified Oct 1 02:43), so I extracted from it. (1) Supplemental Tables S1-S28 are in an Excel appendix that is not among the files I had. All 9 estimates were copied from the Results text (pp. 5-6) and checked against Figures 2-3 and the abstract, but these are not available: exact per-outcome Ns (listwise deletion), the problematic-use exclusion (S12), the continuous-outcome linear mixed models (S14-S22) and the 3-wave longitudinal models (S23-S28). If the Excel file is obtained, the continuous-outcome models could become additional model cards. (2) M2 ORs are inverted by the authors (per 1 year EARLIER acquisition). The SD of age at acquisition is not reported (median 11, IQR 10-11), so d for M2 is per year, not per SD. (3) p0 for M1 is the non-owner prevalence from Table 1. For M2 it is the owner prevalence, since there is no unexposed group. For M3 it is null, because 3-year outcome rates are not reported. Chinn's OR-to-d conversion does not need p0. (4) The race covariate is described as 'race and ethnicity' in the main text but as 'Black race and Hispanic ethnicity' in eMethods 3; I followed eMethods. (5) Three separate cards were used because the analytic samples differ (all youth, owners only, and non-owners at age 12), and M3 adds the prior-year outcome. (6) p-values printed as '<.001' are stored as p = null with p_label.

primary_models.location_in_paper: Analysis 1. Results p. 5-6 (adjusted Model 2 ORs printed in text); Figure 2A (p. 15, Model 2 shown in red); full model output in Supplemental Tables S3-S5 (appendix Excel file, not in the extracted PDFs). Interpreted in Abstract and Discussion p. 7.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Smartphone ownership and all three outcomes are measured at the same visit, the ABCD 2-year follow-up (mean age ~12). One observation per child; no repeated measures. Smartphone ownership was first assessed at the 2-year follow-up, which is why this wave is the analytic baseline. A longitudinal version pooling the 2-, 3- and 4-year follow-ups was run only as a sensitivity analysis (see excluded models).
primary_models.iv: Smartphone ownership at the 2-year follow-up, binary (1 = owns a smartphone, 0 = does not). Caregiver report to "Does your child have their own cellphone?" plus a follow-up item on device type; iPhone or Android counted as a smartphone. 63.6% (6,739/10,588) owned a smartphone at this wave.
primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 12 on smartphone ownership (yes vs no), fully adjusted Model 2
primary_models.estimation: Mixed-effects logistic regression in R 4.5.0, package lme4 (glmer). Nested random intercepts for family within research site. No survey weights reported. Two models per outcome built stepwise: Model 1 adjusts for age and sex only; Model 2 (extracted here) is the fully adjusted model the authors interpret. Listwise deletion of missing data. Bonferroni-type threshold P < 0.017 (0.05/3) for the three outcomes. Sex x exposure interactions tested; none significant in the main analyses. Sensitivity analyses: excluding youth with problematic smartphone use (MPIQ mean > 5; Supplemental Table S12), E-values for Model 2 (S13), linear mixed models with continuous outcomes (S14-S16), and longitudinal models pooling 2-, 3- and 4-year follow-ups (S23-S25); all described as similar in direction and significance.
