d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a).
d_transformation.notes: All estimates are reported as standardized betas, so SD_IV and SD_DV are not needed for conversion. SDs recorded for reference from Table 1 (pp. 4-5): average social media use over 4 years 1.0 h/day; T0 combined ADHD 3.0, inattention 1.9, hyperactivity-impulsivity 1.8. Convertible: M1 social media main effects, M2 cumulative beta 0.15, M3 cross-lagged paths, M4 reverse paths (SM as DV). Caveats: (1) the M1 SM x time coefficients are differences in yearly slope, so a d derived from them is a per-year rate, not a level difference, and is not comparable to cross-sectional d's; (2) the three-way SM x time x PGS-ADHD terms are moderation effects and should not be converted; (3) how the authors standardized variables inside lmer (both sides z-scored vs. partial standardization) is not described; (4) only SEs are reported, no CIs, so d CIs cannot be formed without computing beta +/- 1.96*SE, which the extraction rules prohibit. The M4 total effect has no SE or p. [complete pass] SEs moved into 'se' field for all 13 estimates with printed SEs (Table 2 p.6; Abstract; Results pp.5-6). No CIs are printed anywhere in the PDF; the two docs/pdfs files are the same article (different download), no supplement file is bundled. iv_type = continuous for all models.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 SD of social media use (hours/day) in SD units of the symptom score; for M1 SM x time terms, per 1 SD of average social media use difference in the yearly symptom slope; for M2, per 1 SD of average social media use in the 4-year inattention change score.

primary_models.dv: Parent-reported CBCL ADHD symptoms at every visit, as three continuous scores run in separate models: (1) combined ADHD = CBCL DSM-5-oriented ADHD scale raw score (cbcl_scr_dsm5_adhd; alpha > 0.72 at all time points); (2) inattention = 4 CBCL items retained by factor analysis (loading > 0.3) of the 9 DSM-5 ADHD items, correlated r = 0.93 with the CBCL inattention summary score at T0; (3) hyperactivity-impulsivity = 5 items from the same factor analysis. T0 means (SD): combined 2.7 (3.0), inattention 1.7 (1.9), hyperactivity-impulsivity 1.3 (1.8) (Table 1). Raw item sums, not T-scores.
primary_models.equation: ADHD_DV[i,t] = b0 + b1*SM_avg[i] + b2*time[t] + b3*SM_avg[i]*time[t] + b4*age_T0[i] + b5*sex[i] + b6*SES[i] + b7*PGS_ADHD[i] + b8*SM_avg[i]*time[t]*PGS_ADHD[i] (with lower-order terms) + b9..b18*genPC1-10[i] + u_site + u0_i + u1_i*time[t] + e[i,t]. Focal: b3 (SM x time); b1 (SM level) and b8 (genetic moderation) also printed.
primary_models.design: Longitudinal cohort, ABCD baseline (T0, ages 9-10) and four annual follow-ups (T1-T4). The outcome enters as repeated measures at T0-T4 (not averaged), with random intercepts and slopes. The exposure is a single time-invariant value per child: average daily social media hours across all available visits (T0-T4), chosen by the authors to absorb the COVID-19-era increase in use. The focal longitudinal term is the two-way social media use x time interaction (described by the authors as the between-person longitudinal effect, i.e. difference in yearly symptom slope); the social media main effect is the association with symptom level at time = 0. A three-way social media use x time x PGS-ADHD term tests genetic moderation of the slope. Because the exposure is averaged over the same waves as the outcome, IV and DV are not strictly temporally ordered.
primary_models.estimation: R 3.5 (RStudio), lmer in lme4, restricted maximum likelihood. Random intercepts and slopes; study site as random effect. Separate model per DM category (social media, video games, TV/videos) and per symptom score (combined, inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity). Coefficients reported as standardized beta (SE); no CIs or exact p-values printed in Table 2. Alpha 0.05 with Bonferroni correction for 9 tests (0.05/9 = 0.005); Table 2 footnotes mark a = <0.001 and b = <0.005 (Bonferroni corrected). Authors define yearly standardized beta > 0.05 or cumulative beta > 0.10 as meaningful. Moderation of significant DM x time effects by sex, ADHD diagnosis at T0, and ADHD medication at T0 tested in separate models (Supplemental Tables 1-3, not bundled in the PDF; reported non-significant). Sensitivity analyses (at-term births only; typically developing children only; complete behavioral data only; follow-up truncated at T3) reported narratively as consistent (Supplemental Tables 4-8, not bundled).

primary_models.iv: Average daily social media use (texting + social networking sites + video chat) across T0-T4, hours/day; mean 1.4 (SD 1.0) (Table 1). For Figure 2B the authors split it into quartiles (Q1 <0.54, Q2 >=0.54 to <1.36, Q3 >=1.36 to <1.86, Q4 >=1.86 hours/day in the panel legend; the Figure 2 caption instead gives cutoffs 0.61, 1.22, 1.97), but the reported beta uses the continuous variable.
primary_models.design: Longitudinal change-score analysis. DV is the single difference score in inattention from baseline (T0) to 4-year follow-up (T4); IV is average social media use across T0-T4. One observation per child. Authors present this as the cumulative 4-year effect corresponding to the yearly SM x time slope in M1, and anchor their population-level interpretation (0.15 SD) to it.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. The supplement is not bundled in the 10-page PDF. As a result, the M2 cumulative-change covariates, the CLPM (M3) covariates, missing-data handling and estimator, the full M4 reverse-direction spec, Supplemental Tables 1-8 (moderation and sensitivity analyses) and analytic Ns other than 8,324 could not be checked.
2. The 'social media use' IV is a composite of texting, social networking sites and video chat (YSTS items 4+5+6). All three items are phone/SM, so it qualifies under Step 2. Texting is asked as cell phone/tablet/computer, which is activity-defined and qualifies under clarification 5.
3. The exposure is averaged over T0-T4, the same waves as the outcome, so the IV and DV are not temporally ordered in M1 and M2.
4. In M1 the authors anchor on the SM x time interaction, which gives a difference in yearly slope. A d derived from it is a per-year rate. I included the three-way SM x time x PGS-ADHD terms as estimates and flagged them as not convertible; a coder may prefer to strike them.
5. Table 2 prints only beta (SE) with Bonferroni footnote markers. Cells without a marker are coded sig=false with p null. CIs are null throughout and the SEs are in the notes.
6. In M3 the CLPM cross-lagged values look constrained equal across lags; this is inferred from the figure.
7. The M4 total effect (-0.01) has no SE or p. sig=false is set only because no test is reported.
8. The Figure 2 caption quartile cutoffs (0.61/1.22/1.97) disagree with the Figure 2B panel legend (0.54/1.36/1.86).
9. The year is recorded as 2025 per items.json, but the journal issue is Vol 2, Issue 1, 2026.
10. Spot-checked all 9 Table 2 social media cells plus the in-text values 0.15, 0.03/p=.004, -0.002/p=.64 and -0.01/SE 0.001 against the PDF text layer; all match.

primary_models.estimation: R 3.5 (RStudio), lmer in lme4, restricted maximum likelihood. Random intercepts and slopes; study site as random effect. Separate model per DM category (social media, video games, TV/videos) and per symptom score (combined, inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity). Coefficients reported as standardized beta (SE); no CIs or exact p-values printed in Table 2. Alpha 0.05 with Bonferroni correction for 9 tests (0.05/9 = 0.005); Table 2 footnotes mark a = <0.001 and b = <0.005 (Bonferroni corrected). Authors define yearly standardized beta > 0.05 or cumulative beta > 0.10 as meaningful. Moderation of significant DM x time effects by sex, ADHD diagnosis at T0, and ADHD medication at T0 tested in separate models (Supplemental Tables 1-3, not bundled in the PDF; reported non-significant). Sensitivity analyses (at-term births only; typically developing children only; complete behavioral data only; follow-up truncated at T3) reported narratively as consistent (Supplemental Tables 4-8, not bundled).
primary_models.dv: Parent-reported CBCL ADHD symptoms at every visit, as three continuous scores run in separate models: (1) combined ADHD = CBCL DSM-5-oriented ADHD scale raw score (cbcl_scr_dsm5_adhd; alpha > 0.72 at all time points); (2) inattention = 4 CBCL items retained by factor analysis (loading > 0.3) of the 9 DSM-5 ADHD items, correlated r = 0.93 with the CBCL inattention summary score at T0; (3) hyperactivity-impulsivity = 5 items from the same factor analysis. T0 means (SD): combined 2.7 (3.0), inattention 1.7 (1.9), hyperactivity-impulsivity 1.3 (1.8) (Table 1). Raw item sums, not T-scores.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Data Release 5.0. Of 11,875 enrolled children, 8,324 included at T0 after excluding children born extremely preterm (<28 weeks), birthweight <1200 g, not English-proficient, neurological problems, history of seizures, or MRI contraindication, and keeping one randomly selected child per family. Follow-up >85% through T3 and 43% at T4. Mean age at T0 9.9 (SD 0.6); 4,408 (53.0%) male. Race/ethnicity: White 4,356 (52.3%), Black 1,358 (16.3%), Hispanic 1,763 (21.2%), Asian 496 (6.0%), Native American 183 (2.2%), Pacific Islander 2 (0.02%), Other 106 (1.3%). primary_models.design: Longitudinal cohort, ABCD baseline (T0, ages 9-10) and four annual follow-ups (T1-T4). The outcome enters as repeated measures at T0-T4 (not averaged), with random intercepts and slopes. The exposure is a single time-invariant value per child: average daily social media hours across all available visits (T0-T4), chosen by the authors to absorb the COVID-19-era increase in use. The focal longitudinal term is the two-way social media use x time interaction (described by the authors as the between-person longitudinal effect, i.e. difference in yearly symptom slope); the social media main effect is the association with symptom level at time = 0. A three-way social media use x time x PGS-ADHD term tests genetic moderation of the slope. Because the exposure is averaged over the same waves as the outcome, IV and DV are not strictly temporally ordered.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. The supplement is not bundled in the 10-page PDF. As a result, the M2 cumulative-change covariates, the CLPM (M3) covariates, missing-data handling and estimator, the full M4 reverse-direction spec, Supplemental Tables 1-8 (moderation and sensitivity analyses) and analytic Ns other than 8,324 could not be checked.
2. The 'social media use' IV is a composite of texting, social networking sites and video chat (YSTS items 4+5+6). All three items are phone/SM, so it qualifies under Step 2. Texting is asked as cell phone/tablet/computer, which is activity-defined and qualifies under clarification 5.
3. The exposure is averaged over T0-T4, the same waves as the outcome, so the IV and DV are not temporally ordered in M1 and M2.
4. In M1 the authors anchor on the SM x time interaction, which gives a difference in yearly slope. A d derived from it is a per-year rate. I included the three-way SM x time x PGS-ADHD terms as estimates and flagged them as not convertible; a coder may prefer to strike them.
5. Table 2 prints only beta (SE) with Bonferroni footnote markers. Cells without a marker are coded sig=false with p null. CIs are null throughout and the SEs are in the notes.
6. In M3 the CLPM cross-lagged values look constrained equal across lags; this is inferred from the figure.
7. The M4 total effect (-0.01) has no SE or p. sig=false is set only because no test is reported.
8. The Figure 2 caption quartile cutoffs (0.61/1.22/1.97) disagree with the Figure 2B panel legend (0.54/1.36/1.86).
9. The year is recorded as 2025 per items.json, but the journal issue is Vol 2, Issue 1, 2026.
10. Spot-checked all 9 Table 2 social media cells plus the in-text values 0.15, 0.03/p=.004, -0.002/p=.64 and -0.01/SE 0.001 against the PDF text layer; all match.

d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 SD of social media use (hours/day) in SD units of the symptom score; for M1 SM x time terms, per 1 SD of average social media use difference in the yearly symptom slope; for M2, per 1 SD of average social media use in the 4-year inattention change score.
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a).
d_transformation.notes: All estimates are reported as standardized betas, so SD_IV and SD_DV are not needed for conversion. SDs recorded for reference from Table 1 (pp. 4-5): average social media use over 4 years 1.0 h/day; T0 combined ADHD 3.0, inattention 1.9, hyperactivity-impulsivity 1.8. Convertible: M1 social media main effects, M2 cumulative beta 0.15, M3 cross-lagged paths, M4 reverse paths (SM as DV). Caveats: (1) the M1 SM x time coefficients are differences in yearly slope, so a d derived from them is a per-year rate, not a level difference, and is not comparable to cross-sectional d's; (2) the three-way SM x time x PGS-ADHD terms are moderation effects and should not be converted; (3) how the authors standardized variables inside lmer (both sides z-scored vs. partial standardization) is not described; (4) only SEs are reported, no CIs, so d CIs cannot be formed without computing beta +/- 1.96*SE, which the extraction rules prohibit. The M4 total effect has no SE or p. [complete pass] SEs moved into 'se' field for all 13 estimates with printed SEs (Table 2 p.6; Abstract; Results pp.5-6). No CIs are printed anywhere in the PDF; the two docs/pdfs files are the same article (different download), no supplement file is bundled. iv_type = continuous for all models.

papers.extraction_flags:
1. Where the numbers come from: every estimate is a B copied from the Results text on pp. 730-731. The paper has no results table, and the full edge matrix is in supplementary eTable 10, which is not in the PDF. Fig. 4B hides edges with |B| < 0.05. So only the edges the authors chose to report in the text are extracted. There may be other A2/A3 edges that are non-zero but not reported.

2. pdftotext drops minus signs. I checked the page image: A2→C5 in the female network is B = −0.251. The positive signs on the other A2/A3 edges match the narrative text.

3. No SE, CI or p-value is reported for any edge. I set sig=true on every estimate on the basis that the edge is non-zero after LASSO and the authors describe these as significant associations. A coder should decide whether that is acceptable.

4. The male A2→C1 edge is printed with the symbol β instead of B (0.113). I assume it is the same metric as the other edges.

5. On d_transformable=false: the paper says covariate-residualized standardized residuals were used, so the coefficients may in effect be in SD units. However, they are LASSO-shrunk and conditional on 19 other T2 nodes, including the autoregressive term. Following the rule that network edges are non-convertible, I marked the paper not transformable. A coder could choose to treat them as approximate beta_std instead.

6. E4 (perceived school environment) and E5 (positive school involvement) are reverse-scored. A positive B therefore means a more adverse school environment and lower school involvement. Whether perceived school environment counts as an individual-trait or a contextual variable should be checked.

7. Cross-sectional GGM edges involving social media time (B2), checking (B3), A2 and A3 with CBCL/UPPS/BIS/BAS appear only in figures (Fig. 2A, Fig. 3) and in supplementary eTables 8-9. I excluded them rather than read values off the figures. A coder may want to pull eTable 8 from the online supplement.

8. Whether CBCL raw scores or T-scores were used is not stated. The PDF reports no SDs for SMAQ, MPIQ or the outcomes.

primary_models.dv: T4 nodes on the other side of the cross-lagged edge. CBCL syndrome scales, caregiver-report (C1 anxious/depressed, C2 withdrawn/depressed, C3 somatic complaints, C4 social problems, C5 thought problems, C6 attention problems, C7 rule-breaking, C8 aggressive); impulsivity from the brief UPPS-P (UPPS); Behavioral Inhibition (BIS) and Behavioral Activation (BAS) from the BIS/BAS scale; environmental factors E1 family conflict (FES conflict subscale), E2 prosocial peer involvement (Peer Behavior Profile, reverse scored), E3 delinquent peer involvement / peer rule-break (Peer Behavior Profile), E4 perceived school environment (SRPF, reverse scored, so higher = more adverse), E5 positive school involvement (SRPF, reverse scored, so higher = less involvement), E6 school disengagement (SRPF). Whether CBCL raw or T-scores were used is not stated. All entered as standardized residuals after covariate adjustment.
primary_models.equation: node_j,T4[i] = b0 + a_j*node_j,T2[i] + sum_{k != j} b_jk*node_k,T2[i] + e[i], estimated for each of the 20 T4 nodes, with all nodes as standardized residuals after regressing on age, race, ethnicity, parental marital status, parental education and family income. Focal coefficients: b_j,A2 (problematic social media at T2 -> node j at T4) and b_j,A3 (problematic mobile phone at T2 -> node j at T4). Coefficients are LASSO-penalized (L1) so small coefficients are shrunk to exactly zero.
primary_models.name: Cross-lagged panel network (LASSO-regularized regressions) of T4 psychopathology, behavioral tendencies and environment on T2 problematic social media and mobile phone use, female network, covariate-residualized
primary_models.estimation: R (glmnet for LASSO; qgraph for plotting; bootnet; NetworkComparisonTest). LASSO-penalized maximum-likelihood regression with 10-fold cross-validation to select the tuning parameter. No random effects or weights; one child randomly selected per family to ensure independence. Missing data: minimum-value imputation for structurally missing problematic-use items, predictive mean matching for remaining missingness (MCAR per Little's test, eFigs 2-4). No p-values, confidence intervals or multiple-comparison correction are reported for individual cross-lagged edges; edges reported in text are non-zero LASSO coefficients and the authors describe them as significant associations. Mean autoregressive B: female 0.406, male 0.391; mean cross-lagged B: female 0.012, male 0.013. Stability via CS coefficients (eFig. 12); female/male network structure correlation r = 0.47, t = 10.382, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.39, 0.55]. Sensitivity analyses with pairwise deletion and categorical problematic-use indicators reported only in supplementary eFigs 18 and 21 (narrative: results stable). Sex differences handled by stratification; no formal sex x edge test for the CLPN.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1. Youth with data at both the 2-year (T2) and 4-year (T4) follow-up; one child randomly selected per family. Total CLPN sample N = 3,954 (abstract and Table 1); this female network N = 1,863 (47.12% of the CLPN sample). Females: age at T2 143.21 months (SD 7.77), age at T4 168.53 months (SD 7.88). Race: White 1,250 (67%), Black 225 (12%), Asian 52 (2.8%), mixed/other 336 (18%). Hispanic 394 (21%), non-Hispanic 1,469 (79%). Parents married/living with partner 1,400 (75%); parental education college 1,420 (76%); family income <$25,000 274 (15%) through $200,000+ 207 (11%) (Table 1, p. 727).
primary_models.design: Longitudinal two-wave cross-lagged panel network (CLPN). Predictors are the 20 nodes measured at the ABCD 2-year follow-up (T2, ages 11-12, 2018-2020); outcomes are the same 20 nodes at the 4-year follow-up (T4, ages 13-14, 2020-2022). Each T4 node is regressed on all 20 T2 nodes, including its own T2 value (autoregressive path), so each cross-lagged coefficient is the prediction of a T4 node by a T2 node adjusted for all other T2 nodes. The 20 nodes are 3 problematic-use nodes (A1 problematic video game, A2 problematic social media, A3 problematic mobile phone), 8 CBCL syndrome scales (C1-C8), 3 behavioral-tendency nodes (UPPS, BIS, BAS) and 6 environmental nodes (E1-E6). Screen-time and phone-checking nodes from the cross-sectional networks were not carried into the CLPN. 20 x 19 = 380 possible cross-lagged edges per network. Single follow-up, no repeated measures beyond the two waves. Networks estimated separately by sex.
primary_models.iv: Problematic use at T2, entered as continuous scale scores. A2 = Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ); A3 = Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire (MPIQ; Walsh, White, & Young, 2010). Missing problematic-use items due to not meeting prerequisites (no social media account, no mobile phone) were imputed with the minimum scale value ("never"); other missing data imputed with predictive mean matching in the CLPN. All variables were residualized on covariates and the standardized residuals entered the network. Descriptive statistics for SMAQ/MPIQ are not in the main PDF (supplementary materials only). A1 (problematic video game, VGAQ) is also a T2 predictor node but is not a qualifying modality.

primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1. Youth with data at both the 2-year (T2) and 4-year (T4) follow-up; one child randomly selected per family. Total CLPN sample N = 3,954; this male network N = 2,091. Males: age at T2 143.11 months (SD 7.72), age at T4 168.63 months (SD 8.13). Race: White 1,491 (71%), Black 216 (10%), Asian 55 (2.6%), mixed/other 329 (16%). Hispanic 458 (22%), non-Hispanic 1,633 (78%). Parents married/living with partner 1,612 (77%); parental education college 1,586 (76%); family income <$25,000 319 (15%) through $200,000+ 231 (11%) (Table 1, p. 727).

primary_models.name: Cross-lagged panel network (LASSO-regularized regressions) of T4 psychopathology, behavioral tendencies and environment on T2 problematic social media and mobile phone use, male network, covariate-residualized
primary_models.dv: T4 nodes on the other side of the cross-lagged edge. CBCL syndrome scales, caregiver-report (C1 anxious/depressed, C2 withdrawn/depressed, C3 somatic complaints, C4 social problems, C5 thought problems, C6 attention problems, C7 rule-breaking, C8 aggressive); impulsivity from the brief UPPS-P (UPPS); Behavioral Inhibition (BIS) and Behavioral Activation (BAS) from the BIS/BAS scale; environmental factors E1 family conflict (FES conflict subscale), E2 prosocial peer involvement (Peer Behavior Profile, reverse scored), E3 delinquent peer involvement / peer rule-break (Peer Behavior Profile), E4 perceived school environment (SRPF, reverse scored, so higher = more adverse), E5 positive school involvement (SRPF, reverse scored, so higher = less involvement), E6 school disengagement (SRPF). Whether CBCL raw or T-scores were used is not stated. All entered as standardized residuals after covariate adjustment.
primary_models.equation: node_j,T4[i] = b0 + a_j*node_j,T2[i] + sum_{k != j} b_jk*node_k,T2[i] + e[i], estimated for each of the 20 T4 nodes, with all nodes as standardized residuals after regressing on age, race, ethnicity, parental marital status, parental education and family income. Focal coefficients: b_j,A2 (problematic social media at T2 -> node j at T4) and b_j,A3 (problematic mobile phone at T2 -> node j at T4). Coefficients are LASSO-penalized (L1) so small coefficients are shrunk to exactly zero.
primary_models.estimation: R (glmnet for LASSO; qgraph for plotting; bootnet; NetworkComparisonTest). LASSO-penalized maximum-likelihood regression with 10-fold cross-validation to select the tuning parameter. No random effects or weights; one child randomly selected per family to ensure independence. Missing data: minimum-value imputation for structurally missing problematic-use items, predictive mean matching for remaining missingness (MCAR per Little's test, eFigs 2-4). No p-values, confidence intervals or multiple-comparison correction are reported for individual cross-lagged edges; edges reported in text are non-zero LASSO coefficients and the authors describe them as significant associations. Mean autoregressive B: female 0.406, male 0.391; mean cross-lagged B: female 0.012, male 0.013. Stability via CS coefficients (eFig. 12); female/male network structure correlation r = 0.47, t = 10.382, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.39, 0.55]. Sensitivity analyses with pairwise deletion and categorical problematic-use indicators reported only in supplementary eFigs 18 and 21 (narrative: results stable). Sex differences handled by stratification; no formal sex x edge test for the CLPN.

primary_models.sample: ABCD baseline (enrollment September 2016 to October 2018, 21 U.S. sites); data release not stated. 10,842 children were included, of whom 187 (1.7%) had parent-reported autism. Propensity-score matching (1:5 nine-digit greedy match) produced an analytic sample of 186 children with autism and 930 typically developing (TD) children (N = 1,116); one child with autism could not be matched and was dropped. Matched sample (Table 1, p. 4): age 9 years 45.2%, 10 years 54.8%; mean age 10.0 (SD 0.6); 85.5% boys (159 autism, 795 TD) and 14.5% girls (27 autism, 135 TD); 53.8% non-Hispanic White, 15.6% Hispanic, 13.4% non-Hispanic Black, 1.6% non-Hispanic Asian, 15.6% non-Hispanic other/multi-race; distributions identical across autism and TD groups by design. 35 of 186 (18.8%) children with autism and 134 of 930 (14.4%) TD children were obese. Cell sizes in this model: boys 159 autism vs 795 TD; girls 27 autism vs 135 TD.
primary_models.name: Poisson GEE (log link) of child-reported social/video chat and texting minutes per day on autism status, crossed with gender, in a propensity-matched sample
primary_models.estimation: SAS 9.4. Generalized linear models estimated with generalized estimating equations; Poisson distribution with log link chosen because screen time was count-like and positively skewed; compound-symmetry working correlation for within-site clustering. Effect reported as ratio of means (autism / TD) with 95% CI. Alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. No sample or propensity weights beyond 1:5 matching. No sensitivity analyses reported.
primary_models.dv: Two phone/SM screen-time categories from the child-reported ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, each in minutes per day: (1) social and video chat = visiting social networking sites (e.g., Facebook, Twitter, Instagram) plus video chatting; (2) texting. The 7-point responses (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4+ h) were recoded to 0, 15, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240 min, and daily time = [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)]/7. Overall sample means: 17.1 min/day social networking or video chat and 12.4 min/day texting (p. 4). Group means are in Table 2: social/video chat boys 16.9 (autism) vs 15.5 (TD), girls 45.5 vs 21.9; texting boys 11.4 vs 12.5, girls 14.6 vs 13.8. SDs not reported.
primary_models.equation: log(E[minutes_per_day[i,site]]) = b0 + b1*autism[i] + b2*girl[i] + b3*autism[i]*girl[i]; ratio of means autism vs TD = exp(b1) for boys and exp(b1 + b3) for girls; Poisson GEE, compound-symmetry working correlation within site. Fit separately for social/video chat minutes and texting minutes.

primary_models.iv: Three-category daily duration of each phone/SM screen type, derived from the child-reported ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (weighted daily minutes = [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)]/7, responses recoded 0-240 min). Social and video chat (social networking sites plus video chat): 0 min (reference), 1-44 min, 45 min or more. Texting: 0 min (reference), 1-29 min, 30 min or more. Each non-zero category is contrasted with the 0-min reference.

primary_models.name: Log-binomial GEE of obesity on categorized social/video chat and texting duration, crossed with autism status, in a propensity-matched sample
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional, ABCD baseline only. Phone/SM duration category is the independent variable and obesity (yes/no) the dependent variable. One observation per child; within-site clustering handled by GEE. For each screen-time category a separate model was fit with two fully crossed factors (three-level duration category and autism status). Table 3 reports duration effects for all children; Table 5 reports them separately for children with autism and TD children. Duration x autism interactions were all non-significant (p > 0.05), so the authors anchor on the all-children estimates in Table 3 and describe Tables 4-5 as showing similar patterns.
primary_models.estimation: SAS 9.4. GEE with binomial distribution and log link (log-binomial), compound-symmetry working correlation for within-site clustering. Effects reported as prevalence ratios with 95% CI, each non-zero duration category vs 0 min, plus an overall (omnibus) p-value per screen type. Alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. Duration x autism interactions all p > 0.05 (values not printed). No covariates beyond matching; no weights. No sensitivity analyses reported. Printed prevalences (e.g., Table 5 autism texting 30+ min: 5 of 20 shown as 23.9%) do not equal raw n/N, suggesting model-based prevalences.
primary_models.equation: log(P(obese[i,site]=1)) = b0 + b1*dur_low[i] + b2*dur_high[i] + b3*autism[i] + b4*dur_low[i]*autism[i] + b5*dur_high[i]*autism[i]; prevalence ratio = exp(coefficient) for each duration category vs 0 min; binomial GEE with log link, compound-symmetry working correlation within site. Fit separately for social/video chat and for texting.
primary_models.dv: Obesity (binary): sex- and age-specific BMI z-score at or above the 95th percentile of the CDC 2000 growth reference, from measured height and weight (average of up to three measurements). Prevalence in the matched sample 15.1% overall (169/1,116; 18.8% autism, 14.4% TD). Reference-group (0 min) prevalences printed in Tables 3 and 5 are used as p0 per estimate.
primary_models.sample: ABCD baseline (enrollment September 2016 to October 2018, 21 U.S. sites); data release not stated. 10,842 children were included, of whom 187 (1.7%) had parent-reported autism. Propensity-score matching (1:5 nine-digit greedy match) produced an analytic sample of 186 children with autism and 930 typically developing (TD) children (N = 1,116); one child with autism could not be matched and was dropped. Matched sample (Table 1, p. 4): age 9 years 45.2%, 10 years 54.8%; mean age 10.0 (SD 0.6); 85.5% boys (159 autism, 795 TD) and 14.5% girls (27 autism, 135 TD); 53.8% non-Hispanic White, 15.6% Hispanic, 13.4% non-Hispanic Black, 1.6% non-Hispanic Asian, 15.6% non-Hispanic other/multi-race; distributions identical across autism and TD groups by design. 35 of 186 (18.8%) children with autism and 134 of 930 (14.4%) TD children were obese. Table 3 cell sizes: social/video chat 0 min n = 670, 1-44 min n = 338, 45+ min n = 108; texting 0 min n = 671, 1-29 min n = 306, 30+ min n = 139. Table 5: autism social/video chat 119/45/22, TD 551/293/86; autism texting 121/45/20, TD 550/261/119.
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 (all children, p. 5) and Table 5 (stratified by autism status, p. 6); methods p. 3; results p. 4; abstract and Discussion section 4.2 (p. 7).

papers.extraction_flags: 1) M1 (Table 2) treats phone/SM minutes as the DV and parent-reported autism status as the IV. Autism counts as a clinical-diagnosis trait, so it qualifies, but please confirm. The native metric is a Poisson-GEE ratio of means. No SDs are reported for minutes/day, so d can only be approximated by the rough rate-ratio-as-OR route, which makes M1 effectively non-convertible. 2) "Social and video chat" combines social networking sites with video chat. That composite is entirely phone/SM, so it is extracted as a qualifying IV/DV. 3) The overall p-value for texting and obesity conflicts within the paper: the abstract says 0.02, while Table 3 and the Results text say 0.04. Separately, the pairwise texting 30+ min PR is 1.42 (1.00-2.01) with printed p = 0.05, which I coded sig=false. Please check that call. 4) The paper does not say whether Table 3's all-children PRs come from a model that includes the autism factor or are marginal. Tables 3 and 5 are in one card (M2), with obesity columns for all children, autism and TD. p0 varies by panel, so I put it on each estimate (reference-row prevalence) and left it null on dv_axis. Please confirm the pipeline reads p0 per estimate. 5) The printed prevalences do not equal raw n/N (for example 5/20 is shown as 23.9%), which suggests they are model-based. 6) The ABCD data release is not stated. There are no covariates beyond propensity matching on age, gender, race/ethnicity and SEP, and no multiple-comparison correction.

d_transformation.notes: p0 for M2 comes from the reference-row prevalences in Table 3 (14.8% social/video chat, 15.2% texting) and Table 5 (autism 17.6% / TD 14.2% social/video chat; autism 16.6% / TD 14.8% texting), p. 5-6. Exposure prevalence is not small (e.g., 30+ min texting 12.5% of sample) but p0 is the unexposed-group rate, so the RR-to-OR conversion is exact under the guideline formula. M1 has no SD for any DV (only group means in Table 2), so its d is only the Poisson-rate-ratio approximation, which is weak for skewed continuous minutes; treat M1 d's with caution. Neither contrast is a per-SD contrast, so these d's are not directly comparable to per-SD d's from papers like 394. [complete-stage check 2026-10-01] Whole 9-page PDF re-read (no supplementary file exists). All M1/M2 native values, 95% CIs and exact p are printed and present. M1 SDs of minutes/day are not printed anywhere, so a mean-difference d cannot be formed; group sizes and group means added per estimate.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: autism vs typically developing (within boys, within girls), on phone/SM minutes per day. M2: duration category (1-44 or 45+ min social/video chat; 1-29 or 30+ min texting) vs 0 min, on obesity.
d_transformation.native_metric: M1: ratio of means (Poisson GEE, log link); M2: prevalence ratio (log-binomial GEE)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: M2: OR = RR * (1 - p0) / (1 - RR * p0); d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), with p0 = printed obesity prevalence in the 0-min reference category of the same panel. M1: if treated as a Poisson rate ratio per guidelines §4a, d ~ ln(ratio) * sqrt(3)/pi as a first approximation; an exact d = (M_autism - M_TD)/SD_pooled is not possible because SDs of minutes/day are not reported.
